10317-betty-gordon-at-boarding-school-or:
Alice B. Emerson published this girls' school story in 1921, sending Betty Gordon to Shadyside School after earlier books at home. New plans, letters, and good-byes open the tale, but a lost treasure soon gives Betty and her friends a puzzle to solve. The tone is bright, clean, and full of school fun.

Parties, a nutting trip, a storm, dramatics, and a Saturday race fill term time, while a mysterious four and a secret keep the plot moving. Bob's solution and a second mystery bring the treasure hunt to a close. Readers get a cheerful series tale of friendship, pluck, and schoolgirl adventure.
10372-bunch-grass-a-chronicle-of-life-on:
Horace Annesley Vachell published this ranch chronicle in 1913, dedicating it to his brother Arthur. Vachell, author of Brothers and The Hill, writes of cattle country through linked sketches rather than one straight plot. The tone is warm, comic, and full of local character, with ranch hands, neighbors, and beasts in every scene.

Chapters introduce Alethea-Belle, Pap Spooner, Gloriana, fifteen fat steers, a poisoned spring, and old man Bobo's Mandy. Experiments, pups, and barons fill the ranch year, with humor and hardship in turn. Readers get a lively, old-style portrait of western ranch life, with strong, plain folk.
10577-international-short-stories-french:
Francis J. Reynolds compiled this 1910 volume of French short stories, part of his International Short Stories series. Reynolds gathers masters from Balzac and Merimee to Maupassant, Zola, Hugo, and Daudet, with lesser-known writers beside them. The book serves readers who want French fiction in English, in one handy set.

A Piece of Bread, The Elixir of Life, Mateo Falcone, Zadig, Abandoned, Jean Gourdon's Four Days, and The Last Lesson stand among the pieces. Love, war, wit, and moral surprise recur. Readers get a rich, varied anthology of French storytelling, from classic tales to modern sketches.
10762-impressions-of-theophrastus-such:
George Eliot published Impressions of Theophrastus Such in 1879, a book of essays spoken by an imagined observer of modern life. Its chapters look inward and backward. They take up how we encourage research, a man surprised at his own originality, a too deferential man, moral swindlers, and the shadows of the coming race. Theophrastus judges his age in the manner of his ancient namesake.

Eliot writes with irony and moral seriousness, turning small social types into lessons on honesty, vanity, and thought. The essays are short, sharp, and quotable. Readers get the great novelist as a critic of her own society, in her last published work.
10946-three-frenchmen-in-bengal-the-comm:
S. C. Hill, officer in charge of India's government records, wrote this 1903 history of French Bengal's ruin in 1757. Three chiefs carry the story: Renault at Chandernagore, Law at Cossimbazar, and Courtin at Dacca. Maps and plans show the Ganges valley, the Hugli River, and the forts where French trade centred.

Hill explains why France lost: Calcutta's English merchants traded freely across Bengal, while French traders faced restrictions and poorer sites, though Calcutta, Chandernagore, and Chinsurah stood within thirty miles of one another. War with England then destroyed the French settlements. The book uses official records to tell a sharp story of commercial rivalry, and it remains a clear account of a forgotten imperial contest.
11248-the-delights-of-wisdom-pertaining-:
Emanuel Swedenborg's Delights of Wisdom Pertaining to Conjugial Love, put into English from the Latin work printed at Amsterdam in 1768. argues that true marriage continues in heaven, while its companion section treats the pleasures of scortatory, or illicit, love as insanity. Swedenborg opens by saying plainly that the visions he recalls, visions of angels, weddings in heaven, and spirit groups, were seen in perfect wakefulness over twenty-five years, not invented as fiction.

The book's teaching on God is ordered and odd: angels debate, companies from north and south assemble, and earthly marriage matches a heavenly pattern. Readers need not accept Swedenborg's visions to follow his argument about love, fidelity, and the afterlife. The work remains central to his school's thought and to the history of mystic writers.
11363-bayard-the-good-knight-without-fea:
Christopher Hare's Bayard, the Good Knight Without Fear and Without Reproach, with colored illustrations by Herbert Cole. retells the joyful history of Pierre Terrail, born at Bayard Castle in Dauphiné about 1474, when Louis XI ruled France. Second son of a large, heroic family, Bayard grew up in a castle built on a rocky hill in 1404, commanding a deep valley. Illustrations show his horsemanship, the battle of Fornovo, his defense of a bridge, and his death.

Hare writes for young readers, presenting Bayard as chivalry's model: brave, loyal, and courteous. The book's old-fashioned title promises exactly what it delivers, a life of heroic deeds. For readers of historical biography for children, it remains a charming introduction to late medieval France.
1206-the-flying-u-ranch:
B. M. Bower returns to the Flying U ranch in Montana, where the Happy Family of cowboys, led by Chip Bennett, rides, jokes, and brawls through a season of work and trouble. A new foreman, a schoolteacher, and a nest of rustlers stir the crew, and the ranch's fortunes hang on wit and nerve.

Bower writes cowboy life with humor and affection, and her dialogue crackles with range talk. The novel is episodic and warm, more about a crew than a single hero. It gives a lively picture of the working West and still pleases western fans.
12486-indian-nullification-of-the-uncons:
William Apes, an Indian and preacher of the gospel, published this 1835 defence of the Mashpee tribe against Massachusetts law. Apes addresses the white people of Massachusetts directly, calling them descendants of men who crossed the sea to escape tyranny, and asking why that refuge now denies Indians self-rule.

The pamphlet explains the pretended riot at Mashpee, arguing that tribal resistance to state laws was lawful nullification, not disorder. Apes sets tribal rights, Christian preaching and American principle side by side. The tract stands as an early Native American political text, written by a Mashpee advocate in his own voice, and it remains a sharp record of the Mashpee struggle.
12629-language-an-introduction-to-the-st:
Edward Sapir's Language, an Introduction to the Study of Speech, first published in 1921 and reprinted in 1939, defines language as a cultural, not biologically inherited, function. Sapir dismisses interjectional and sound-imitative theories of origin as futile, and builds a definition on the psycho-physical basis of speech.

Chapters move from elements of speech and sounds of language through forms, grammar and types of linguistic structure. Words, sentences, feeling-tones, concepts and thought without language all receive treatment. Sapir writes with clarity for general readers, and the book remains a classic introduction to linguistics, humane and systematic.
12769-how-to-teach:
George Drayton Strayer and Naomi Norsworthy published How to Teach in 1917 as a practical guide for classroom teachers. It treats education as a group enterprise, aimed at making pupils active for the common good, not merely polished as individuals. Chapters cover attention, habit, memory, imagination, play, moral conduct, and study methods.

Later sections weigh verbal images against object images, arguing that words save time and travel further, while concrete images ground creative work and hard thinking. Tests and measures of children's progress close the book. Teachers will find here the psychology of its day turned into plain classroom counsel.
13084-back-to-methuselah-a-metabiologica:
Bernard Shaw's 1921 Back to Methuselah, subtitled a metabiological pentateuch, is a five-part play cycle on evolution, long life, and the future of man. Its long preface moves from Darwin and the neo-Darwinians to creative evolution, voluntary longevity, and the hope, or lack of it, in education. Shaw argues that life strives upward by will, not by blind chance alone.

The plays range from Eden to a far future where men live for centuries and debate whether to kill, drink, or wait for tomorrow. One scene hears Beethoven's Hammerklavier as a picture of whirling electrons, sane and methodical beneath its difficulty. Shaw's cycle is bold, talkative, and comic, a philosopher's drama dressed as science fiction.
13482-what-the-schools-teach-and-might-t:
Franklin Bobbitt, of the University of Chicago, reports what Cleveland schools teach and might teach in this 1915 survey volume, directed by Leonard P. Ayres for the Cleveland Foundation. Tables measure time given to reading, spelling, handwriting, language, composition, and grammar, with sets of supplementary books per building.

Bobbitt argues that spelling for the few who need it unusually well should not be forced on all. Spelling practice should run through high school, with teachers refusing written work full of errors. Drawing, taught in measured hours across grades, gets its own tables. The survey is a practical audit of an American city school system, asking what each subject is worth in time and result.
14641-the-golden-calf-which-the-world-ad:
John Frederick Helvetius, doctor at The Hague, wrote The Golden Calf in Latin in 1666, and this English version, printed in London in 1670, tells how lead was transmuted into gold. The title names the world's adored metal.

A grave stranger in plebeian habit visits Helvetius, asks leave to discuss the pyrotechnic art, and demonstrates the philosopher's stone in a tiny particle. Helvetius dedicates the work to physicians of Amsterdam and Brandenburg. The book is a famous alchemical testimony, credulous to modern eyes but central to the history of chemistry's dreams. Alchemists cited Helvetius for generations after.
15429-thomas-henry-huxley-a-character-sk:
Leonard Huxley wrote this short life of his father, Thomas Henry Huxley, for the Rationalist Press Association in 1920. It is a character sketch rather than a full biography, tracing a scientist who became a public voice for science in Victorian Britain. Portraits from youth to old age illustrate the text.

Chapters follow Huxley's medical training, his voyage on the Rattlesnake, and his long fight for Darwin's Origin of Species in lecture halls and print. Later sections cover his work for popular education, for teachers and women students, and his views on ethics and the Church. Family scenes and letters close the book, showing the private man behind the debater. It suits readers who want a compact, humane portrait of a famous Victorian mind.
16285-the-way-of-salvation-in-the-luther:
Rev. G. H. Gerberding, pastor of St. Mark's Lutheran Church in Fargo, Dakota, wrote this book for the common people, with an introduction by Rev. M. Rhodes. Published by the Lutheran Publication Society in Philadelphia, copyright 1887, it reached an eleventh thousand in a revised and improved printing. Gerberding dedicates it hopefully to the united English Lutheran Church of the future, joined in one faith and one body.

Chapter one declares that all are sinners, and later chapters lay out the Lutheran way of salvation in plain, pastoral language. The book speaks to farmers, shopkeepers, and families rather than scholars. Readers studying American Lutheranism will find a clear, popular statement of its teaching.
16497-the-moon-out-of-reach:
Margaret Pedler's 1921 romance follows a heroine through a long chain of trials: a shining ship, a skeleton in the cupboard, a forgotten fan, a skirmish with death, and a flight. Chapter titles like The Double Barrier, By the Lovers' Bridge, Till Death Us Do Part, and The Width of a World Between trace a love tested by pride, honor, and fate.

Pedler writes in the lush style of popular romance between the wars, with country houses, family pressure, and strong feeling at every turn. The plot keeps shifting ground, from near partings to fresh hope. Readers who enjoy a full, emotional love story will find the book generous and absorbing.
16583-the-yoke-a-romance-of-the-days-whe:
Elizabeth Miller's 1904 romance tells of Israel's redemption from Egyptian bondage, with a plot her brother Percy helped construct. Chapters run from choosing the tens and the ban of the ritual through the procession of Amen. The heir to the throne, the lady Miriam, the plagues, the conspiracy, and light after darkness follow. Rameses' love and the idols' crumbling fill the later course.

Miller writes a full, colorful historical romance, rich in Egyptian court detail. The tale mixes love, faith, and Exodus drama. Readers of biblical fiction will find a grand, old-fashioned novel of Moses' age, told with warmth and spectacle.
1697-madam-how-and-lady-why-or-first-les:
Charles Kingsley wrote this book of talks for children, in which a father answers his son's questions about the world outdoors by telling stories of Madam How and Lady Why. Madam How stands for the forces that shape the earth — water, ice, fire, and weather — while Lady Why stands for the reasons behind what those forces do.

Chapters take the reader to seashores, chalk cliffs, volcanoes, and coral reefs. Each walk ends with a plain account of how a valley was cut or a rock was laid down. It is an early work of popular science for the young, meant to be read aloud, and it still works as a friendly first step into geology.
1720-the-man-who-knew-too-much:
Gilbert K. Chesterton links eight detective stories around Horne Fisher, a man who knows too much about the powerful and too little about how to use what he knows. A face in a target, a prince who vanishes, a schoolboy's soul, and a temple of silence each hide a crime that polite society would rather not name.

Fisher solves his cases by seeing the political motive behind the puzzle, and Chesterton uses each mystery to poke at privilege, war, and the press. The stories are witty and compact, and they reward readers who like their detection mixed with argument about how England is really run.
17939-a-statement-on-the-future-of-this-:
John Haynes Holmes, minister of the Church of the Messiah in New York, printed this short statement in 1918 as number six of the Messiah Pulpit series. It sold for five cents, and it spoke to his flock at a turning point in his work.

Holmes tells his people that All Souls Church in Chicago has called him, by unanimous vote, to take up the work of the late Dr. Jenkin Lloyd Jones. The call would also bring the Lincoln Centre and the journal Unity. The pamphlet is frank, warm, and personal, a rare look at how a minister weighed a great call in public.
18286-the-miller-of-old-church:
Ellen Glasgow's novel opens on a sunny October day at a country crossroads. A stranger rides the corduroy road from Applegate to Old Church and stops near a small public house called Bottom's Ordinary. The square brick building has sunk over generations from a chapel to an inn, and three roads meet at its gate.

The book is built in parts, the first called Jordan's Journey. Its chapters bring in the Revercomb family, the mill, a preacher named Orlando Mullen, and a young woman named Molly, with quarrels, flirtation, and a flight. Glasgow sets village talk, work at the mill, and church life side by side. Readers get a portrait of a rural community and the people trying to find their place in it.
18336-the-lighted-match:
Charles Neville Buck, author of The Key to Yesterday, wrote this novel, published by W. J. Watt and Company in New York in 1911, with pictures by R. F. Schabelitz. The Lighted Match opens with an omen construed on a cabin porch. When a fellow and a girl wash hands in the same basin, a farmer says, they will not marry that year. A setter pup gnaws at his boot heels as the girl bends over her basin.

Chapters follow Benton playing magician, the moon overhearing, a masquerade, Romeo becoming Dromio and Dromio becoming Romeo, a princess consulting Jonesy, and a toreador appearing. Later chapters bring a mistaken countess, farewells and warnings, a cabinet noir, and a toreador turned ambassador and admiral. Readers get a Ruritanian romance of disguise, courts, and love, lit by a match struck in fun.
18530-elsie-inglis-the-woman-with-the-to:
Eva Shaw McLaren wrote this life of Dr. Elsie Inglis, published at London in 1920 in the Pioneers of Progress series on women. It traces Inglis from childhood in India and school days in Edinburgh through medical study and twenty years of practice. She founded the Hospice for poor patients in Edinburgh in 1901 and worked hard for votes for women.

At the outbreak of war she helped build the Scottish Women's Hospitals, serving in Serbia, where a 1916 photo shows her after her return. McLaren draws on friends, letters, and Inglis's own unpublished novel for color. The book honors a doctor whose work joined medicine, reform, and war service.
18767-stories-about-animals-with-picture:
Francis C. Woodworth, editor of The Youth's Cabinet, published this animal book at Boston in 1851 with Phillips, Sampson and Company, entered in 1849. It groups anecdotes on quadrupeds, showing their habits, tempers, intelligence, and affection, with pictures to match. Woodworth stresses that he offers no scientific treatise and no full natural history of any beast.

Instead he picks lively tales meant to entertain young readers while teaching useful knowledge of animals. He hints at later volumes on other great divisions of the animal kingdom if this one pleases. The book is a kindly, old-style introduction to animal character for children.
18926-judith-of-blue-lake-ranch:
Jackson Gregory published this western novel in 1919, illustrated by W. Herbert Dunton. Its heroine, Judith, takes a hand in ranch affairs from the first chapters. She rides an outlaw horse that bucks as only a devil-hearted horse knows how, and she puts matters straight with a firm hand. Bud Lee wants to know what she plans, and the ranch watches her.

Judith's story gives the western a capable woman at its center, handling horses, men, and trouble without waiting for rescue. Gregory writes her with admiration and humor. Readers get a lively ranch novel with a strong heroine, popular in its day. It shows how westerns began to make room for women who could ride and rule a ranch.
1902-the-old-peabody-pew-a-christmas-rom:
Kate Douglas Wiggin's Old Peabody Pew, a Christmas romance of a country church, is dedicated to a handful of dear New England women. Their names are unknown to the world, and they dwell in a quiet village. They worked together to make their corner of the universe pleasanter. The story follows those women as they prepare the church for Christmas.

Household work done and luncheons laid out for the men of the family, the women turn to the pew itself, and to the old romance it holds. Wiggin writes the tale with warmth and a light touch. Its charm lies in its setting: a village church at Christmas, and the love story that its oldest pew remembers.
19376-mrs-piper-the-society-for-psychica:
Noralie Robertson translated and abridged this study of Mrs. Piper, a famous Boston medium, from the French of M. Sage, with a preface by Oliver Lodge. It follows the Society for Psychical Research as it tested her trances, from early sittings watched by William James of Harvard to later work under Richard Hodgson.

Each theory gets a hearing: fraud, muscle-reading, thought-transference, and talk from the dead, including the control known as Phinuit. Automatic writing, misplaced syllables, and careful minutes all appear as evidence. The book is a clear short record of how serious researchers weighed an uncanny case.
20055-historic-tales-the-romance-of-real:
Charles Morris wrote Historic Tales, a set of books that retell great events as stories. Volume six turns to France, under the subtitle The Romance of Reality. One scene opens on a grand plain in the centre of France. There stands an old, rich city that stood before France itself began.

Morris moves from Rome's wide rule to later French history in vivid scenes. He aimed to make the past read like a tale, not a list. Readers get battles, kings, and cities told in a flowing style. The volume suits those who learn history best through story.
2086-the-slowcoach:
E. V. Lucas writes a children's story about the Avory family of Chiswick, whose mother and four children take to the road in a caravan called the Slowcoach. Janet, Robert, Hester, and little Gregory Bruce travel with high spirits. Lucas wrote the book for children who loved caravans, camps, and the open road.

Adventures follow at every stop: a second caravan, a runaway pony, a lost baby, a giant, and a visit to Stratford-on-Avon. Lucas keeps the tone kind and funny, and the book charms as a gentle road tale for young readers. Stratford-on-Avon gives the journey a literary stop, since Shakespeare's town draws every traveller.
2099-a-history-of-the-moravian-church:
J. E. Hutton writes a full history of the Moravian Church, from the Bohemian Brethren of 1457 through Hus, Peter of Chelcic, and the society at Kunwald to the modern church. The second edition of 1909 revises and enlarges the work. Hutton revised and enlarged the history for its second edition in 1909.

Hutton follows the Brethren through persecution, exile, and renewal, with chapters on Poland, missions, and church order. The history suits readers who want a clear, detailed account of one of Protestantism's oldest communities. The Moravians, heirs of the Bohemian Brethren, spread missions from Herrnhut across the world.
21035-the-adventures-of-a-three-guinea-w:
A watch scarce a month old settles to business at once, Talbot Baines Reed observes. Watches, he jokes, outgrow infancy far faster than human babes ever do. The Adventures of a Three Guinea Watch lets that watch tell its own tale.

From pocket to pocket, the watch sees school, city, wealth, and want at close range. Owners come and go while its small voice judges them all with wit. Reed's device lets him tour all ranks of life in one tale. The book charms as both school story and social sketch, ticked out in a watch's own dry time.
21068-under-the-meteor-flag-log-of-a-mid:
On March 9, 1793, the gun-brig Scourge sailed from Spithead to cruise for a month in the Channel. A young midshipman kept the log in Harry Collingwood's novel. Britain was entering the French Revolutionary War. The boy narrator serves under orders to watch for enemy activity close to home.

Gales, shipwrecks, rafts, and hand-to-hand fights fill his service, in the manner of the boys' sea tales of Kingston. The young midshipman proves smarter and luckier than his years suggest. One odd note is the title: the meteor flag appears only once, at a burial at sea.
21346-the-sot-weed-factor-or-a-voyage-to:
Ebenezer Cooke published this satire in London in 1708, a burlesque poem about a tobacco factor's voyage to Maryland. Sot-weed is tobacco, the colony's money crop, and its factor its often-duped agent. The title page promises the laws, courts, buildings, feasts, and drunken humours of the inhabitants of that part of America.

Cooke's newcomer finds courts, food, drink, and manners all turned upside down for an English gentleman. Shea's Early Southern Tracts reprinted the poem in the nineteenth century, noting how personal and earnest its mockery feels. It is among the earliest comic poems written about America, and still one of the sharpest colonial satires.
21471-mountain-moggy-the-stoning-of-the-:
Old Mountain Moggy lives alone on a Welsh hillside in W. H. G. Kingston's short tale Mountain Moggy. Local children call her a witch who can never be hurt or die. They amuse themselves by taunting her and throwing stones at her hut.

One evening a stone knocks a burning stick from her fire, and the flames catch her. A young midshipman, lost nearby, helps her and brings word to the village. The clergyman, once a doctor, hurries up to treat her wounds. Moggy's pardon of William, a ringleader in the stoning, gives the tale its theme of forgiveness.
22534-a-biographical-sketch-of-the-life-:
A Biographical Sketch of the Life and Character of Joseph Ch. preserves a grandfather's memory for his descendants. The writer addresses beloved children directly in its opening lines. Your grandfather, he tells them, was a truly great man.

Not as a warrior, the sketch insists, nor as a statesman. His greatness was not of the earth, earthy kind at all. He possessed a rare combination of moral worth and Christian excellence. That made him a blessing to his race and family. In other words, he was great because he was truly good. Such family memorials kept private virtues in public print. Readers get Victorian praise of character over fame or wealth.
22578-the-girl-and-the-kingdom-learning-:
The Girl and the Kingdom, subtitled Learning to Teach, is a work of fiction about a young woman finding her calling as a teacher in a crowded city neighborhood. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its setting is a poor immigrant district where shop signs carry names from many nations.

The sample pages describe tailors and secondhand shops run by Jewish families alongside liquor sellers with Irish and Scottish names. Against that lively street scene, the story follows its heroine's path into teaching. Readers get both a character story and a close look at city teaching in an era of heavy immigration. The book speaks to readers drawn to education, social work, and urban life of the period.
23054-the-dean-s-watch:
Erckmann-Chatrian waylay a traveler in The Dean's Watch, their tale dated 1897 in this edition. A stranger hails traveling musicians on the Heidelberg road, guessing their errand, and presses advice on them. Wilfred studies him sidelong and answers shortly, asking what business it could possibly be of his. The stranger's counsel comes free all the same, and entirely unasked.

The Alsatian writing pair built their fame on village tales where small objects carry long histories. A dean's watch, ticking through the story, measures out guilt, memory, and time itself. Their manner is plain and patient, letting dread accumulate in ordinary rooms. This translation brought their Rhineland world to English readers who prized its solidity.
23227-aucassin-and-nicolette-translated-:
Aucassin and Nicolette is an old French tale, presented here in a translation by Francis William Bourdillon. Its young hero, Aucassin, is pressed hard by both his parents. They urge him to take up his arms, mount his horse, fight for his land, and stand by his father's men.

If his men see him in their midst, his parents promise, they will fight harder for their lives, their goods, and his land. That pressure sets the tale's core tension: duty in war against the pull of love. Readers get one of medieval France's best-loved short tales in plain English dress.
23881-the-history-of-punch:
M. H. Spielmann published The History of Punch in 1895, with numerous illustrations, through Cassell and Company in London, Paris, and Melbourne. His preface weighs the sources: George Hodder's Memories, Mr. Punch's Origin and Career, and Joseph Hatton's delightful but fragmentary True Story of Punch.

Hatton's papers, Spielmann judges, are untrustworthy where they rest on others, but valuable where they rest on his own knowledge, his documents, and his intimacy with Mark Lemon. Spielmann draws on all three, and on more besides, to tell how the comic paper began and grew. The Mahogany Tree, drawn by Linley Sambourne for Punch's jubilee number, fronts a history of Victorian humor itself.
24092-critical-miscellanies-vol-3-of-3-e:
John Morley included this biographical sketch of W. R. Greg in the third volume of his Critical Miscellanies, published in London and New York in 1904. Greg was born at Manchester in 1809, went to Edinburgh University in 1826, started in business at Bury in 1833, joined the Board of Customs in 1856, and died in November 1881.

Morley admits he did not share Greg's views and once crossed swords with him in print, yet he writes with respect for Greg's character and courtesy. The sketch follows Greg's family, friends, and books, including Enigmas of Life from 1875. Readers get a fair-minded portrait of a Victorian thinker by an opponent who came to like the man.
24204-the-lost-despatch:
Natalie Sumner Lincoln wrote this novel of 1865, published by D. Appleton and Company in New York and London in 1913. It is dedicated to Brigadier-General Sumner H. Lincoln, a gallant Union soldier and veteran of two wars. The story opens on a bitterly cold December night in 1864, with wind sighing through the Maryland woods and the moon breaking through heavy cloud.

Chapters follow a pigeon's flight, brains against brawn, a knot of ribbon blue, and Banquo's ghost. Later come a scrap of paper, a signal light, the fight at the ford, a trial, sensational evidence, a thunderbolt, and a close with malice toward none. Readers get a Civil War tale of messages, spies, and love, set in the war's last winter.
24356-sixty-years-with-plymouth-church:
Stephen M. Griswold wrote this memoir of sixty years with Plymouth Church, published by Fleming H. Revell Company in New York, Chicago, Toronto, London, and Edinburgh in 1907. It is dedicated to his New England mother, long since entered into rest. Griswold was urged for years to record his recollections of Plymouth Church and Henry Ward Beecher. The original members had nearly all passed away, and almost no one else could give the record personal value.

Chapters run from Coming to New York and Early Plymouth through a Plymouth usher, services, and members. Buying a slave girl, Beecher in England, and the Beecher trial lead to the church tested and church thought and life. The church staff, the Fort Sumter expedition, and future Plymouth close the book. Readers get a first-hand church history, centered on Beecher's Brooklyn pulpit.
25005-the-shadow-witch:
Gertrude Crownfield's 1922 fairy tale, published by Dutton with illustrations by Anne Merriman Peck, opens beside a hearthstone, gazing into low-burning fire. Among scarlet and gold coals and shadows flitting over embers lies the Land of Fire, home of the good and peaceful Ember Fairies, entered by a golden gate. There stand Prince Ember's Palace of Good Cheer and the Shadow Princess dancing in trailing garments of rose and amethyst.

Long ago, in the dim Land of Shadows between the Land of Fire and the Chimney Back, lived the Shadow Witch, that land's one beautiful and loving creature. Nearby lie the Plain of Ash, giant Curling Smoke, crafty Ash Goblin, boisterous Wind in the Chimney, and her brother the Wizard in his Cave of Darkness. The tale tells how she left that grim land to dance happily among the fire fairies, and how Prince Ember fared on his high quest.
25556-heroes-of-the-middle-west-the-fren:
Mary Hartwell Catherwood writes the French volume of Heroes of the Middle West, published by Ginn in 1898 with a front picture of Count Frontenac from his statue at Quebec. Her preface warns that covering French discovery and occupation of the middle west is no easy task.

From Marquette and Jolliet to the pulling down of the French flag on Fort Chartres, Catherwood condenses events into a moving picture for young minds. She seeks a light, sure touch for readers used only to modern scenes, vivifying explorers, soldiers, and settlers as living men.
25578-the-sunbridge-girls-at-six-star-ra:
Eleanor Stuart writes this 1913 girls' ranch story, illustrated by Frank J. Murch and published in Boston by L. C. Page. A first impression came in April 1913, with a second in January 1914. A picture shows Reddy right there every time, a hint of ranch liveliness inside.

Chapters open with Aunt Sophronia, plans for Texas, and the coming of Genevieve. The girls travel onward, and the boys prepare a welcome at Six Star Ranch. Stuart, writing for girls who loved horses, camps, and new places, mixes ranch work, friendship, and high spirits in a Texas setting.
25809-the-mascot-of-sweet-briar-gulch:
Henry Wallace Phillips, author of Red Saunders and Plain Mary Smith, writes The Mascot of Sweet Briar Gulch, published by Grosset and Dunlap in 1908 with pictures by F. Graham Cootes. The gulch runs in a trough of beauty to Jones's Hill, rising in a sweeping curve into clouds.

Wildflowers, leafy trees, and tangled vines blanket scarred ground beneath a clear spring-like sky, the air thick with stirring scents. Phillips writes a western tale of a gulch, its people, and a mascot whose luck or charm shapes fortunes, in the humorous, colourful style of his Red Saunders books.
25866-the-search:
Grace Livingston Hill sets a romance of faith and second chances in 1919, opening on a suburban train to Bryne Haven. Two young officers in uniform trade talk of girls met at dances, with Harry praised as a fine fellow and Bobbie keen to set him up again. Beneath the light talk lies a deeper quest, for love that lasts and for a life set right after the follies of youth.

The tale moves to country houses, motor cars, and a great stone barn where a car chase ends in tense silence. Cameron, his mother's hand on his shoulder, whispers that the pursuers are near, and names Passmore's voice among them. Letters between Ruth Macdonald and John Cameron thread the book, and the search of the title runs through courtship, peril, and a turn toward home.
25901-the-new-testament-translated-from-:
Leicester Ambrose Sawyer gives a strict, literal rendering of the New Testament from the original Greek, printed in Boston in 1858. Sawyer says the work avoids both compromise and loose paraphrase: it sticks close to the Greek, aiming for clarity, force, and precision. Modern style, save in the prayers, makes the text plain for practical religion as well as for biblical study.

The edition arranges the sacred books in chronological order and improves the divisions of chapters and verses, with verse numbers set in the text. Stephen's stoning, with Saul standing by as witnesses lay their clothes at his feet, reads in Sawyer's plain, close English. The book stands as a scholar's bid to let English readers hear the Greek as nearly as words allow.
26117-sketches-of-the-fair-sex-in-all-pa:
Theodore Abbot's 1841 miscellany gathers narratives and anecdotes meant to illustrate female character, from delicacy and sweetness to gentle or heroic virtues, amiable weaknesses, and strange defects. The editor claims little method, preferring a rich profusion of stories to a formal analysis of what he calls the hardest subject man ever tried to master.

Added rules promise to fix a woman's precise figure, degree of beauty, habits, and age, notwithstanding the aids and disguise of dress. Advice to readers warns against marrying a man lacking virtue, good nature, and understanding, and against expecting infallible men. The book couples instruction with amusement, in the editor's own phrase.
26193-the-rover-boys-in-southern-waters-:
Arthur M. Winfield's 1907 volume, the eleventh Rover Boys book, shifts the scene to the lower Mississippi and the Gulf of Mexico. Dick, Tom, and Sam hunt a missing houseboat, hear Harold Bird's strange tale, and push through swamps and mud. Chapters promise fights with bobcats, a houseboat found in bushes, two young prisoners, and a chase on the river.

On the Gulf, the boys find a deserted steam yacht and take possession, only to face storms, peril in the engine room, and an enemy bid to seize the prize. Dan Baxter, their old foe, shows repentance before the homeward-bound close. The book offers river and sea adventure in the series' familiar mix of fun, danger, and brotherly pluck.
26389-dorothy-on-a-ranch:
Evelyn Raymond's Dorothy novel, copyrighted in 1909, sends Dorothy and her friends west in the private rail car Erminie, lent by railway boss Dan Ford. From a siding at Denver they travel on to a ranch in the Rockies, where the party settles into western life. The book belongs to a long series that follows the same heroine from book to book.

Chapters take in a spill on the road, a midnight search, rifle practice, a moonlight concert, and a modern horse fair. A sheep herder's cabin, a hen kept by a Chinese cook, and a grizzly with Native people figure in later chapters. The story ends with prosperity and parting, after days of work that often feels like play.
27102-the-ground-plan-of-the-english-par:
A. Hamilton Thompson's The Ground Plan of the English Parish Church, a Cambridge Manual of Science and Literature published in 1911, explains how to read a parish church from its plan. The chapters cover nave, tower, and porches, then transepts and chancel, with sections on each part.

Thompson shows how western towers of the mid-twelfth century, at Birkin, Brayton, and Riccall, derive from Saxon types, while the main entrance moved to a south doorway with elaborate late Norman ornament. The handbook gives walkers and students a clear key to England's parish churches.
28316-bournemouth-poole-christchurch:
Sidney Heath wrote Bournemouth, Poole, and Christchurch in 1915 for Blackie's Beautiful England series, with paintings by Ernest Haslehurst. Heath describes Bournemouth's pier and sands, square and gardens, winter gardens, chines, and Talbot Woods, then Poole Harbour and Christchurch Priory. The frontispiece shows Branksome Chine, once a smuggler's landing place.

The series, priced at two shillings net, covered Oxford, the Lakes, Canterbury, and many other places in the same small format. Heath writes for visitors, with history, scenery, and walks. The book offers a charming, illustrated guide to the Dorset coast before the First World War changed it.
28322-pioneer-surgery-in-kentucky-a-sket:
David W. Yandell wrote Pioneer Surgery in Kentucky in 1890 as the president's address to the American Surgical Association, delivered at Washington on May 13, 1890. Yandell, professor of clinical surgery at Louisville, chronicles Kentucky pioneers who were men of deeds, not of fruitless promise. He sets aside village Hampdens and mute Miltons for surgeons who worked.

The earliest great Kentucky operation he records, an amputation at the hip-joint in 1806, was the first of its kind in the United States. Yandell rescues overlooked names and honours famous ones. The sketch offers a vivid history of frontier medicine.
28482-sawtooth-ranch:
B. M. Bower's Sawtooth Ranch, first published in Britain in 1921, pits a small ranch against a powerful cattle company. Hunter and Johnson own only a section and a half of land along Quirt Creek. Their herd numbers some three hundred cattle, while the Sawtooth Cattle Company counts its cattle by tens of thousands.

Chapters follow Lone, Swan, and their neighbours through accidents, threats, a kidnapping, and a coyote trail, as the Sawtooth shows its hand again and again. Bower writes with dry humour and first-hand knowledge of ranch work, turning a land and cattle feud into a tense western story.
28660-phebe-the-blackberry-girl-uncle-th:
Phebe, the Blackberry Girl, published by Livermore and Rudd of New York in 1856, belongs to Uncle Thomas's Stories for Good Children. The series promises young readers information joined with amusement, in unpretending little books. Phebe's father is poor, with many little ones, and cannot buy her a church gown.

He bargains instead: if Phebe gathers blackberries in her play time and sells them for bonnet and shoes, he will try for the gown. Climbing a fence, her apron catches a stake, and her fruit spills into sand and dirt. A kind young lady stops to comfort her. Short pieces on good children, pets, flowers, and industry follow.
28861-dave-porter-in-the-far-north-or-th:
Edward Stratemeyer wrote this 1908 Dave Porter novel, subtitled The Pluck of an American Schoolboy. Dave and his friends leave Oak Hall after a row in a restaurant, a confession by Gus Plum, and a sleigh ride for Job Haskers. A mysterious letter and an adventure on Robber Island lead to a hunt for an ice boat and a meeting of the Gee Eyes.

The boys then say good-bye to Oak Hall and travel to London, before the story turns to the far north itself. Stratemeyer keeps the school story moving into travel adventure, with Dave's courage as the through line. Readers get a lively period boys' book, mixing school scrapes with northern journeys, illustrated by Charles Nuttall.
28987-sunlight-patch:
Credo Harris wrote this 1915 novel, Sunlight Patch, published by Small, Maynard in Boston. The chapters open out of the wilderness, with an unexpected rescue and a wounded mountaineer, then bring a human enigma, an interrupted breakfast, and a burned cabin. Later chapters follow Dale Dawson's philosophy, the spirit of Sunlight Patch, and a light above the mountain, through a meeting of rascals to a call that means surrender.

A frontispiece shows a man springing like a panther at an offender's throat. Harris, author of Toby, a novel of Kentucky, writes of mountain folk, engineers, and old houses with color and pace. Readers get a Kentucky romance of action and feeling, in the popular style of its day, with a heroine and hero worth following.
29122-mammals-obtained-by-dr-curt-von-we:
E. Raymond Hall wrote this 1951 paper, Mammals Obtained by Dr. Curt von Wedel from the Barrier Beach of Tamaulipas, Mexico, in the University of Kansas natural history series. Hall asks what mammals live on the coastal island barrier beach of Tamaulipas, and whether their closest kin live on Padre and Mustang islands of Texas or on the Tamaulipas mainland. Von Wedel arranged air transport from Brownsville, Texas, to Boca Jesús María, a tidal inlet through the beach.

The two men arrived March 18, 1950, and left March 22, working from one-story buildings just north of the inlet. Their study compares beach mammals with island and mainland kin, specimen by specimen. Readers get a short, exact piece of mammal fieldwork, showing how a week's collecting on a barrier beach can answer a question of geography and kinship.
29525-the-leech:
Phillips Barbee's short tale opens with a leech waiting for food, drifting for millennia through the huge void of space. Unconscious, it spends countless centuries in the void between stars, until a sun's radiation flares around its hard, dry spore. Gravitation tugs it, a planet claims it with other stellar debris, and winds blow it around the Earth until it falls.

On the ground the spore stirs, nourishment soaks in, and it grows and feeds. A guest, the tag line warns, deserves feeding, but this guest could devour a household, literally. Frank Conners and Professor Micheals meet it next. Fans of horror science fiction will enjoy a chilling tale of hunger from the stars.
2993-samuel-butler-a-sketch:
Henry Festing Jones wrote Samuel Butler: A Sketch, first published in The Humour of Homer and Other Essays in 1913 and reissued by Jonathan Cape in 1921. Butler was born on December 4, 1835, at the rectory in Langar, Nottinghamshire, son of the Reverend Thomas Butler, later a canon of Lincoln Cathedral, and Fanny Worsley of Bristol. His grandfather was Dr. Samuel Butler, the famous headmaster.

Jones follows Butler as artist as well as author, noting a dozen pictures exhibited at the Royal Academy between 1868 and 1876, including Mr. Heatherley's Holiday, hung on the line in 1874. Butler left the painting to his college friend Jason Smith, whose representatives gave it to the nation. The sketch gives a compact life of a singular Victorian thinker.
30055-the-1893-duryea-automobile-in-the-:
Don H. Berkebile describes the 1893 Duryea automobile held by the Museum of History and Technology, in Paper 34 of the museum's Contributions series. Charles and Frank Duryea began work on a self-propelled vehicle with an internal-combustion engine about 1892. Their carriage ran on the streets of Springfield, Massachusetts, in 1893, where newspapers noted its trials. An 1897 photograph shows the car with gear sprockets already missing and its chain loose on the pinion.

Berkebile traces early automotive experience, the start of construction, and each part of the car, then notes its later restoration as a prized exhibit. The paper suits readers who want hard detail on one of America's first motor carriages, rather than a broad history of the car. Smithsonian photographs, including a view after restoration, help the text along.
30264-lie-ge-on-the-line-of-march:
Glenna Lindsley Bigelow tells what an American girl saw when German forces came through Belgium, in a John Lane volume from 1918, issued in New York and London. The book is dedicated to the King of the Belgians, with a sonnet praising a small nation that refused to bow to overmastering force and stand aside. Belgium, the verse says, stands transfigured and glorified, friend of France and England, thanking the men who died.

Bigelow writes from the line of march at Liège, where armies thronged and thickened beyond numbering, bidding peoples tremble and obey. Her account belongs to the first-hand literature of invasion, told by a civilian witness rather than a soldier. Readers of Great War memoirs will find here a personal, urgent view of Belgium under the shock of 1914.
30764-ham-sandwich:
This June 1963 Analog story by James H. Schmitz turns on a talent that will not work when its owner knows it is real. Its central problem is a man with a gift badly needed by others, who cannot use that gift once he knows it is honest. The tale opens at the Institute of Insight, where Wallace Cavender arrives late for a Sunday night meeting of advanced students.

Even Dr. Ormond's secretary, Mavis Greenfield, has left her desk, though the attendance book lies open with a pen beside it. Cavender signs in and follows the distant voice of Dr. Aloys Ormond down a corridor to a lecture room, where some thirty advanced students sit, most on the right side. Schmitz turns a puzzle about insight, honesty, and need into a witty story of mind reading and its limits.
30880-pope-adrian-iv-an-historical-sketc:
Richard Raby wrote this historical sketch of Pope Adrian IV, published in London, Dublin, and Derby in 1849, with a preface signed from Munich in May 1849. Raby says he wrote to give fellow Catholics in England an account of the only English pope who ever reigned. He claims no novelty of research, but a connected narrative drawn from old chronicles and from modern writers who had touched the story only in passing.

Raby defends Adrian in some acts that readers commonly condemn, and he hopes the spirit behind that defense, a love of practical policy, public order, and lawful authority, will win approval. He also notes a striking likeness between the troubles of Pius IX in his own day and Adrian's troubles in the twelfth century. It is a short, sympathetic life for readers of church history.
30935-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Held here is a slice of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, volume 7, running from Constantine Pavlovich to Convention. As a dictionary of arts, sciences, literature, and general information, the Britannica packs each entry with dates, lineage, and judgment. This slice opens with its fullest kind of biographical entry. Constantine Pavlovich, grand-duke and cesarevich of Russia, was born at Tsarskoye Selo on April 27, 1779.

He was the second son of the tsar Paul Petrovich and Maria Feodorovna, née princess of Württemberg. He resembled his father more closely than any brother in body and mind. His upbringing lay entirely in the hands of his grandmother, the empress Catherine II, who regulated every detail of his physical and mental education. She left the carrying out of her views to men in her confidence, including Count Nicolai Ivanovich Soltikov. It is a solid slice of the great eleventh edition.
30989-mystery-ranch:
Arthur Chapman, author of Out Where the West Begins and Cactus Center, wrote this 1921 western mystery. It was published by Houghton Mifflin in Boston and New York, with copyright held by Doubleday, Page and Company. It opens at an Indian agency, where Walter Lowell, the agent, looks up from his desk as Plenty Buffalo, his chief of Indian police, arrives at an unaccustomed pace. The police chief brings news of a murder on the road just off the reservation.

Lowell, who knows better than to press an Indian narrator, listens as the clerk-interpreter translates Plenty Buffalo's rapid speech in his tribal tongue. The dead man, found just beyond the reservation line, sets the mystery in motion. It is a western tale of an agency, its people, and a killing that tests the agent's judgment from the first chapter.
31261-the-defects-of-the-negro-church:
Orishatukeh Faduma's 1904 paper, number ten in the American Negro Academy's Occasional Papers, examines the leading defects of the Black church with a surgeon's sympathy and a healer's aim. Its three heads are the tendency to stress outwardness rather than inwardness, the neglect of rural communities, and the state of the ministry.

Faduma insists he writes as an optimist, that these defects are not inherent in the race but grow from environment. He adds that churches of other races show the same faults in kind, differing only in degree. Since no church was ever perfect, he argues, frank criticism should drive the Black church toward as few defects as possible. The paper remains a candid early voice in Black church reform.
31298-the-trial-of-theodore-parker-for-t:
This 1855 volume prints the trial of Theodore Parker, minister of Boston's Twenty-Eighth Congregational Society, before the United States Circuit Court at Boston on April 3, 1855. It covers the misdemeanor of a speech in Faneuil Hall against kidnapping, together with Parker's own defence. Dedicated to his lawyers John Parker Hale and Charles Mayo Ellis, the book opens with Parker's preface to the people of the free states.

Parker insists the case is not personal. After fourteen years of attacks without reply, he speaks now because the case involves the great human right to freedom of speech. The actual question before the court, he says, was never brought to trial. The volume is a primary record of the Fugitive Slave era's collision between pulpit, courtroom, and conscience.
31518-trusia-a-princess-of-krovitch:
Davis Brinton's Trusia, a Princess of Krovitch, published by George W. Jacobs and Company of Philadelphia and London in September 1906, is a romance of an imaginary kingdom. Its contents open with a wager made, strange countries for to see, a duel of wits, and the gray man, before the heroine declares, in chapter five, "I am the Lady Trusia." Later chapters bring the gray man again, a cool reception, and the spectre of the star.

Brinton, with illustrations by Walter H. Everett, writes the Ruritanian romance popular in his day: invented royalty, disguise, and court intrigue in a small European state. The pleasures are those of the form, with a spirited princess at the center. Readers who enjoy Graustark-style adventure will find a light, well-paced tale of wagers, wit, and a princess claiming her name.
31641-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Drawn from the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, this slice runs alphabetically from Cincinnatus to Cleruchus, in the catalog's spelling, Cleruch. It gathers entries across history, geography, and culture, from ancient Rome to modern institutions. The transcriber's notes name articles corrected in the slice, including Cistercians, Cithara, Ciudad Real, Civil Service, and Clairon, showing the range a single alphabetical run could hold.

One note is telling: in the Civil Service article, fitness for office often counted less than party loyalty, with honesty and capacity secondary at best. Such sentences capture the Britannica's early twentieth-century voice: confident, comparative, and frank. Readers can use the slice as reference, or read across it for a portrait of its age.
31664-once-a-greech:
Evelyn E. Smith's science-fiction story Once a Greech, illustrated by Dillon and produced from Galaxy Science Fiction of April 1957, opens a fortnight before the S. S. Herringbone of the Interstellar Exploration, Examination, and Exploitation Service was due to begin her voyage home. One of her scouts disconcertingly reports intelligent life in the Virago System. Captain Iversen snarls at the news: thirteen planets explored for a full year, with intelligent life turning up on the eleventh planet's nineteenth moon, discovered by Harkaway of all people.

Iversen had sent Harkaway to the moons precisely to keep him from getting in his hair, sure they were cinders. The story's sidenote jokes that Iversen, mildest of men, could still kill to disprove Harkaway's claim that amid life we are in life.
31892-the-old-die-rich:
H. L. Gold's short story The Old Die Rich, printed in Galaxy in March 1953, opens with a narrator the medical examiner greets wearily: you again, Weldon. Weldon looks around a shabby room with hopeful eagerness, thinking that maybe this time he will get the answer he seeks.

On the bed lies an old woman whose thin white hair shows the tight-drawn scalp. Her body is so emaciated that flesh between bones forms parchment pockets, while the examiner goes over her like a side of beef. Readers get a dark science-fiction mystery about the kind of news item read a dozen times a year, whose real story reporters cannot cover.
32435-every-day-errors-of-speech:
L. P. Meredith's handbook, published in Philadelphia in 1876 and entered for copyright in 1872, corrects every-day errors of speech. Meredith, a doctor of medicine and dental surgery, also wrote a book on saving teeth. Here he gives a key to pronouncing respelled words, marking long and short vowel sounds and sounds such as a in air, far, and all. The book then works through words and phrases commonly misspoken.

Its aim is practical: to help speakers, readers, and students say words clearly and correctly in ordinary talk. Short entries, plain rules, and pronunciation marks make it easy to consult. The volume offers a period picture of American speech standards and remains useful for readers interested in language, elocution, and nineteenth-century usage.
33627-frederick-hale-a-biographical-sket:
An anonymous campaign sketch presents Frederick Hale of Portland, Maine, as a candidate for the United States Senate. Hale was the son of former Senator Eugene Hale of Maine and the grandson of former Senator Zachariah Chandler of Michigan. The sketch traces his ancestry, his admission to the Maine bar in 1901, his business prospects, and his military service, in which he reached the rank of colonel on a governor's staff.

Further chapters cover his brief service in the Maine Legislature as a representative for thirteen weeks in 1903. They also cover his public addresses and his qualifications for the Senate and as a candidate. Short and promotional in purpose, the pamphlet offers a compact record of a political family's next generation and of the case made for him to voters.
33628-emma-goldman-biographical-sketch:
Charles A. Madison sketches the life of Emma Goldman in this pamphlet, reprinted from his Critics and Crusaders. It was published by the Libertarian Book Club in 1960 as a tribute on the twentieth anniversary of her death on May 13, 1940. Madison opens with the hanging of several anarchists in 1887 after the Haymarket bombing in Chicago, an event that turned many Americans toward sympathy with the condemned and suspicion of state power.

Goldman was one of those converts, though resentment of authority was no new experience for her. Madison traces her girlhood under a quick-tempered, deeply harassed Orthodox Jewish father, whose strict discipline she refused and whose love she craved. The sketch follows her path toward anarchism and public life. It offers a concise, sympathetic introduction to one of America's most famous radicals.
33853-jessica-trent-her-life-on-a-ranch:
Evelyn Raymond wrote this ranch tale for girls, published at Racine, Wisconsin, in 1902. Jessica Trent lives and rides on a western ranch, and the story opens on a narrow canyon trail, where a meeting with a stranger turns into a wild race uphill. Her horse and his mount press on where the trail allows no passing.

Later chapters follow Jessica through ranch work, rides, and the company of ranch folk. Raymond, author of other Jessica Trent books, writes briskly for young readers. The novel offers a lively picture of ranch life from a girl's point of view.
34372-fra-angelico-a-sketch:
Jennie Ellis Keysor wrote Fra Angelico, a sketch of the painter-monk, copyrighted in 1900 in Boston. Keysor had written sketches of American authors. Ruskin and other critics supply the opening praise: Angelico's work glows like opal among common marbles, and the light of his studio came from Paradise.

Keysor sets the scene at a monastery above Florence, in the vale of the Arno, when the Renaissance was new. Angelico lived from 1387 to 1455. His Madonnas and angels, she says, are beings of unearthly beauty, and the drawing of their hands is most exquisite. The sketch tells his life and art in short, warm chapters meant for students and general readers.
34480-campobello-an-historical-sketch:
Kate Gannett Wells wrote Campobello, an historical sketch of a Maine-coast island. She thanks a local history of Eastport and Passamaquoddy for exact knowledge. That book serves all who want the story of the boundary line, she says. Friends gave her the names of a few of the island flowers. The sketch opens with the charms that cluster round the island.

Ancestry and yellow parchment, royal grants, and feudal loyalty hang about it. On the charts it is Passamaquoddy Outer Island, a plainer name. Campobello is the name men love for it, she writes. The French first discovered the region under Sieur de Monts in 1604. They named an isle of magpies and sailed up the St Croix river. Winter's severity drove them from their first settlement there. Wells gives the island from discovery to her own day.
34878-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Slice eight of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, eleventh edition, runs from Dyer to Ecclesiastical topics. The set calls itself a dictionary of arts, sciences, literature, and general information. Copying notes at the front explain signs for sums and accents. They also list small fixes made to named articles. John Dyer the poet and the anatomy of the ear both appear in those notes.

Long articles treat the figure of the earth and the book of Ecclesiastes. One note weighs Greek thought in Ecclesiastes against the book of Job. Church law gets space under its own head. The slice mixes science, scripture, and biography in one stretch of the alphabet. It shows the depth the edition gave to both facts and faith.
35231-serbia-a-sketch:
Helen Leah Reed wrote Serbia: A Sketch for the benefit of the Serbian Distress Fund. The fund published the book at Boston in 1917, a year after her copyright. Reed had written of Napoleon's young neighbor before.

A poem to Serbia opens the sketch. It calls the land a valiant daughter of the ages, long assailed by Bulgar, Turk, and Magyar. A fair tomorrow, it promises, will soon gleam on her valleys. A front plate shows Karageorges, liberator of Serbia. Reed wrote while the Great War ground Serbia between empires. Her sketch gave American readers the small nation's history and its claim on their pity, with all proceeds sent to relieve its suffering.
35490-seaside-studies-in-natural-history:
Seaside Studies in Natural History treats the marine animals of Massachusetts Bay, and in this part the group called Radiates. Its authors are Elizabeth C Agassiz and Alexander Agassiz. The book was issued at Boston in eighteen seventy one. It is dedicated to Professor L Agassiz, whose system of grouping has been its main guide.

In their preface the authors say a want was often felt for a seaside book of a popular kind. English books of the sort treat the animals of Great Britain, they note. Those differ in species from the animals of the American coast. So a local book was needed, they argue. Most of its cases come from their own bay, they say. A few from other places fill out the sketch of the group. The aim is a fair picture of the type within small limits.
35859-aunt-jane-s-nieces-on-the-ranch:
Edith Van Dyne wrote Aunt Jane's Nieces on the Ranch, printed at Chicago with a copyright of 1913. The nieces, with their rich Uncle John, travel to El Cajon Ranch in the West. A blessed baby stands at the center of the household, with little Jane's two nurses in attendance.

Inez threatens, a dinner with the neighbors passes, and then the baby is gone. A fruitless search, wild conjectures, and the major's encounter with a ghost fill the middle. Prisoners of the wall and an unexpected arrival bring the tale to its turn. Van Dyne, who also wrote as Baum's pen name in other series, keeps the tone sunny and the mystery light.
3632-poor-miss-finch:
Wilkie Collins writes a sensation novel about a blind heroine, Lucilla Finch, called Poor Miss Finch. Collins notes in his dedication that many charming blind girls had appeared in fiction and drama before, but almost always from an ideal and sentimental point of view. His attempt, he says, is to appeal to a different interest: blindness as lived, with its practical limits and its sharp senses.

The story mixes romance, mystery, and a villain's plot around Lucilla, whose blindness makes her both vulnerable and keenly observant. Collins keeps the suspense moving while treating his heroine with respect. The novel suits readers who enjoy Victorian sensation fiction and a heroine who sees more than sighted people expect.
36566-the-roycroft-dictionary-concocted-:
Elbert Hubbard's Roycroft circle concocted this mock dictionary on rainy days, copyrighted in 1914. The title page credits Ali Baba and the Bunch, and the Roycrofters printed it at their shop for the divertisement of the gloomsters. The definitions are jokes with teeth.

Advertising, it says, is the education of the public as to who you are and what you have to offer. Abel is the first squealer. An abode may be a place to clean one's teeth, a bar counter, or a grave. The abnormal man is simply one less stupid than his neighbor. Hubbard's Arts and Crafts wit runs through the alphabet, half sagebrush philosophy and half vaudeville, in the manner of his Philistine magazine.
36658-tales-from-the-old-french:
Tales from the Old French holds old French tales in English dress by Isabel Butler, out in nineteen ten. The tales stand in three bands by kind. The first band holds lays, short verse tales of love and fate. The next holds jest tales of plain folk. The last holds tales of faith and of right ways.

Named hands of the old age stand past two of the lays, and past lays stand the work of a famed wife of that age. The first lay tells of a rich plain man whose manor had no match in the world. Round it ran a stream, and its walled fruit yard held herbs of such strength that one night in it could heal the sick. A tale stock and a note on the tongue close the book.
3724-the-house-of-heine-brothers-in-muni:
Anthony Trollope sets this tale in the dingy Munich office of Heine Brothers, bankers of good repute but modest scale. The two elderly brothers sit daily in the Schrannen Platz, and the younger handles any business that needs more than a word or two. Into their quiet world comes Herbert Onslow, a young Englishman in love with their daughter Isa, and the tale turns on whether prudence will let the match proceed.

Isa has promised her mother that nothing shall change between the pair in manner, since they are not betrothed and may never be. Herbert frets and fumes at the delay, while daily meetings keep hope alive. The story is a gentle study of family caution against young love, with a Bavarian banking house as its unlikely stage.
37806-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
The eleventh Britannica volume here runs from Franciscans onward. Its front pages carry a list of the volume's contributors. Corrections gathered by its transcribers stand in the same front matter. One note amends a name in the author list of the volume. Another mends a sentence in the article on francs-tireurs.

Their soldierly qualities improved with experience, that article holds. The Franklin article is corrected on a point of latitude. A place was set four degrees too far north, it says. The alternative course in Franklin's instructions is mended there too. Frauenburg was founded in 1287, a further note states. In the Freemasonry article a diarist records his making as a mason. He was made a Free Mason at Warrington with a colonel, it quotes. The volume gives the great dictionary in one thick alphabetical slice.
38626-heimatlos-two-stories-for-children:
Heimatlos holds two stories for children by Johanna Spyri, in a translation by Emma Stelter Hopkins issued by Ginn and Company. The copyright page dates the translation to 1912. Spyri wrote for children and for those who love children, as the subtitle says. Pictures by Frederick Richardson go with the tales.

The first story, by Lake Sils and Lake Garda, follows a boy named Rico. Chapter heads name his quiet home, his school, and the schoolmaster’s violin. A distant lake without a name draws the boy’s longing. His mother, a precious legacy, and a precious prayer shape his path. The tale moves at last to Lake Sils itself. Spyri writes of Swiss lakes and hills with a warm moral touch. Her children learn through loss, work, and faith in these pages.
38963-the-history-of-the-negro-church:
The History of the Negro Church, by Carter Woodson, editor of the Journal of Negro History, was published by the Associated Publishers at Washington in 1921. Woodson dedicates the book to the cherished memory of his mother, and a plate of a Christianized African serves as frontispiece.

Fifteen chapters run from early missionaries and the dawn of the new day through pioneer Negro preachers and the independent church movement. Later chapters treat the schism, preachers of versatile genius, the Civil War and the church, the call of politics, and the socialized church of recent growth. The illustrations gather the founders' faces: Lemuel Haynes, Andrew Bryan, Richard Allen, James Varick, Lott Cary, and Josiah Henson among them. The opening chapter argues that one cause of America's discovery was the zeal to extend the Catholic religion.
39172-a-safety-match:
Ian Hay wrote A Safety Match, a novel from the author of A Man's Man and The Right Stuff, both of which went through many impressions. Hay was a soldier and a humorist, and his tales of British life sold by the shelf. The title plays on a match that lights only when struck right, a neat image for the spark of marriage.

Hay tells of a wedded pair and the rubs and warmth of their life together. His touch is light, but the feelings under it are true. Readers of the day loved his mix of fun and sense. The novel still reads as a kind word on the work of staying in love, from a writer who knew men under strain.
39283-letters-to-the-clergy-on-the-lord-:
John Ruskin addressed these Letters to the Clergy on the Lord's Prayer and the Church in 1879 and 1880. Malleson, the vicar of Broughton in Furness, edited them with replies from clergy and laity and an epilogue by Ruskin himself. The first edition sold out in a week. Then the publisher failed, and the book lay in suspended animation, as Malleson says, for twelve years.

This third edition, published by George Allen in 1896, adds further letters. Malleson explains how he rescued the volume at last. Ruskin, the great critic of art and society, turns here to prayer and the state of the Church of England. Clergymen answer him, sometimes sharply, and he answers back. The exchange shows Victorian religion arguing in public.
4000-the-immortals-masterpieces-of-ficti:
Georges Ohnet's volume belongs to the French Immortals series of fiction crowned by the French Academy, and it gathers prize-winning short tales. A sampled chapter, The Little Boots, opens on worn laced boots set in a line by a door, their leather marked by the feet that wore them.

Such small, telling details carry these stories, which favor character and feeling over grand plot. Ohnet and his fellow laureates write of French homes, work, and love with warmth and care. Readers who enjoy short, humane fiction will find the volume a pleasant door into the Academy's chosen storytellers.
4001-widger-s-quotations-from-project-gu:
David Widger gathered this set of short sayings from the Project Gutenberg editions of French novels crowned by the French Academy. The lines come from many hands and many plots, yet they share a plain, sharp way of judging life.

Readers will find maxims on dignity and revenge, on love earned by desert, on self-interest as the law of the world, and on sense that looks like nonsense. Each line stands alone, so the book works well in small bites, for browsing or for copying into a commonplace book. It offers a quick taste of the wit and moral bite of the French Immortals series.
4020-arcadian-adventures-with-the-idle-r:
A comic novel of New York's idle rich follows the members of a plutocratic club through dinners, lectures, and college follies. Notices in a college hall tell of classes suspended and professors struck down by overwork, while bronze busts watch from niches.

The humor turns on wealth without work, as rich men take up causes, cures, and learning with grand seriousness and small sense. The book satirizes a gilded world of clubs, yachts, and good intentions gone idle. Readers who enjoy light social satire will find a funny, old-fashioned portrait of money at play.
40521-an-etymological-dictionary-of-the-:
John Jamieson made An Etymological Dictionary of the Scottish Language for his land. Archibald Constable printed this short form at Edinburgh in eighteen hundred eighteen. The great quarto of eighteen hundred eight stands behind the abridged book. Jamieson cut his own vast work to fit more hands and purses.

Each word stands in its Scots senses, with proof from named books. Writers who used a term, or works where it lives, back each sense. Roots in old tongues close each entry in Jamieson’s set plan. His plan tracks the short Johnson word book, save one change. Roots come last here, not first, in his set Scottish scheme. A star marks words that hold a Scots sense apart from English use. Scots speech in those years bent its spellings from page to page. The book guards a tongue that print was fast smoothing away.
40604-art-in-america-a-critical-and-hist:
Benjamin wrote Art in America as a short history and critique of painting and sculpture in the United States. Harper and Brothers printed it in New York in 1880, with many pictures. Benjamin had already written on art in Europe of his own day.

The book traces American art from its early days to the present tendencies of 1880. Long chapters survey painters who worked between 1828 and 1878. A separate chapter covers sculpture, which Benjamin treats with more room for artists living abroad. Pictures show works by Copley, Stuart, West, Trumbull, and others. Benjamin says he judged artists by how well each showed a stage in the growth of American art.
40661-a-daughter-of-the-rich:
Waller wrote A Daughter of the Rich, a tale put out by Little, Brown at Boston in 1903. Ellen Bernard Thompson drew the plates, and the front plate shows Hazel. The book opens with a night call between Rose and Martie, her friends at home. Chapters bear names like Molasses Tea, Mrs. Blossom's Valentine, and A Little Millionaire. A prize chicken, a secret tree, a Christmas prelude, and a snow-bound day all turn up in the list.

Hazel, Rose, and their kin move through small joys, small ills, and kind deeds. One part tells of a wish tree, one of a lost nation, and one of a girl who learns to give. Waller wrote tales for young folk in a warm, plain voice. This one shows a rich girl who learns that worth lies in love, not in wealth.
40704-franklin-a-sketch:
John Bigelow's sketch of Benjamin Franklin, printed at Boston in 1879 and sold for 25 cents, traces Franklin from his Boston birth on 17 January 1706. Franklin was the youngest of ten children; his father came from Ecton in Northamptonshire in 1682 and took up the trade of tallow-chandler and soap-boiler in New England. Benjamin was meant for the church and put to school at eight.

At ten he was taken out to help his father, and at twelve he was apprenticed to his brother James. The young printer was newly set up with a press and a newspaper, The New England Courant. The boy formed his style on the Spectator and the Pilgrim's Progress. He slipped unsigned pieces into his brother's paper, and they were accepted and noticed before he owned them.
41048-the-church-index-a-book-of-metropo:
William Pepperell, a clergyman, compiled The Church Index, printed in London in 1872 as a book of metropolitan churches and church work. Part one covers the fifty churches, Anglican and Nonconformist, of the crowded parish of Kensington. The title page promises full and fair facts on each: history, building, clergy, faith, and social reach. Notes on church questions and pictures of church building fill out the volume.

The contents run from Saint Mary Abbots and All Saints, Notting Hill, to Baptist, Wesleyan, and Congregational chapels across the parish. Kensington Palace Chapel stands in the list beside mission halls. Pepperell meant the book as a lasting work of reference, a church history of his own day. For the modern reader it freezes one London parish at a moment when church building raced to keep up with the new streets.
41057-our-people-from-the-collection-of-:
Charles Keene drew these sketches for Punch, and Osgood published the Boston collection in 1881. Keene was the magazine's quiet master of the common scene. His people are sorted by where Punch found them: at home, in street-life, in the country, travelling, professional, official, and in the army. Further sets cover art and artists, volunteers, business, domestics, working folk, Ireland, and Scotland.

The jokes live in the captions. A school inspector demands who signed Magna Charta, and the scapegrace, thinking matters serious, protests that it was not him. A club buttons announces he has resigned to the committee, not been sacked. One boy's father is an officer, a corporal; another's is a general, a general dealer. Keene's London of landladies, waiters, and boys is drawn without malice. The book was companion to a volume of Du Maurier's society pictures.
41487-ian-hamilton-s-march:
Winston Spencer Churchill, then a young war correspondent, wrote these letters on the South African war for the Morning Post. The book came out in 1900 as a sequel to his London to Ladysmith via Pretoria. It is inscribed to Lieutenant-General Ian Hamilton, whose march the letters follow.

Hamilton's column marched on the flank of Lord Roberts's main army from Bloemfontein to Pretoria. Far from the railway, it covered more than four hundred miles through rich enemy country. It fought ten general actions and fourteen smaller affairs, and took five towns. Few reporters went with it, so Churchill's letters form a near-complete record. His preface owns the debt with pride.
41518-the-battle-of-sempach:
Robert Walser wrote The Battle of Sempach, a story of a proud armed host. The Future Press issued the book at Berlin in nineteen hundred eight. Walser lived from eighteen hundred seventy eight to nineteen hundred fifty six. A summer march toward the Luzern district fills its bright start.

Sun dazzles on armour, plumes, and prancing horses in the host. Dust clouds veil the long line like a train trailed by proud dames. Now a shimmering snake, now a cloth of rich figures, it winds. Knights trade gay banter through their iron bound mouths as they ride. Footmen lift dainty bits on silver forks to their swaying lords. Wine and poultry pass on the move in care free, lordly ease. No earnest war is this, the host feels, but a chastising raid. Cut heads in heaps on the meadow dance in each man’s proud dream.
41681-breton-legends-translated-from-the:
Breton Legends, Englished from the French and printed in London, gathers the old fireside tales of Brittany for English readers. Its preface notes how the Grimm brothers made such work honoured, and how Norse and German sets have gone before: now Brittany puts forward her claim. The editors choose some of the best of her legends.

Brittany's rocks, deep bays, and lone heaths breed tales of saints, spirits, and the dead who walk. Much is shared with other lands, yet the Breton cast is its own. The book is a small, early door into a rich store. Folk tale fans get a rare corner of the great gathering age.
41846-bolax-imp-or-angel-which:
Bolax, Imp or Angel, Which, is a children's book by Josephine Culpeper, published in nineteen o seven. It came out in Baltimore and New York from the John Murphy Company. A letter at its head recommends the work warmly to all Catholics. That letter praises it as a study in child life and sound training.

The book is dedicated to the author's own pupils of her governess years. Sixteen chapters follow the boy Bolax through rides, parties, picnics, and fights. A picnic, a talk about our boys, and a trip to the seashore are included. Christmas and first communion get chapters of their own in the set. Later chapters take Bolax to college and then away on vacation. A verse at the front calls him only a boy, full of mischief and glee.
41926-friar-tuck-being-the-chronicles-of:
Robert Alexander Wason recorded Friar Tuck, the chronicles of Reverend John Carmichael of Wyoming, printed under copyright in 1912. The tales are set forth and embellished by the parson's friend and admirer, Happy Hawkins, whose own books Wason also wrote. Stanley Wood drew the pictures, and a front scene shows a quick hand on a gun while Horace sits still with a friendly smile.

Carmichael is a fighting parson in a wild cattle land, a Friar Tuck of the West who can preach, ride, and shoot. Happy tells his deeds in rich cowboy talk. Readers get a warm, funny western, where a minister earns respect the hard way and keeps his humor through every scrape.
42283-the-san-rosario-ranch:
Maud Howe wrote this novel of a ranch household, published by Roberts Brothers at Boston in 1884. She dedicates it to her beloved sister, Laura E Richards.

A guest is expected at the San Rosario Ranch, and the house knows it. The big square house stands draped in roses and clematis. Old Tip, the hunting dog, is routed from his sunny spot for a bath he does not want. The kittens gloss their coats. Barbara Deering steps from the wide doorway, tall and commanding. Howe builds the welcome first, and lets the visitor's arrival carry the tale.
42366-the-cozy-lion-as-told-by-queen-cro:
Frances Hodgson Burnett wrote The Cozy Lion, a picture story published by the Century Company in 1907. Harrison Cady drew the pictures. The tale is told by Queen Crosspatch, a fairy. She claims full credit for reforming a very rude lion.

The lion had moved into a cave near a village. He liked society and was fond of children, in the worst way. Parents armed themselves and locked their children in top rooms and cellars. Crosspatch scolds the lion soundly at the start. A fairy is too small and light for a lion to bite, she explains. The book invites the adult reader to roar well when reading aloud.
42507-a-tenderfoot-bride-tales-from-an-o:
A Tenderfoot Bride, tales from an old ranch, is a memoir by Clarice Richards. Doubleday, Page brought the book out at Garden City in 1927.
