Richards held the rights from 1920 and gives the book to her husband. Pike's Peak seen from the old ranch fronts the printed pictures. Thirteen chapters run from first impressions to echoes of the past.

A surprise party, a root cellar, and a state contract fill the early list. Runaways, the sheep business, and the measure of a man come next. Blizzards and a Christmas fire warm the back half of the ranch year. The tale opens on a train out of Colorado Springs eastward. Prairie spread like a green sea from the foot of Pike's Peak. Owen studies a map of their new holdings as they ride on. She felt like Columbus sailing for a new world that day.
42559-the-story-of-scotch:
Enos A Mills wrote The Story of Scotch, his collie's life. Houghton Mifflin Company issued it in 1916. Mills took the photos that fill it. Copyright dates run 1909, 1911, and 1916. The book goes to Mary and John King Sherman. They knew and prized Scotch, it says. Eight years of companionship fill the tale.

A famed collie bore five puppies in the first lines. A Swedish farmer of Mills's acquaintance owned her. Mills had done his children a small kindness once. The farmer gave him the wisest puppy for it. Wee Scotch gave pleasure to hundreds, Mills writes. Photos show the pup's first kennel and football play. Scotch stands guard at a timber-line cabin in one plate. A mountain naturalist's dog memoir joins pet love to the wild Rockies both of them roamed.
42562-mason-of-bar-x-ranch:
Mason of Bar X Ranch is a western tale by Henry Bennett. It came out in New York from the A. L. Burt Company, with a copyright date of 1920. The book is given to the author's brother, in memory of a vacation spent in the Adirondacks. The contents set out a fast tale of the range. The first chapter is A Hard Proposition.

The Girl stands second, then Mason Meets the Sheriff and A New Arrival. The Abduction of Josephine and Josephine's Peril stand next in the list. The Rescue, The Mexican Escapes, and Mysterious MacNutt carry the plot on. Welcome Visitors, Ricker's Warning, and The Raid stand later, then The Counterfeiters and The Fight in the Secret Passage. The Dance at the Gaylor Ranch and The Shot in the Night stand in the list as well.
42895-arius-the-libyan-a-romance-of-the-:
Nathan Chapman Kouns wrote Arius the Libyan, a romance of the early church, first dated eighteen eighty-three. Appleton reissued the novel at New York and London in nineteen fourteen. The tale turns on Arius and the great fight over his teaching.

Book one opens with an old tale of Crete, where King Etearchus plots against his daughter Phronime. Chapters move through hermits, sea waifs, and talks on faith and reason. Theckla finds one God and hears of another. Book two brings Constantine, church politics, and the one great battle of Christendom. Kouns ends with the fall of the early church order he prized.
43649-over-the-front-in-an-aeroplane-and:
Over the Front in an Aeroplane, a war report by Ralph Pulitzer, was published by Harper and Brothers in 1915. Pulitzer flew over the front lines of the First World War and went down into the trenches on both the French and Flemish sectors. Photographs mark the flight and the tours.

Eight chapters move from the flight to the firing line through a grenade throwing school and the Belgian batteries. He shows how visits to the front were arranged and what a typical day's tour looked like. A final chapter draws lessons from what he saw. The book gave American readers an early view from the air, when flight at war was still new.
43650-bach:
Abdy Williams wrote this life of Bach for The Master Musicians, a series of short composer biographies edited by Frederick Crowest. The series also covered Beethoven, Brahms, Chopin, Handel, Haydn, Mendelssohn, Mozart, Schubert, Schumann, Tchaikovsky, and Wagner, many in several editions. Such handbooks put the lives and works of the great composers into a single portable volume each.

Williams himself also wrote the Handel volume. His Bach follows the standard plan of the series: the composer's life, his posts and travels, and a survey of the music, with pictorial and musical illustrations. The notes to this edition warn that musical symbols may not print cleanly in plain text copies. The series served students, teachers, and concert goers who wanted sound knowledge without a library of scores.
4377-mrs-wiggs-of-the-cabbage-patch:
Alice Caldwell Hegan wrote this little story of Mrs. Wiggs, first published in 1901 and dedicated to her mother, the good angel of the Cabbage Patch. The Cabbage Patch is a poor Louisville neighborhood, and Mrs. Wiggs meets its cold mornings with cheer, even when her elbows stick through a boy's coat. Her philosophy opens the book.

Later chapters bring ways and means, the Christmas lady, the annexation of Cuby, a theater party, and Mr. Bob. Mrs. Wiggs at home, spring in the patch, and a benefit dance complete the picture. Hegan's tale is warm and funny, and it made Mrs. Wiggs a beloved figure of American humor.
43810-woodstock-an-historical-sketch:
Clarence Winthrop Bowen read this sketch of Woodstock, Connecticut, at the town's two-hundredth birthday in Roseland Park on September 7, 1886. Putnam printed it the same year. Bowen notes that a full history of the town was in preparation, and offers this brief account as it was spoken at the celebration.

He begins with the settlement of Massachusetts Bay and Roxbury, and the quarrels that drove Puritans into the wilderness of New England. The Nipmuck country and the planting of Woodstock follow. Bowen tells the town's story as a family tells its own: settlement, church, war, and growth, with names and dates treasured. It is a model town-birthday history.
44071-the-sin-and-danger-of-self-love-de:
Robert Cushman preached this sermon at Plymouth in New England in 1621, the year after the Pilgrims landed. A Boston edition of December 1846 adds a memoir of the author and a life by Judge John Davis. A plate of the landing of the Pilgrims fronts the pamphlet.

Cushman, a leader of the Leyden congregation, warned the young colony against self-love. A settlement built for gain alone, he argued, would fail both God and itself. His sermon is held to be the first preached in New England that survives in print. Readers get the voice of Plymouth at its founding, stern, plain, and still searching.
44195-flower-o-the-peach:
Flower o' the Peach is a novel of South Africa by Perceval Gibbon, published in New York by the Century Company in 1911. The book is dedicated to Jessie and Joseph Conrad. Its first chapter opens at sunset on a sheep farm. Sheep flow out from a cactus-ringed fold toward sparse pastures.

Paul, the hero, stands on the path between the house and the dam, watching them go. Gibbon sets the scene with care: dust hanging in a bronze haze, the farmhouse behind, miles of level veld ahead. The title quotes Browning on the peach flower as a sign of death and life. The novel tells a hard story of the South African farming country.
44568-a-comprehensive-history-of-norwich:
Bayne wrote A Comprehensive History of Norwich, transcribed from the Jarrold and Sons edition of 1869. Its title page promises a survey of the city and its public buildings, plus full lists of mayors and sheriffs. Political history comes with full election returns and lists of members of Parliament for the city.

Religious history covers bishops and deans and the rise of nonconformity, while a trade section prints prize essays on the making and selling of Norwich goods. Bayne opens by telling readers where his facts came from, so they can trust the tale. The book is a Victorian city history in full form, made for citizens who wanted their town's whole past in one thick volume.
44576-the-girls-of-silver-spur-ranch:
Grace MacGowan Cooke and Anne McQueen wrote a novel of ranch life in Texas. John Spooner's small cattle farm bears the grand name Silver Spur, chosen by his second daughter Elizabeth. She has hung a spur dressed in silver leaf over the door. The neighbors laughed at first, but the name stuck.

The story opens with the girls hard at work on wedding sewing. Mary, the eldest, is to wed a young man named Bellamy in a few days. Elizabeth teases her about the plain name Spooner and the spoon brand their father chose. Chapters ahead promise a guest named Roy, a bakery at the ranch, and a cut wire fence. The book is a warm tale of sisters, work, and courtship on a small ranch.
45452-connie-carl-at-rainbow-ranch:
Connie Carl at Rainbow Ranch, by Joan Clark, was published in Chicago in 1939. Connie comes home by train to Red Gulch, watching the blue line of New Mexico's mountains, her mountains, draw closer beyond the telegraph poles. At first glance no one would take her for a Westerner: she has just graduated from a stylish Eastern finishing school. The chapters promise a rodeo, bad news, a foreman's boast, Pop Bradshaw's treachery, and the kidnapping of a horse named Catapult.

A midnight escapade, a holdup, dude wrangling, a stampede, and a roundup fill out the tale. The Goldsmith Publishing Company sold the book as wholesome western adventure for girls. Connie's two worlds, the finishing school and the ranch, give the story its pull: polish on the surface, and a rider underneath.
46076-sebastian-bach:
Sebastian Bach is a short life of the composer by Reginald Lane Poole, in the Great Musicians series edited by Francis Hueffer. Sampson Low, Marston and Company published it in London. Poole was a fellow of Balliol College, Oxford, and a doctor of philosophy of Leipzig. Companion volumes treat Wagner, Handel, Mendelssohn, and Mozart.

The preface makes a modest promise. No one will expect a life of Bach to be amusing, Poole writes. Yet the essay should interest, and interest of a high and varied character. He notes the disadvantage of writing the master's first biography in England. Against that stands his direct use of German scholarship. The series sold at three shillings a volume, uniform in cloth. Poole's Bach introduced English readers to the composer as a working church musician, not a marble saint.
46085-the-boy-allies-with-pershing-in-fr:
Clair Hayes wrote The Boy Allies with Pershing in France, part of the Boy Allies army series rushed out while the Great War still ran. Its subtitle promises to go over the top at Chateau Thierry. The front picture shows Hal calling sharply for Sergeant Bowers to take a house with a dozen men.

Hal and Chester, the boy allies of many volumes, serve with the American forces in France. The series put boy heroes beside real generals and real battles, from the Marne to the Argonne. Hayes wrote fast, patriotic, and close to the headlines, for readers who followed the war in the papers each morning. This volume shows the formula at full tilt, with Pershing's name on the cover as the prize.
46152-the-last-ditch:
Will Levington Comfort wrote a novel of travel and longing that Doran copyrighted in 1916. A prologue set at Hankow opens the tale. Romney, on a small river steamer a day below that city, sees a rug before he sees the woman who holds it. The rug is the yellow of India, thin as silk, heavy in its folds, and like no other weave.

The woman takes a missionary's small boy into her arms and wraps the rug round him to hold him close. Her face shows a hunger that burns in Romney's chest as he watches. The parts that follow bear the names The Great Drift, The Gobi, and Tientsin. Two figures of the Gobi are named, Anna Erivan and Rajananda. A hunchback marks the Tientsin part. The close is set in the hill country, and the yellow rug stands at the heart of the tale.
47076-the-art-of-drinking-a-historical-s:
Georg Gervinus, a noted German scholar of history and letters, wrote this short sketch on the art of drinking. It was turned into English for the United States Brewers' Association and printed in New York in eighteen ninety. Gervinus had won fame for bold stands on the rights of the people under German princes.

He treats drink as a fit subject for grave study, not as a box of curios. The sketch sketches what a full history of the subject would need: customs, songs, laws, and habits across ages and lands. He asks how peoples have used wine and beer in joy, in worship, and in daily life. Brewers backed the book, but the mind behind it is a scholar's, and the tone stays high.
4760-tillie-a-mennonite-maid-a-story-of-:
Helen Reimensnyder Martin tells Tillie, a Mennonite Maid, as a story of the Pennsylvania Dutch. Its chapters open with Tillie crying, Oh, I love her, and with a teacher promising, I'm going to learn you once. Later chapters ask what is hurting Tillie, show the Doc combining business and pleasure, and declare that novels are not moral, Doc. Jake Getz falls into a quandary, and the last days of Pump-Eye pass.

Miss Margaret runs an errand, Tillie promises to do her darn best, teacher, and Adam Schunk's funeral follows. Tillie feels plain, Absalom keeps company, Ezra Herr the pedagogue appears, and a Harvard graduate arrives. The Wackernagels at home, Tillie revealing herself, telling a lie, and being set back lead to a revolt of Tillie and a last fight. Readers get a warm, dialect-rich novel of a bright girl among strict Mennonite ways.
48247-prayers-of-the-early-church:
Prayers of the Early Church was edited by Manning Potts. The Upper Room issued the book at Nashville in 1953. Potts edited that devotional guide, named the world's most widely used. Contents arrange the prayers by century, from the first to the fifth. Chapter one gives New Testament prayers first: Simeon, Mary, Jesus, Stephen, Paul, and Peter. Other first century prayers follow, from Clement of Rome and old liturgies. The prayer's text of Simeon and the Magnificat stand at the head of the book.

Second century names include Polycarp, Ignatius, and Irenaeus. The third adds the Liturgy of St Mark and Eastern vespers. Ambrose, Basil, Chrysostom, and Augustine fill the fourth. The fifth closes with the Leonine and Gelasian sacramentaries. The small book gathers the church's oldest words of prayer for daily use.
48395-the-lives-of-the-saints-volume-03-:
Volume three of The Lives of the Saints, by the Reverend S. Baring-Gould, covers the saints of March. The set ran to sixteen volumes, and this new edition came out in London in 1897 with over four hundred pictures across the whole work. Baring-Gould, a clergyman and writer, spent years gathering these lives from old sources.

The March volume holds lives in date order, from Saint Chad and Saint Casimir to Saint Benedict and Saint Catherine of Bologna. It adds lives of English martyrs and of Cornish and Welsh saints not in older sets. Each life gives the saint's tale, death, and feast day in plain, full form. The book remains a rich store of church lore and folk history.
48977-johann-sebastian-bach:
Herbert F Peyser wrote this short life of Johann Sebastian Bach, copyrighted in 1945 by the Philharmonic-Symphony Society of New York. The society issued it for concert and radio listeners who wanted a quick background. Peyser claims no new findings; he offers a few high points of Bach's outward life and a glance at a handful of great works.

The foreword notes how plain that life looks beside the riches of the music. Bach travelled only a few hundred miles in central and northern Germany, and mostly on sober professional business, far less than his contemporary Handel. His drama is in the scores. Peyser begins with a remark of Goethe. Long-lived families, Goethe said, bring forth one figure who gathers up the gifts of all who came before. Peyser holds that Bach, sprung from generations of musicians, fits it exactly.
49114-proposed-surrender-of-the-prayer-b:
William J Irons wrote a letter to the Lord Bishop of London on the proposed surrender of the Prayer Book and Articles of the Church of England. Theodore Wright and Rivingtons in London issued the pamphlet in eighteen sixty three. Irons was a prebendary of Saint Paul and incumbent of Brompton. The letter is dated from Brompton at Whitsuntide, eighteen sixty three. Professor Stanley views on subscription are the spur.

Irons warns that a call to end subscription to the English formularies would once have seemed grave disloyalty. Twenty years past, he says, some clergy had claimed leave to hold all Roman doctrine. Now others claim free thinking inside the church and seek court backing. To sweep away the sober restraints of orthodoxy at once strikes him as bold and risky. Church readers get a fierce defence of set forms in a time of strain.
49645-the-mentor-belgium-the-brave-vol-8:
Belgium the Brave is an issue of The Mentor, volume eight, number three, serial number 199, dated 15 March 1920. Ruth Kedzie Wood wrote the text. The Mentor's motto was Learn One Thing Every Day, and the copy sold for twenty cents. Its subject is the cloth hall of Ypres, pictured on the cover.

Ypres has a past of war and magnificence. Her main square, next to that of Brussels, is called the most beautiful in the world. Her town hall, her cathedral, and her market hall combine all the splendours. The market hall is more than beautiful, for it is unique. In time of peril the whole town could gather there for shelter. For centuries it has stood there, the wonder of Ypres, the business centre of the cloth makers and weavers. A sketch of the Belgian poet Emile Verhaeren, who died in 1916, accompanies the article.
4983-slips-of-speech:
John H. Bechtel's Slips of Speech opens with taste as a universal gift, found in some degree in all nations and ages, from the savage's love of decoration to civilized man's love of art. Taste differs among people as faces and languages differ, and the same person shows it differently at different periods of life.

That variety, Bechtel argues, implies a susceptibility to improvement, and good taste in writing is no exception. The book collects common errors and lapses in speech and writing, correcting them with examples. Readers who want cleaner English get a practical guide, written before style books became standard, and still useful for its plain advice.
49840-the-present-method-of-inoculating-:
The Present Method of Inoculating for the Small-Pox is a medical tract of the eighteenth century, from the years when inoculation was new and feared. The writer, a physician, begins by saying that from the time he entered practice he saw the danger of smallpox taken in the natural way, and wished for a safer road.

Inoculation meant giving a patient the disease on purpose, in a mild, managed form, so the body would learn to fight it. The tract sets out the present method, its preparation, diet, and course, with cases. Before vaccination, this was the best shield medicine had against a killer. The book is a window on doctors weighing risk with honest care.
50186-brigadier-frederick-and-the-dean-s:
Brigadier Frederick and The Dean's Watch pairs two tales by the French writing partners Erckmann-Chatrian, in English translation. Collier of New York issued the volume, with a critical introduction by Professor Richard Burton of the University of Minnesota. Portraits with notes by Octave Uzanne illustrate the book.

The introduction praises the partners' lasting claim. Fashions change in literature, the critic says, but their work is saturated with humanity that all men can understand. Their duality, he notes, is lost in the long association of their names, since the two wrote as one. The tales draw on French provincial and military life. A frontispiece and other portraits support the text. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
50307-fifteen-sonnets-of-petrarch:
Fifteen Sonnets of Petrarch is a small bilingual selection translated by Thomas Wentworth Higginson, published by Houghton Mifflin in Boston and New York in 1903. Each sonnet appears first in Italian, then in Higginson's English. His introduction grows from an earlier paper called Sunshine and Petrarch.

The first sonnet blesses the flowers and grass where his lady walks. The plain that hears her sweet words and keeps the print of her foot wins his envy. Rivers, trees, and violets share the praise. The transcriber's note at the end matches each piece to its number in the Canzoniere. Higginson, a man of letters and a former colonel, made Petrarch readable for American parlours. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
51158-the-train-wire-a-discussion-of-the:
Anderson wrote on the science of train dispatching in a book printed at New York in 1891 by the Railroad Gazette. Adams wrote the introduction. The second edition was revised and enlarged from the first of 1883, when Anderson was superintendent of the Belvidere Division of the Pennsylvania Railroad. Chapter one treats train dispatching itself, then the dispatcher, the operator, and the order.

The manifold, the record, the train order signal, and transmission follow in order. One wire ruled a whole division in those years. A dispatcher's orders, copied by operators at small stations, kept trains from meeting head on on single track. Anderson modestly disclaimed perfection for his work, Adams says, while venturing a bold prediction for it. Railroad men get the craft rules of a vanished wire world here.
51291-narrative-and-critical-history-of-:
Volume four of a grand survey of the past of America came out in eighteen eighty-four. Justin Winsor, head of the Harvard book hall, shaped the whole work. This part treats the French probes and towns in North America from fifteen hundred to seventeen hundred. It takes in the work of three more lands in that same span.

Chapters treat the first sea men, the maps of the east coast, and the great French probe chief and his heirs. Each part pairs its tale with sharp notes on the proofs and with maps and drawn plates. Past three hundred plates fill the book, drawn from old charts and hands of the age.
51696-the-brownie-scouts-at-silver-beach:
Brownie Scouts at Silver Beach is a children's story by Mildred A Wirt, copyright nineteen fifty two. Contents run to twenty chapters. Sand dollars open the list, and a turtle race follows. Fog, a ship house, and an old sea captain take their turns. A locked door and high tide build the middle of the tale.

Chapter one opens on the beach as Vevi McGuire shouts that she is a fish. She runs along the sand toward the ocean in a red bathing suit. Her dark hair and freckles make a bright flash against the blue sky, the tale says. Connie Williams calls out to be careful, for the tide is coming in. Vevi does not heed the warning. She flings her arms wide and runs to meet a big wave, hoping to be first in the water.
51803-the-lost-dispatch:
An unnamed writer printed The Lost Dispatch at Galesburg, Illinois, in 1889, as a piece of Civil War literature. The preface warns that every person in the narrative appears under a made-up name. The author, who knew the truth, chose to stay unknown.

Fewer than twenty-five people alive, he says, could name the real men in the story. The lost dispatch of the title belongs to the war's famous paper trail of orders found and lost, which changed campaigns. By hiding names he frees himself to tell what official reports left out. The pamphlet is part memoir, part detective note, and wholly a veteran's act of custody over a secret.
51861-victoria-c-woodhull-a-biographical:
Theodore Tilton wrote this sketch of Victoria C Woodhull for The Golden Age tracts. The paper issued it at Nine Spruce Street, New York, in eighteen hundred seventy one. Tilton knew Woodhull well and held her in rare respect, he says. A proverb on slander fronts his defence of her name.

Victoria Claflin was born in Homer, Ohio, on September twenty third, eighteen hundred thirty eight. She was the seventh of ten children of Roxana and Buckman Claflin. Queen Victoria’s crown year gave the babe her proud name. The Queen had set gifts by for such namesakes of that year. Tilton hints she might claim hers at Windsor one day. Woodhull now stands as a candidate for the Presidency, he notes. Her sex’s great reform gives her life its wide public stake. Suffering and slander mark the drama of her path so far.
52098-tachyhippodamia-or-the-new-secret-:
Willis Powell wrote Tachyhippodamia, or the new secret of taming horses, printed at Philadelphia in 1872. Its title page promises full directions to break and ride colts, to tame the most vicious horses, and to gentle them to all kinds of vehicles and work. Tricks are taught too, down to making turkeys and other animals dance, and taming deer.

Receipts for diseases of horses, mules, and cows fill the back, with ways to fatten stock. Rarey's famous method of breaking and taming is added at the end. Powell writes in the showman's voice of the American horse tamer, part craft, part wonder, for farmers and teamsters of the horse age.
52293-on-the-various-forces-of-nature-an:
On the Various Forces of Nature is a set of talks on the powers of the world and how they hang as one. House ads at its front name the science books of its age: star lore, sky flowers, and a ringed world and its moons. A work on the growth of kinds, by a Scot doctor, stands in those ads.

The talks come from a famed set first spoke to work men and the young. Their theme is the great law that no force is lost. Heat, light, the spark, the pull of the earth, and the bonds of stuff pass one to the next, they show. Each force is a coin that can change its stamp but not its worth, in the plan of the tale.
52509-the-crimson-patch:
Augusta Huiell Seaman wrote The Crimson Patch, a mystery tale for girls, issued by Appleton-Century. C M Relyea drew the pictures. Seaman had written The Slipper Point Mystery and The Sapphire Signet before it. Suite Number Four Hundred Three heads her first chapter.

Friends or Enemies follows, and The Shadow on the Wall after that. The crimson patch itself appears as a chapter title at last. Who Took It and The Mystery Deepens keep the questions hot. A piece of paper and a message in the night turn the hunt. The House with the Green Shutters waits near the close. Seaman was a master of the girls' mystery shelf, all clues and courage.
53109-the-witch:
Mary Johnston, a well known American novelist of her day, published The Witch in 1914 with Houghton Mifflin. The story is set in England in an older century, when fear of witchcraft still shaped village life. Its chapters move from a queen's chamber to a rose tavern, a forest road, and a plague struck town, with a heroine named Joan at the center.

Along the way the reader meets physicians, a squire's brother, and a man with a hawk. Scenes at an oak grange, a heron's cottage, and the village church build the period world. Talk of magic hangs over daily life, and accusation is a real danger. The novel blends romance, history, and the dread that drove the old witch trials.
54281-the-voiage-and-travayle-of-sir-joh:
John Ashton edited this edition of the travels of Sir John Maundeville, the famed medieval knight and storyteller. Pickering and Chatto printed it in London in 1887, with old pictures copied in facsimile. The book tells the way toward Jerusalem and the marvels of India and other lands.

Ashton says he loved Sir John despite his tall tales. Good editions, he argues, were either too hard in old spelling or too bare in modern dress. He chose a reprint of Pynson's early printed edition, kept in the British Museum. The text keeps its old flavor while staying readable. Generations of readers met dog-headed men, fountains of youth, and other wonders through Maundeville's book.
54322-norwich:
Norwich, a sketch book by Cole, was published in London. Black issued the artist's volume there. Twenty four sketches are listed at the front. The Erpingham Gate serves as the title page plate. The cathedral is drawn from the south east, and through its apse. The Prior's door in the cloisters follows. The Ethelbert Gate and the grammar school gateway stand next. Houses in the Close and Pull's Ferry vary the subjects. Bishop's Bridge and the castle from the cattle market come midway. Bigod's tower and a Norman arch of the keep are drawn. St Peter Mancroft is seen from the market place. The Guildhall and Stranger's Hall doorway follow.

St Helen's Hospital and its cloisters close the church subjects. Elm Hill and Dutton's Court end the street scenes.
54709-the-galleon-s-gold-or-frank-reade-:
Number 74 of the Frank Reade Weekly Magazine, dated March 25, 1904, sends Frank Reade the younger hunting sunken gold. Frank Tousey published the five-cent weekly in New York, at $2.50 a year by subscription, and the tale is signed only Noname.

The chapters promise the sunken treasure, the young inventor, the bottom of the sea, a divers' battle, and what became of the Dolphin. The story opens aboard the clipper Aurelian, in from Belize, with Captain Hartley watching for New York harbor. His passenger, Cecil Clifford, has come back from Honduras with a secret plan touching a matter of perhaps millions. Both men hope that Gilbert Parker, the most penurious man in America, got their cable from Havana.
55131-the-camp-fires-of-napoleon-compris:
The Camp-Fires of Napoleon is a popular military history by Henry Watson, printed at Philadelphia in 1867. Its subtitle promises the most brilliant achievements of the emperor and his marshals. A frontispiece shows Napoleon crossing the Alps. A table of embellishments lists the book's many plates. The work was made for the American parlour of the eighteen-sixties.

Watson writes battle as story. His chapters gather round the camp-fires of the title, where the emperor's genius and his marshals' daring could be retold as fireside tales. The publisher's age loved such books: war, the preface-trade of the day held, excites a pleasing thrill, and men love excitement. The volume delivers the Napoleonic legend whole, marshals, charges, and all, two generations after Waterloo and in the afterglow of America's own great war. It is history as the gift-book trade sold it, bright and stirring.
55305-the-black-patch:
Black Patch is a mystery novel by Fergus Hume of England. John Long published it in London, first issued in the year 1906. Hume also wrote The Mystery of a Hansom Cab and many like tales. His past list spans The Silent House in Pimlico to The Silver Bullet. Chapters open in a Garden of Eden and pass to hints of Durban.

A proposal, a sight seen in lightning, and a discovery build the case. An inquest runs two chapters, then a will changes the stakes for all. Lady Watson, a major, an ex butler, and past secrets fill the middle. What Orchard knew and a curious coincidence tighten the net in turn. Hume piles clue on clue in his brisk, popular manner.
55386-the-girl-scouts-on-the-ranch:
Edith Lavell wrote The Girl Scouts on the Ranch, for Burt at New York, with rights held in 1923. Lavell had written five Girl Scout books before this one, on school, camp, and canoe trips. The tale opens in commencement week at Miss Allen's Boarding School. Each door and window stands wide open to welcome the guests of the graduating class. Goodbyes, a week-end at the shore, and Daisy's sister fill the first chapters.

Two lieutenants, the ranch itself, and a rival for Marjorie raise the stakes. A stampede, a picnic, a scout meeting, and a pack trip fill the middle. Night fears and a search lead to revelations, and a trip to Yellowstone crowns the fun. A plate shows Kirk, Marjorie, and Daisy at breakfast, bound back for camp.
56331-the-historical-growth-of-the-engli:
Hamilton Thompson wrote The Historical Growth of the English Parish Church. Cambridge University Press put it out in 1911, in a manuals series. A plate shows the west tower of a Cambridge church from the north-west. The first chapter traces the development of the parish church in England. Early parish churches come first in his contents list.

Monastic mission settlements and church building on private estates follow. The Danish invasions and the monastic revival take their section next. The early history of these churches is obscure, the book owns. Stone remains of the earliest fabrics are scanty, and records are thin. Thompson works from what walls, plans, and documents survive. He shows how the parish church grew from mission post to the center of village life.
56542-philipp-reis-inventor-of-the-telep:
Silvanus Thompson, a professor of experimental physics at Bristol, wrote this life of Philipp Reis in 1883. Spon published it in London and New York that year. A front plate shows a medallion and autograph from the monument to Reis at Friedrichsdorf, his home town in Germany.

Thompson calls Reis the inventor of the telephone in his plain title. Documentary testimony, translations of Reis's original papers and contemporary publications support the claim in the book. Thompson says the labour was not slight, with inquiries pressed in England and Germany among Reis's surviving contemporaries to set the record forth.
57989-the-sea-monarch:
Percy Westerman wrote The Sea Monarch for The Captain, a magazine for boys and old boys. George Newnes of London ran the tale in volume twenty-five, from April to September 1911. Six installments carried the story through that half year. It opens with the mysterious case of the Zietan, then brings in the yacht Playmate and her skipper. A huge vessel looms from fog and runs the small yacht down.

The hero is taken prisoner on the mysterious ship and meets Captain Brookes. The conning tower of the Olive Branch, rumors of war, and an act of piracy follow. Mine fields, a crippled submarine, and foes in Patagonia raise the pace. A missing wireless set and an airman add new craft to the tale. Westerman gives boys a sea war of invention, daring, and narrow escapes.
58017-a-few-remarks-on-the-scripture-his:
A sermon pamphlet by J Church of the Surry Tabernacle. R Thomas printed it at Southwark in 1816. Church sold it in the vestry. His subject is Saul and the witch of Endor. Three texts stand on the title page. They command readers to try the spirits. They warn that Satan transforms himself into an angel of light.

Church addresses the tract to all who love Christ in sincerity. His opening pages praise the person and work of Jesus at length. Christ's righteousness justifies, and his blood atones. His intercession grounds the believer's hope. Only then does the argument turn to Endor. The question is what truly appeared to Saul that night. Church writes as an evangelical preacher for his own flock.
58018-the-rod-in-pickle-or-an-answer-to-:
The Rod in Pickle is a polemical pamphlet by the Reverend Latham, printed in London in 1817. Hay and Turner published it at four pence. Its subtitle calls it an answer to the appeal of John Church. Church is named the Obelisk preacher on the title page. The pamphlet promises an authentic narrative of his leaving Banbury. Charges exhibited against him are set out in full. 

Church's own letters to the Banbury meeting house managers are added. In them he begged that his dismissal's cause not be known in London. A proverb motto says the nearer to church, the farther from God. The answer opens by calling an attack on a fallen foe ungenerous. Only duty to the public could induce the publishers, it says. The piece is a chapel scandal fought out in print.
59145-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
The Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of John Leech is a list book by David Widger. It names the works in that store that bear the cuts of John Leech. A Christmas Carol heads the list with its plate names in full. Marley ghost, Fezziwig ball, and the last ghost stand in that plate rank. The Cricket on the Hearth stands next with its own plate list.

Comic past books of Rome and England stand in the scheme with Leech cuts. Mrs Caudle talks, the Book of Ballads, and Disraeli heads fill more ranks. Four hundred laugh cuts and a small tour in Ireland join the list. Punch books on meals, rail, hunt, and love close the shown part ranks. Each work bears its full part scheme in the list for search ease.
59400-the-history-of-christianity-consis:
The History of Christianity is an old popular account of the Christian faith, its title promising the life and teachings at its heart. The text keeps the spelling of its period, with words spelled in more than one way. Its punctuation has been made uniform for modern readers. The editors note that italics and small capitals are marked in special ways in this copy.

Works of this kind retold the life of Christ and the growth of the church for general readers at home. They served family reading and Sunday study in the nineteenth century. The book's plain aim was instruction in the story of the faith, from the Gospels onward.
59567-our-summer-migrants-an-account-of-:
J E Harting wrote a guide to the birds that spend each summer in the British Isles. Bickers and Son issued it in London in 1875, with designs by Thomas Bewick. Harting had first shared parts of the work in the paper The Field in 1871. He then checked the text and added new chapters for the book.

The chapters trace when each bird comes, where it rests, and how it nests and sings. They also ask where the birds spend the cold months and how they cross wide seas to get here. Country readers who watch fields and woods gain a clear aid for naming what they see each spring.
59751-arnold-of-winkelried-the-hero-of-s:
Arnold of Winkelried, the Hero of Sempach retells a Swiss legend for young readers. Gustav Höcker wrote the tale in German, and George P Upton put it into English. A C McClurg printed the book at Chicago in 1908, with three pictures.

In his preface, Upton admits that some scholars doubt Winkelried lived at all. He answers that the hero lives on in Swiss hearts, like William Tell. Sketches lead through the 1300s: the fight at Morgarten, a mystery play, and the Black Death. Robber knights and castle attacks fill the middle. The book ends at Sempach, where Winkelried gathers the Austrian spears to his chest and opens a path for his friends.
59764-brazil-and-her-people-of-to-day-an:
Nevin Winter wrote this travel book on Brazil, printed in Boston in 1910. The catalog title is a scrap, but the title page gives the full name, Brazil and Her People of To-Day. Winter had written like books on Mexico and Guatemala. His chapters move from the coast to Rio de Janeiro, then inland to mines, farms, and the Amazon.

Winter describes the land, the cities, schools, railways, and the coffee trade in detail. He also writes on the army, the church, the old empire, and the new republic. Photos from his own trip fill the book. It gives American readers of 1910 a broad, hopeful picture of a fast-growing South American nation.
59849-filthy-rich:
Fred Sheinbaum wrote Filthy Rich, a science fiction story in Worlds of If in April 1957. Its tagline calls the hero worse than Dillinger, the James boys, Captain Kidd, and Benedict Arnold together, all because he is filthy rich. The scene is a future America run by one great corporation.

An assistant vice-president for cotter pin production attends the Thursday executive meeting, which closes with the Consumer's Pledge recited in schools nationwide. Common workers put in three-day, twenty-one-hour weeks while management works behind the scenes raising living standards. Sheinbaum aims his satire at corporate cant and the religion of consumption, in the sharp, sour style Worlds of If favored under its editor of the day.
60135-mexico-and-her-people-of-to-day-an:
Mexico and Her People of To-Day, by Nevin O Winter, was first published in 1907 and revised in a new edition of 1912. The subtitle promises an account of the customs, characteristics, amusements, history, and advancement of the Mexicans, with the development and resources of their country. Photographs by the author and C R Birt illustrate the book. Winter wrote matching volumes on Brazil, Guatemala, and Argentina for the same Boston house, L C Page.

The series sold Latin America to American tourists and businessmen in the years of Porfirio Diaz and after. A belle of Tehuantepec fronts this volume in national dress. Winter writes as a friendly guide, confident that his readers will invest, travel, and approve. The revised edition of 1912 had to reckon with a Mexico entering revolution, which gives the book its interest as a before picture.
61417-the-colored-man-in-the-methodist-e:
The Colored Man in the Methodist Episcopal Church is a history by the Reverend Hagood of the Lexington Conference. It was published at Cincinnati in 1890. A portrait of the author forms the frontispiece. His preface states the book's claim plainly: the history of the ties between his church and the colored man had never been written.

Hagood argues that the subject demands a record. From the landing of twenty African slaves at Jamestown, he says, the colored man has been the subject of much discussion. On his status as a man there have always been two sides, one for enslaving him and one against. Both sides have always found champions in the church's world. The book sets out to trace where the colored member stood inside one great Methodist body across that long argument.
61514-captain-sparkle-pirate-or-a-hard-m:
Nicholas Carter wrote Captain Sparkle, Pirate, a Nick Carter detective story copyrighted in 1905 by Street and Smith of New York. The tale opens in Carter's study, where his valet Joseph shows in Maxwell Kane, a sportsman whose name opens any door. Kane counts his wealth in hundreds of millions, yet still comes to his friend the detective for help.

A pirate chief who calls himself Captain Sparkle stands at the center of the case, and the subtitle calls him a hard man to catch. Carter must use his wits, disguise, and nerve against a foe who works at sea and ashore. The story is a fine sample of the cheap, fast dime novels that made Nick Carter one of the best known detectives in American popular print.
61976-shadrach:
Shadrach, by Nelson Bond, is a science fiction story from Planet Stories, Fall 1941. The teaser recalls the three men cast into a fiery furnace in Bible times, then promises the same test of godship for three space bitten men on frozen Titania. The tale opens far from Titania, in Xuerl's Cosmobar on the drab edge of Mars Central.

There Chip Warren watches a drunk Earthman, a Venusian, a Jovian, and a runt gathered at the bar, and a flower headed Martian barman pipes his offers of drink. Bond builds his space frontier out of dives, mines, and mixed crews. The bar scene alone is worth the price.
62002-a-plain-statement-of-the-doctrines:
A Plain Statement of the Doctrines Objected to in the Church of Rome is a Protestant controversial pamphlet by Joseph Reilly. Reilly describes himself as late a Roman Catholic student. The third edition was printed in Dublin by M. Goodwin in 1827.

The pamphlet gives the reasons fairly assigned for separating from Rome's communion, as its title promises. Reilly writes to the reader with reluctance, saying he appears in defence of his own character. He had tried every means to quiet an anxious, troubled conscience before leaving. Two mottoes frame the argument: follow the ancients only so far as they follow truth, and prove all things, holding fast what is good. The work belongs to the fierce pamphlet wars of Irish religion in the eighteen twenties.
62268-money-making-men-or-how-to-grow-ri:
Ewing Ritchie's Money-Making Men; or, How to Grow Rich was transcribed from the 1886 edition of Brain and Company, Paternoster Row, and entered at Stationers' Hall. George Peabody's portrait stands with the cover. Ritchie had written lives of Palmerston and the Prince Consort before it.

The chapters sort the money makers by kind. In the City opens the book, Across the Atlantic follows, and Charles Bianconi, the Irish car-man, gets a chapter of his own. Fortunes made by a vegetarian and by teetotalism come next, then money-making publishers, men in the provinces, and odd, eccentric winners. George Moore, citizen and philanthropist, artists and writers, and a closing set of reflections fill the rest.
62328-the-dream-coach:
The Dream Coach is a book of dream tales for children by Anne and Dillwyn Parrish, printed by Macmillan in 1924. The authors also drew its pictures and its map. Its coach, the fare set at forty winks, leaves every night for no one knows where.

Inside, four young travellers take their trips in the coach. A princess rides in it into sleep. So do a little Chinese emperor, a French boy, and a Norwegian boy. The contents name the parts: the seven white dreams of the king's little daughter, and Goran's dream. A bird cage with tassels of purple and pearls holds three dreams of the Chinese emperor. King Philippe's dream closes the set. A short verse opens the coach door, telling an unhappy child to wait with patience for the night.
62743-grace-harlowe-s-overland-riders-at:
Jessie Graham Flower wrote a Grace Harlowe adventure copyrighted in 1923, one of a long series of Overland Riders books. Earlier rides crossed the old Apache trail, the great American desert, and Yellowstone. Chapter one is set in the peace of the Coso Valley. Chapter notes say Stacy's dream is interpreted and a guide can howl like a coyote.

Mules, the notes warn, are contrary creatures like some fellows. The peace is rudely broken. In chapter two the Overlanders prepare for defence, with Stacy armed with a tent stake. Emma Dean falls into toils, and a shot stops a roper. A picture caption cries that a newcomer is Pap.
62803-chitimacha-notebook-writings-of-em:
Chitimacha Notebook holds the writings of Emile Stouff, a chief of the Chitimacha people. Marcia Gaudet edited the book for the Lafayette Natural History Museum in Louisiana. It came out in 1986, with facsimile pages of the notebook.

Four parts frame the whole: an introduction and the Chitimacha story of creation. A history of the Chitimacha Indians follows, then a list of earlier writings about them. Photographs from 1908 show Chief Benjamin Paul with children by a pirogue at Charenton. Basket weaving, the book notes, is a traditional craft of the tribe. One plate shows the Regis Darden family with finished baskets set before them. Another shows Stouff's kin: his mother, sister, great-aunt, and father. A portrait of Stouff and a basket pattern head the volume.
62965-eugenie-empress-of-the-french:
Erich Holm wrote Eugénie, Empress of the French, and George Upton turned it into English for a Chicago edition of 1910. The book is one of the Life Stories for Young People. Four pictures show the empress in youth, in power, and in widowhood, with Napoleon the Third beside her in his turn.

The tale begins in Malaga in Spain, where a merchant named Kirkpatrick dwelt at the start of the last century. His granddaughter Eugénie rises to marry Louis Napoleon and share the throne of the Second Empire. Chapters cover her part in politics, her lead in fashion, and Paris in her reign. The war of 1870, her flight to England, exile, and the death of her son close a sad royal life.
63001-the-passing-of-the-idle-rich:
The Passing of the Idle Rich is a social critique by Frederick Townsend Martin. Doubleday issued it in New York in 1911. The contents list eleven chapters. The kingdom of society opens the book. The madness of extravagance follows. A Lincoln quote on labour serves as a motto. Useful labour alone is meritorious, it says. Idleness lives as a pensioner on that labour.

Martin begins by claiming his ground. He was born in society and has lived in it all his life. He knows its courts in Europe as well, he says. American society, for all its faults, is his theme. Later chapters name a social nemesis. The death-knell of idleness closes the argument. A rich man indicting riches drew wide notice. The book belongs to the muckraking temper of its years.
63192-the-fairy-and-the-witch:
Nelson wrote a small play of a fairy and a witch for stage fun. The play sold for fifteen cents from a house in Franklin, Ohio. That house sold plays for school and stage of all kinds. Its ads list plays for women and song plays for the young. Mock trials and tale books fill more of its cheap list.

Such play books gave small towns a show in one thin wrap. Parts are few, dress is light, and the plot is plain. A fairy and a witch in clash make a clear core for kids. Lines are short and built to be heard from the back rows. School stage groups were the chief buyers of such fare. Gay, brief fun is the whole aim here.
63389-homestead-ranch:
Homestead Ranch is a novel by Elizabeth G Young, published by D Appleton and Company of New York and London in 1923. Appleton copyrighted it in 1922; earlier copyrights of 1915 and 1919 stand to the Perry Mason Company. The book is dedicated to Mary Tracy Horne, kindest of critics.

Harriet Holliday rides the tourist car west across the Rockies toward her brother's ranch, watching solitary homesteads and wondering if his will look the same. The desert of sand and sagebrush makes Connecticut feel unutterably far, as if she had left 1912 behind for pioneer days. Her fellow passengers carry the westward hopes of the year: an apple orchard in Oregon, an orange grove in California, a timber claim in Washington. A Chicago teacher has quit her post to teach in Montana and homestead there herself.
63648-defense-mech:
Defense Mech is a science fiction story by Ray Bradbury, taken from Planet Stories for the spring of 1946. Halloway, a crewman on a rocket bound for Mars, stares down at Earth from a million miles past the Moon. His brain, he says, tore loose and screamed.

Halloway begs the captain for sedatives, or to turn the rocket back to New York. His hands tremble and his heart whirls like a hot pinwheel at the sight of all that space. The captain calls the ship's psychiatrist, who comes down the ladder. The two men weigh the problem: the crew is small, every man is worth his weight in uranium, and Halloway has to be cured. Drugs for the whole trip are ruled out. The psychiatrist refuses the demand to go home yet thinks he has an idea, and the story turns on his idea.
63934-patch:
William Shedenhelm wrote Patch, a science tale printed in Planet Stories in the fall of nineteen fifty. Old pilots like Pop Gillette, a head note says, are no longer needed to run the big ships. Craft are now boosted and held by automatic gear, and Pop warns that one day something will go wrong. The scene is the control tower at Venusport, where Joe takes a call from the Lorelei.

Pop is near two hundred years old and still the best pilot in the system, Joe says. He quit the great runs when automatics came in, bought his tub at a surplus sale, and roams the odd corners of space. Now his ship comes in at a strange angle, jets dead, dropping tail first toward the ramp. Joe watches to see whether the old man still has his famous landing trick.
64131-under-the-turk-in-constantinople-a:
Under the Turk in Constantinople is a record of Sir John Finch's embassy, drawn from his papers in the age of the old style calendar. Dates are given in the Julian form unless marked new style, a note warns. Short forms of words are kept as first printed. Macmillan issued the book at London and in India and Australia.

Finch served as English envoy at the Ottoman court. The record holds letters, notes, and daily acts from that post. Blank spaces left for dates are shown as lines in the text, a note says. Footnotes sit at the close of each chapter. The book gives a close view of court life, trade, and statecraft under Turkish rule. Scholars of the Stuart age and of the Levant are its chief readers.
64288-against-tetrarch:
Gilmour wrote "Against Tetrarch," a story printed in Planet Stories in the fall of 1947. On that evil planet, broken men who once trod Earth knew two things for sure: they all were dying at twenty five, and lovely Mona Darlanan was a dirty traitor. The mines of Tetrarch the Fourth grind men down early.

Rod Harrow paws at the whirling sands in the gryxon mines, where lines of bobbing lamps etch the tunnels. The slave next to him crumples against the rock, ghastly under his helmet, his face lined and old. I was twenty five yesterday, he cackles through the audiphones. I'll be glad to die. Foam spatters his helmet as his feet beat a weak tattoo and stop. Rod watches, pity and vengeance fighting in him.
64738-phil-may-sketches-from-punch:
Phil May's sketches from the comic paper Punch are gathered here by the Punch Office in Bouverie Street, London, printed by Bradbury, Agnew and Company. May was born on April 22, 1864, and died on August 5, 1903. The volume opens with a tribute by Owen Seaman taken from Punch of August 12, 1903.

Seaman calls May's death an irreparable hurt to his wide circle of friends. He praises his gentleness, modesty, and reckless generosity, and the sketches he made on the backs of Punch dinner menus. The contents then list the drawings one by one with their dates in the paper, running from 1893 to 1896. Titles such as Self-Criticism, The Finishing Touch, Wasted Efforts, and A Sunday Dinner promise the street scenes, sporting types, and London characters May was loved for.
64812-eyes-that-watch:
Raymond Gallun wrote this science fiction tale for Comet magazine, in its December 1940 issue. Its tagline reads: the Guardians of Space keep constant vigil. A picture of the lone watcher sets the mood of the thing.

Sam Conway has come home from Mars, the first man to walk its red deserts and live. He has seen the ruins of a dead Martian civilization and the cold that killed it. Now, safe among autumn maples and boys playing football, he cannot shake what followed him back in his mind. Gallun builds the dread quietly, on memory and watching eyes. Readers get a thoughtful early tale of the space age.
64834-the-origin-of-thought-and-speech:
Moncalm, a French thinker, wrote this inquiry into the origin of thought and speech, translated from the French by Whitmarsh and published at London in 1905. Two sayings of Max Müller stand at the front: language is the autobiography of the human mind, and language is our Rubicon, which no brute will dare to cross. The translator owns that, with leave, he sometimes follows Müller's exact words where the French differs.

The book asks the oldest question in the science of mind: how did speech begin, and did thought come before it or with it? Müller looms over the whole debate as both master and target. Such books were the seedbed of what is now the study of language origins. Moncalm writes with the faith of the French spiritual school.
64892-the-real-lady-hilda-a-sketch:
The Real Lady Hilda, subtitled A Sketch, is a novel by Bithia Mary Croker, printed in New York and London in 1899. Croker was a popular writer of Anglo-Indian and society tales, among them Pretty Miss Neville and Diana Barrington. A French line at the front says we sometimes suffer more from the death of an illusion than from the loss of a reality.

The tale is told by Gwen, who waits for the lamp in poky lodgings in a small Sussex market town with her stepmother. Poverty, touched on only by a shrug, has brought them low. Lady Hildegarde's photograph, a question of taste, and getting into society drive the plot. Croker writes bright, knowing comedy of manners with a warm heart.
65322-how-to-get-rich:
A recipe booklet fills this entry, How to Get Rich. It is number 8 of the Multum in Parvo Library, billed as the smallest magazine in the world. Courtney published it at Boston in August 1894 for five cents. Valuable money-making secrets, it promises. These recipes have sold for five dollars each and founded many good-sized fortunes. The formulas make household articles in constant use. Some cost two or three cents to make and retail at twenty-five.

The booklet points out the proper method of manufacture. It leaves the selling to the reader's judgment and discretion. Goods may go direct to consumers by canvassing house to house, or wholesale to storekeepers. Such mail-order recipe books were the get-rich literature of the 1890s, sold on hope. This one preserves the pitch whole: big margins, plain directions, and fortune one formula away.
65572-the-new-york-cake-book-fifty-recip:
A famous New York chef, who keeps his name off the title page, gives fifty cake recipes in this small book. It came out in New York in 1904. General directions for making cake open the work, before any single recipe appears.

Good cake, he insists, starts with good materials: flour white and dry, sugar free of lumps, eggs above suspicion. Butter must be sweet and fresh, and the milk whole. Measures must be exact, and each step of mixing rightly taken. Flour is sifted before it is measured, and egg whites are beaten in a cool room until they slice. Readers get a pro's discipline from the age of the great hotel kitchens.
65747-johann-sebastian-bach:
Ludwig Ziemssen wrote a life of Johann Sebastian Bach, Englished by George Upton for McClurg in 1905. The book stands in a line called Life Stories for Young People, with five plates. Upton says no life can be studied by the young with more profit than Bach's. An old saying holds that genius is the highest capacity for work. Bach may have coined that saying, and his life proves it in any case.

Bach worked with vast industry in ill times and good, Upton says. On his great pieces he wrote the letters SDG, to the glory of God alone. Gounod said all music since Bach could be rebuilt from what Bach wrote, if it were lost. The book gives a noble, God-fearing cantor to young readers as a model of work.
66132-du-bose-heyward-a-critical-and-bio:
Hervey Allen, poet and fellow Charlestonian, wrote this critical and biographical sketch of Du Bose Heyward, published at New York after 1926. The bibliography at the front lists Heyward's books: Carolina Chansons, written with Allen, in 1922, then Skylines and Horizons, Porgy, and Angel.

Allen opens by mocking the old critical fashion of hunting the great American novelist with dark lanterns. The steamroller of an industrial democracy, he says, leveled the literary scene for decades. Then came the war, and a paradox: a standard American type had arrived, and was not altogether desirable. Against that background he sets Heyward, whose Porgy the New York Times praised for its lavish yet reticent prose.
66372-daffydowndilly-and-the-golden-touc:
Daffydowndilly and the Golden Touch is a small school reader in the Little Classic Series. Such booklets held thirty two pages each and sold for seven cents. They carried the most popular works of standard authors, arranged for use in schools with notes and sketches.

The series page lists readers from Aesop's Fables to Little Red Riding Hood by grade. Daffydowndilly is Hawthorne's tale of a boy and his schoolmaster. The Golden Touch retells King Midas, whose wish turned his gold and his child alike to metal. Teachers graded the set from the first school years upward. Readers get two of Hawthorne's tales for children in a penny school dress.
66476-the-palmer-method-of-business-writ:
The Palmer Method of Business Writing is a penmanship manual by Palmer, editor of The American Penman. It offers a series of self-teaching lessons in rapid, plain, unshaded, coarse-pen, muscular movement writing. Copyrights run from 1901 to 1915, as the method spread through the schools.

Palmer's explanation states the aim. The book teaches rapid, easily executed business writing. It was not written to show off any one's skill as a pen artist. It seeks to serve those who wish to become good, practical business writers. The lessons, he says, are not experiments. They have guided millions of boys and girls, young men and women, to a good business hand. The Palmer method replaced the ornate Spencerian hand with a plainer, faster script, and for decades it was how American schoolchildren learned to write.
66961-plet-a-christmas-tale-of-the-wasat:
Alfred Lambourne wrote Plet: A Christmas Tale of the Wasatch, first held under copyright in 1891 and printed by the Deseret News in 1909. Lambourne gave the book to his children, to hold the memory of hours at the place he calls our home. The Wasatch hills of Utah form the scene.

The tale opens in verse, as a frame for the story that follows. Two old bachelors, long past their prime, sip wine alone on Christmas Eve. Their talk runs back over old times, in the mood of Auld Lang Syne. Readers get a western Christmas piece that mixes verse, memory, and home ground, made by a Utah writer who knew the place at first hand.
67045-the-cholera-the-claims-of-the-poor:
Thomas Beggs wrote The Cholera: The Claims of the Poor upon the Rich, a penny tract. Charles Gilpin published it at London, at five shillings the hundred for distribution. Beggs had been secretary of the Health of Towns Association. He had also written on the causes of juvenile depravity. The Asiatic cholera first reached Britain in 1831, he writes. It spread consternation wherever it went.

The pestilence had swept the fairest parts of the earth and destroyed fifty millions of people, he says. Born among the swamps of India, it revelled in the crowded, neglected districts of great towns. It gathered its victims from the homes of the poor. The authorities were startled into exertion: whitewash, soap, and a clearing of filth followed. When the cholera passed, the exertions died with it. Beggs presses the rich to keep the lesson.
67046-virginia-of-v-m-ranch:
Grace May North wrote Virginia of V M Ranch, a girls' book copyrighted in 1924 and published at New York by Burt. It belongs to the Virginia Davis series, stories for girls of twelve to sixteen, alongside Virginia at Vine Haven, Virginia's Adventure Club, Virginia's Ranch Neighbours, and Virginia's Romance. North dedicates the book to three girls by name and to all other girls in their teens who like adventure and the desert.

The first chapter brings sixteen-year-old Virginia down a winding mountain trail. A frontispiece shows a man in a gay peaked hat taking a letter from it to hand to her. Ranch life, letters, and desert adventure drive the series.
67113-boy-a-sketch:
Marie Corelli wrote Boy, a Sketch, issued in London by Hutchinson and Company in nineteen hundred. A publisher note calls it her most important volume for some years, and the first since her serious illness, dated May thirty first, nineteen hundred. Corelli gave the book to her dearest friend Bertha Vyver, witness of all her literary work. Chapter one opens on first impressions. Boy sits in a feeding chair as the tale begins.

Our life is often influenced by the first impressions we receive of its value or worthlessness, the tale holds. Some affirm that an infant disgusted at his parents manner will stay disgusted at most events for life, it adds. If any truth exists in such a statement, Boy had cause to be disappointed early, the teller says. A bar guarded him from falling forward in his chair. Novel readers get Corelli sentimental tale of a spoiled child.
67193-the-truth-about-lynching-and-the-n:
The Truth About Lynching and the Negro in the South, by Winfield Collins, was published at New York in 1918 by the Neale Publishing Company. Collins, author of a history of the domestic slave trade of the southern states, states his plea in the subtitle: that the South be made safe for the white race. The book is a defense of lynching and segregation.

Seven chapters run from lynching before the Civil War through the war and carpet-bag rule to the present time. Later chapters treat the criminality of the Negro, segregation, Negro wealth or poverty, and the future of the Negro. Chapter one traces the word to a Virginia farmer named Lynch, who kept order in his section during the Revolutionary War. Early lynching seldom meant death. Punishments were riding on a rail, whipping, or tar and feathers.
67344-myths-of-china-and-japan-with-illu:
Donald Mackenzie wrote Myths of China and Japan, a book printed in London by the Gresham Publishing Company, with pictures in colour and in black and white after paintings and photographs. The first chapters trace the dawn of settled life in the East, far-travelled inventions, and ancient sailors and explorers. Mackenzie then turns to the wide search for wealth that drew ships across the seas.

Dragon lore fills a large share of the book, with bird and serpent myths and dragon folk tales. Later chapters visit the kingdom under the sea, the islands of the blest, and the mother goddess of China and Japan. Readers get a broad tour of East Asian myth in clear, lively prose.
67873-volcanoes-what-they-are-and-what-t:
Volcanoes: What They Are and What They Teach is a geology primer by John W Judd. Judd taught geology at the Royal School of Mines. This sixth edition came out in London in 1903. The book belongs to the International Scientific Series as volume XXXV. Ninety-six illustrations support the text.

Judd explains in his preface that the book carries out a design of Poulett Scrope. Scrope's own works on volcanoes had appeared in 1825 and 1827. They prepared readers for Lyell's doctrines of uniformity. Since then, Judd notes, inquiry had changed the questions. His frontispiece shows sections of igneous rock, from glassy to fully crystalline. The chapters teach what an eruption is, what builds a cone, and what old lava fields reveal. Dead volcanoes in France and elsewhere serve as evidence for how active ones behave.
67953-questions-at-issue-in-our-english-:
Edwin Bowen, author of Makers of American Literature, wrote Questions at Issue in Our English Speech, a set of essays printed in New York in 1909. Bowen gathered most of the pieces from journals such as the Popular Science Monthly and the Atlantic Monthly. His subject is the state of the English language in America.

The essays ask how English should be spelled, who rules its pronunciation, and what slang is and does. One takes up vulgarisms with a pedigree, words now low that were once fine. Another weighs Briticisms against Americanisms, the same ground Brander Matthews worked. Bowen writes as a teacher who loves the tongue and distrusts both pedants and careless speakers.
68059-the-man-among-the-monkeys-or-ninet:
The Man Among the Monkeys, or Ninety Days in Apeland, was printed in London by Ward, Lock, and Tyler in 1873, in Beeton Boy Own Library. Added tales treat a philosopher and his monkeys and a professor and a crocodile. Many plates are by Gustave Dore.

The hero, Polydorus Marasquin, tells how a tiger deprived him of his father, whose trade he took up. He loved animals and was skilled in stuffing them, though they played him terrible tricks. Malay pirates proved less tame than his beasts. English stations set to crush them were wasted by yellow fever and something else. Vice Admiral Campbell visits his menagerie, full of baboons and chimpanzees with passions and rivalries of their own. Boys of the day got a wild beast tale with fine art.
6818-the-arctic-prairies-a-canoe-journey:
Ernest Thompson Seton, author of Wild Animals I Have Known, canoes two thousand miles in search of caribou, north of Aylmer Lake, in The Arctic Prairies. Seton dedicates the book to Sir Wilfrid Laurier, premier of Canada. It opens with a wish. What young man would not give a year to roll back time five decades? He could live in the romantic Wild West. Buffalo would pasture by the Missouri, and traders would swap news by horse and canoe, months apart.

Seton's own voyage, by canoe through northern lakes and prairies, seeks the caribou herds in a land still wild. His prose mixes naturalist care with adventure. The Arctic Prairies is a classic, stirring account of a northern journey, full of wildlife and wonder.
68352-the-sociable-sand-witch:
Sappington wrote The Sociable Sand Witch, a book of fairy tales for children published in New York in 1923. The author had earlier written The Grateful Fairy. The title story presents a witch who lives under the sand at the edge of the ocean, where children dig in summer.

Unlike the witches of older tales, the Sand Witch rides no broomstick and climbs down no chimney. She sinks into the sand when scared and rises when she sees a chance to make a friend. Nine more tales follow, among them The Fountain of Riches, Obstinate Town, Toobad the Tailor, and The Dancing Pearl. The stories mix magic, humor, and gentle lessons in a style meant for young readers and for reading aloud.
68486-the-kobzar-of-the-ukraine-being-se:
The Kobzar of the Ukraine gathers select poems of Taras Shevchenko in English verse, translated by Alexander Jardine Hunter and printed at Winnipeg. Shevchenko, born in 1811 and dead in 1861, spent twenty four years a serf and ten years a prisoner in Siberia. Hunter, a medical missionary among Ukrainian settlers in Manitoba, learned the poems through John Bodrug and the newcomers he served.

The poems are sorted as ballads, social and political verse, poems of exile, religious poems, early poems, and satire, closing with My Testament. Between them stand short life pieces: who Shevchenko was, the Cossacks, serfdom, exile, and the return home. The pictures show Ukrainian art, drawn from the embroidery of peasant women, which Shevchenko himself likened to his verse. The book carries Ukraine's national poet to English readers on the prairies.
6857-indian-games-an-historical-research:
Andrew McFarland Davis studies Indian games as history, opening with Father Brebeuf's 1636 note on the Hurons. Three games were in vogue, Brebeuf says: cross, platter, and straw, the first two deemed supreme for health. A sick man, hot with fever and foreseeing death, might be ordered a game of cross as his only cooling remedy, or might dream he must die unless his country plays.

Davis traces those games, their rules, meanings, and rites, with scholarly care. His work shows play as medicine, ritual, and social bond. Indian Games is a learned, early study of Native play, valuable to readers of anthropology and history.
69021-women-and-economic-evolution-or-th:
Women and Economic Evolution, by Theresa Schmid McMahon, is a study of how trade changes reshaped the place of women. McMahon wrote it as her thesis for the doctor's degree at the University of Wisconsin. It ran in the university bulletin at Madison in 1912, priced at twenty-five cents.

The full title adds the effects of industrial changes upon the status of women. The work spans pages 103 to 234 of its bulletin volume, so it is a long and full study. McMahon had been a fellow in sociology at Wisconsin and taught at the University of Washington. Her theme fits a live debate of her day. Mills, shops, and offices were drawing women out of the home in growing numbers.
69145-caleb-trench:
Caleb Trench is a novel by Mary Imlay Taylor, published in Boston in 1910. Little, Brown and Company issued the book, with a frontispiece by Emlen McConnell. Taylor is named as author of The Reaping and The Impersonator on the title page. The tale opens at once in a long room with a piano.

Diana Royall pushes back the music rack and rises from her seat at the piano in the first lines. She orders the person shown in, and her companion at solitaire asks who it can be. Caleb Trench, she replies carelessly, the shopkeeper at Eshcol in the parish. Her mentor reacts as if Diana had named the chimney sweep to her salon. That clash of rank, a great lady receiving a storekeeper as an equal, sets the social tension of the novel from its first page.
69356-the-x-bar-x-boys-on-the-ranch:
X Bar X Boys on the Ranch is a western story for boys by Ferris. James Cody Ferris wrote it for Grosset and Dunlap in nineteen twenty six. Walter Rogers drew the pictures, from riders sweeping down toward a road. Sister volumes take the boys to Thunder Canyon and Whirlpool River.

Big Bison Trail and the Round Up complete the X Bar X list here. Chapters open on the road to Eagles, then a disheartening loss follows. A puncher in a checked shirt, a clue, and Rimor place build the case. Rattlers, a fall, and facing a mountain lion fill the middle chapters. The man with the scar, pursuit, and the round up close the tale.
69632-the-cynic-s-breviary-maxims-and-an:
The Cynic's Breviary gathers maxims and anecdotes from Nicolas de Chamfort. William Hutchison selected and translated the pieces. Elkin Mathews published the book in London in 1902. Chamfort was a French writer whose sharp sayings outlived his other work. The opening maxim sets the tone: Nature never told man to be rich, but she cries out for him to be independent.

Page after page gives short, pointed thoughts on life and society. A man of wit, one says, is lost without energy of character. The worst wasted day is the one on which a man has not laughed. Education needs two foundations, morality and prudence, held in balance. Public opinion is treated as a court no honest man should fear or flatter. The breviary form suits the matter: brief readings for a sharp mind.
7007-the-true-story-of-my-life-a-sketch:
Hans Christian Andersen's true story of his life appears here in Mary Howitt's translation, sent to Munroe and Company as proof sheets of an unpublished life. Howitt notes this is the author's edition, with Andersen sharing in the proceeds, and she dates her letter from London on June 29, 1847. The English translation is inscribed to Jenny Lind, in admiration of her beautiful talents and still more beautiful life.

An editor's note warns many words lack letters, since diacritic marks were missing from the digital file's character set at production. The sketch itself tells Andersen's rise from poor beginnings to fame, in his own voice as Howitt renders it. It remains a short, direct autobiography from the storyteller himself.
7021-indian-frontier-policy-an-historica:
General Sir John Adye sketches Indian frontier policy on the North West frontier, with a map, at a time of large military operations against a combination of independent tribes. He warns the present troubles are no sudden outbreak by turbulent neighbors, since their causes lie far deeper in events of bygone years. His short historical summary traces the varying phases of policy, hoping to help the public grasp its general bearings.

Adye writes for readers who must form a correct opinion of the policy to pursue in future, not merely follow the news of a campaign. The sketch weighs Britain's Eastern Empire, tribal independence, and the cost of force against patience. It is a soldier's brief for understanding before judgment on the frontier.
70258-the-last-age-of-the-church:
John Wycliffe's The Last Age of the Church was first printed at Dublin in 1840 by the University Press, from a manuscript in the University Library there. James Henthorn Todd, a fellow of Trinity College, edited it with notes. His preface takes up a live charge: that Wycliffe's merits as a reformer have been much exaggerated.

Todd will not settle that charge himself, but he shows why it is hard to settle at all. To judge Wycliffe, a reader must go to the original records, and those records have never been examined with due care. Bishop Bale's list of the writings, he notes, remains the base of all later work, with the labours of John Lewis and Baber built upon it.
70321-the-riddle-club-at-sunrise-beach:
Alice Dale Hardy wrote The Riddle Club at Sunrise Beach, published in New York in 1925 by Grosset and Dunlap, with pictures by Walter Rogers. It is one of a series about a group of young friends who form a riddle club. The title page promises how they toured to the shore, what happened on the sand, and how they solved the mystery of Rattlesnake Island.

Early chapters cover an informal club session, hard luck for a boy named Ward, and a Fourth of July outing. Hardy wrote many series books for young readers under house names and her own. This one mixes holiday fun at the beach with a light mystery to solve.
70626-the-tragedy-of-monomoy-beach:
Clarkson P Bearse wrote The Tragedy of Monomoy Beach, called the Graveyard of the Atlantic. The Goss Print on Cape Cod designed and printed it at Harwich in nineteen forty-three. Bearse was a native Cape Codder and postmaster of Harwich Port. An introduction tells his strange tie to the tale.

Bearse had served in the Coast Guard station that figured in the Monomoy disaster. An injury in the line of duty kept him from reporting that night. But for that, he would have been a victim, not the author. He kept the facts for years out of modesty. A Grange lecture hour drew the story out at last. The wreck ranks, he says, next to the Portland.
712-thomas-jefferson-a-character-sketch:
Edward S. Ellis wrote this sketch of Thomas Jefferson for a series on great Americans, with a supplementary essay by G. Mercer Adam. It traces Jefferson from birth and youth to the presidency, stressing his learning, his democratic faith, and his role in shaping the young republic. An account of the Louisiana Purchase and a set of anecdotes and dates round out the portrait.

Ellis paints Jefferson as wise, prudent, and deeply patriotic, a man who saw both the promise and the perils of the new nation. The sketch is laudatory, as such popular lives often were, yet it gathers the key facts of his career in short compass. It serves as a friendly first life of the third president for general readers.
7125-catherine-booth-a-sketch:
Colonel Mildred Duff sketches Catherine Booth, reprinted from The Warriors Library, with a preface by General Bramwell Booth. Duff penned this warm and moving portrait of his mother at Bramwell Booth's urging, hoping readers might walk the same faithful path she did. Booth answers the doubt: was not Missus Booth exceptional, gifted, and specially trained, so how can ordinary people follow her.

Let me tell you, he replies: Missus Booth walked with God. As a shy young girl lending her mother a hand at home, she kept reaching toward God. Years later, famous across many countries, praised in print, and cherished by good people everywhere, she lived exactly as before. The sketch that follows traces that steady faith.
71388-the-man-who-talked-too-much:
Roy Norton wrote a western tale about two partners known to frontiersmen as David and Goliath. One is a magnificent giant, and the other a blocky, red headed runt with shoulders too large for him. They ride the westbound Overland on the Santa Fe Railway at fifty miles an hour. The journey still seems at a snail's pace to them.

They have lately escaped a district in Mexico where they gambled their lives. Ordinary talk between them is long exhausted. Into their car comes Lucky Cochran, an eloquent talker. Cochran boasts that he owned the ranch at Placides where oil was struck. He says twenty thousand was paid him last week, with a million more in sight.
71401-ran-away-from-the-dutch:
Ran Away from the Dutch, or Borneo from South to North, is a tale of flight and travel by Perelaer, late of the Dutch service in the east isles. It was made into English by one hand and shaped by an other, and put out at London in the late eighteen eighties. Its plates show rafts, night graves, and gold hunts.

The parts open with a war report, four men fled from the ranks, and a kind doctor with deep thoughts. A chief of the land, a cholera grave rite, and shots of rifle and great gun fill the first part. Then come whispers, a feast lord took for a beast in the dark, and the long trek north through the great isle of Borneo.
71513-book-of-needs-of-the-holy-orthodox:
Book of Needs of the Holy Orthodox Church was Englished by Shann. Nutt published the translation in London in 1894. Shann gives it to Pobedonostzeff of the Holy Synod of Russia. The Slavonic original is called Trebnik, he explains. It holds what a Christian needs from the cradle to the grave. An appendix adds offices for the laying on of hands.
