Those come from a bishop's service book printed at Moscow in 1890. The Trebnik itself is taken from a Moscow edition of 1882. The preface lists what was left out. Lessons are given by their first and last words only.

Questions for penitents and rules of penance are also passed over. Some occasional prayers and Nomocanon extracts are cut. The kalendar and paschal tables stand in Shann's earlier Euchology.
71798-delight-and-power-in-speech:
Nattkemper, a teacher of public speaking, and George Wharton James made a reader for speech that the Radiant Life Press of Pasadena published in 1919. Its full title promises a new and practical method. The aim is delight and strength in silent reading, in reading aloud, and in private and public speech.

The editors say they made an almost wholly new choice of pieces. The old stock of the elocution schools is left aside. Much of the prose and verse comes from modern American writers, with a stress on the literature of the West. The West lives fast and hard, they argue, and its writing has force to match. Chapters on training the memory and on after dinner speaking stand with the pieces. The book also points readers to standard authors they can find in any good library.
71819-the-statistomat-pitch:
Chan Davis wrote this science fiction story, printed in Infinity magazine in January 1958, with pictures by Schoenherr. The pitch of the title is a sales pitch, and the blurb warns that the product looked fine but the salesman was sharp, dangerously sharp. The little salesman buzzes into Borch's hotel room exactly at ten, plainly waiting in the corridor for the second hand. He shrugs off his raincoat and hangs it up without asking.

Then come the flat brief case of charts and a large, oddly shaped suitcase holding a model of the computer. The Statistomat is a personalized machine for modern estate planning, he explains, for a man of wealth with heavy duties. Borch watches from a deep chair, eyelids drooping. Davis turns a sales call into a duel of wits.
71995-the-strange-story-of-the-dunmow-fl:
J W Robertson Scott, writing as Home Counties, wrote The Strange Story of the Dunmow Flitch, with thirty four illustrations, sold at two shillings. D Carter at Dunmow issued the book. A motto from a former Dunmow lord runs, Nothing unless you are able to swear. Plates show the earliest official records of the flitch in the chartulary of Dunmow Priory.

Chapter one is A Narrative of Nine Hundred Years. The Priory and the Rhymester follow. The top chartulary entry records the presentation of the Baron in fourteen forty five. A second entry records Thomas le Fuller in fifteen ten. Two bacon receipts show the Parsleys and Reynoldses in seventeen oh one. The Shakeshafts received theirs in seventeen fifty one, the last legitimate ceremony. Local history fans get a famed Essex custom in full.
72312-far-enough-to-touch:
Far Enough to Touch is a space tale by Stephen Bartholomew of a moonship. The story ran in Amazing Stories for December nineteen sixty two. Schelling drew the pictures for this tale of Rene Duport in space. Rene was the quiet member of the moonship crew on the home run.

He was so quiet that minutes passed before anyone saw he had jumped. The ship crew of six was the most mixed yet sent to the Moon. An American pilot, a Russian co pilot, and a Finn navigator flew her. An African engineer and an American observer complete the named crew list. Rene, a Belgian radioman, was the youngest man ever to reach the Moon.
72730-the-religion-of-plutarch:
John Oakesmith wrote The Religion of Plutarch, an essay subtitled a pagan creed of apostolic times, published in London and New York in 1902 by Longmans, Green, and Company. A Greek line from Aristotle heads the book: the lover of myth is in a sense a lover of wisdom. Oakesmith's note says the pages reprint a volume issued for private circulation a year earlier. Its title there named Plutarch's religion as expounded in his Ethics. Greek and Latin quotations are now translated or removed.

Plutarch, priest at Delphi and moral essayist, set out a gentle pagan faith in the age of the early church. Oakesmith asks what that faith held. The essay suits students of religion.
73385-woman-s-touch:
Woman Touch is a science fiction story by Evelyn E Smith, taken from Super Science Fiction for February 1957, with art by Emsh. A blurb says the orders were to leave the natives of the new planet strictly alone. But surveyors wives were women, and women do not obey orders, or leave people alone.

Captain Harnick warns four young people that the job is no universe shaking task. The planet is of no great weight, or an untried team would never have got it. Ned McComb and Danny Field answer with care, yet Harnick fears the gleam in their wives eyes more. Men could take wives along only because the Extrasolar Survey Service could not fill five year terms on remote planets without that term. A contact tale with a light hand follows.
73558-the-thin-match:
The Thin Match is a story by Henry Whitehead, billed at its head as a different story, off the beaten path. It tells of a match that fulfilled its destiny. The heroine began her life as a match along with several hundred million near kin of the great pitch pine family. Her birthplace was a match factory in a town in New Jersey, the tale says.

She had not known her own lowliness until she was shut up tightly in close quarters. Fate placed her in a box of the kind labeled as a product of Finland. Its stated average contents were sixty sticks. Life in a family of sixty, the narrator notes, differs much from being one item in a host of millions, all exactly alike. Just here the thin match's troubles began. She was different, and not by a mere slip of the machine.
74095-the-life-watch:
The Life Watch is a science fiction story by Lester del Rey, from Fantastic Universe of September nineteen fifty four. Its hero, Norden, keeps watch over the whole human race from an asteroid. He cannot trust his own dark thoughts and urges, the headnote warns. A ship with blue atomic flame drops toward his wrecked dome.

Norden's laboratory lies in ruins, and his air has run tank by tank. He barely recalls what the Aliens did when they caught his mate Hardwick. Somehow he lived, unseen, and dug out a transmitter to call for help. The ship that lands half a mile off should mean rescue and joy. Instead a senseless dread knots his mind as he watches it settle. His hands stay steady while the fear works inside him without show.
74331-the-remains-of-the-late-mrs-richar:
Selections from the journals and letters of Mrs Richard Trench appear in a volume issued in London in 1862. Her son, the Dean of Westminster, chose and edited the papers after her death. In his preface he admits that printing a private woman's writing needs defense, and lets the work speak for itself.

Inside, letters and journal pieces run in date order, tied by short notes on the life around them. The editor warns that much of the early journal writing has been lost or has gone astray. What survives shows a keen, devout mind at work on books, faith, family, and events of her day. Readers get an intimate record of a well-read English matron whose name was made by her son's care, not by print in her lifetime.
74738-fairview-boys-on-a-ranch:
Fairview Boys on a Ranch, or riding with the cowboys, is a boys' adventure by Frederick Gordon. Gordon had written three Fairview Boys books before, and they are named on the title page. The contents open with great news. In a bad fix and getting ready follow in quick order. Off for the ranch is the fourth chapter's errand.

A boy named Sammy scents a mystery, and the troop rides hot on the trail. Not so bad as it looked, a new world, and an exciting chase fill the middle heads. Keeping under cover, a cave by the river, and an ugly customer raise the stakes. In great danger and out in the storm lead to a jolly party at the end. The first chapter opens with a shout: boys, this is the best ever, a chance to go out on a ranch and play cowboys.
7496-jack-ranger-s-western-trip-or-from-:
Clarence Young's Jack Ranger series begins at Washington Hall, the boarding school of Dr. Henry Mead on Rudmore Lake, sometimes called Lakeside Academy. The crowd of boys starts forth on mischief bent. The early chapters are schoolboy comedy: fun at Washington Hall, Jack in trouble, a threatening letter, a lesson in chemistry, and a burglary scare foiled by quick wits.

Then comes Nat's invitation, and ho for the West. The second half moves to ranch and range: an old acquaintance, a professor's trick, shooting an oil well, a wild steer, an old stockman, and a thief in the night. Jack hears news of his father as the trail leads toward finding Orion Tevis. The book is a sturdy boys' adventure, half school story and half western.
75565-the-man-with-a-grouch:
H De Vere Stacpoole spins a South Seas tale about a trader who wants to spend Christmas in England. It opens on the island of Levua, with its old forest and copra trade.

Flexner runs the station there for Lombard, Drex and Company of San Francisco, and the trade is going wrong though prices rule high and the trees bear well. Flexner does not drink to excess and seems straight and honest, so old Reuben Lombard sails out himself to find the fault. Reuben has spent a month before on such errands, soaking up the place and its people, who range from the quietly drunk to the thriving. Stacpoole knew the Pacific trade at first hand, and the tale rests on that grit: copra, sandalwood gone, pineapples on trial, and one man's grouch at the centre.
75602-an-historical-sketch-of-the-first-:
A short church history read before the New Brunswick Eastern Association in July 1893. The association asked for its publication. The story begins in May 1763. Six German families then left Pennsylvania for a northern climate. Their sloop reached the place now called Hillsboro on the first of July. The Steeves family landed there and stayed.

Hendrick Steeves, his wife Rachel, and their seven sons built a log house. They cleared land and planted a few turnips. Fishing and hunting carried them toward winter. The promised sloop never returned the next spring. Provisions ran out with no source of more. From that hard planting, the sketch traces the settlers and the Baptist church that grew among them at Hillsboro.
75653-the-treasure-on-the-beach:
The Treasure on the Beach is a story printed in 1906 for the passenger department of the Seaboard Air Line Railway. Street and Finney wrote it, and the railway gave it out to travellers from Portsmouth, Virginia. Its hero tells the tale himself. His great uncle Abner was always a queer old codger, he begins, a half cracked fellow living alone in a shack on a sandy key off Florida.

The narrator had money enough and thought little of the old man, who seemed to have few goods. Then, one morning when he felt beastly at breakfast, a large legal looking envelope came beside his plate. Uncle Abner had died at Lone Palm Key that December. His letter, sent a month after his death by his lawyers, sets the hunt in motion. The tale is a railway giveaway with a Florida treasure plot, made to charm passengers south.
75895-the-great-beach:
The Great Beach, by John Hay, was published by Doubleday in 1963, with illustrations by David Grose. The book is dedicated to Conrad and Mary Aiken and to Henry and Gertrude Kittredge. Hay writes of the long outer beach of Cape Cod, the shore he had already treated in Nature's Year. Chapters view it from a distance, as an unimagined frontier, and as dune country.

Hay blends natural history with human history. He quotes the Pilgrims' bleak first sight of the coast, then turns to the resources of the sea, barren grounds, deer week, and the question of who owns the beach. His theme is impermanence: the shore is a landscape in motion. The book completes his Cape Cod writings with a wider, deeper meditation.
75898-jack-and-his-ostrich:
Eleanor Stredder wrote Jack and His Ostrich, an African story for young readers, printed by Nelson in 1900. Jack Treby is an English boy born in South Africa who has never seen England. He lives with his father on a lonely farm on the wide, hot veldt.

Their nearest neighbor is twenty miles away, and farm hands come and go. Chapters promise African neighbors, a black antelope, and Jack lost on the veldt. Jack falls ill with fever, writes to his grandfather, and makes friends in the district. The title points to his bond with an ostrich. Stredder writes warmly about farm work, wild animals, and a boy growing up far from home.
76604-the-long-march:
William Styron wrote The Long March, a novella printed in New York with rights held in 1952, set down between his first novel and his later famed books. One noon in a blaze of Carolina summer, eight dead boys lie strewn among poison ivy and pine needles, killed in a training blast. Lieutenant Culver stands by the ambulance in the shade and takes in the waste of them.

A forced march in the heat is ordered on the shattered company, and the tale weighs duty, blame, and the men who must give and take such orders. Styron writes of Marines with a poet's eye and a soldier's knowledge. Readers get a short, hard classic.
76654-the-new-science-of-space-speech:
Gaddis wrote this report on man's coming problem: how to talk with minds not human. A giant ear is rising at Sugar Grove, West Virginia, a six hundred foot radio telescope meant to catch whispers from stars sixty to eighty light years away. It will cost a hundred million dollars.

In the Virgin Islands, a scientist talks with a dolphin, and the dolphin answers in imitation. Scholars elsewhere build word lists and math charts for a language any creature could learn. A space agency chief admits we have not yet heard any message aimed at Earth. The problem splits in two: talking face to face on Mars, and trading ideas by radio across the void. Gaddis writes as a reporter of wonders, certain the call may come tomorrow.
77769-freedom-of-speech:
Zechariah Chafee, a professor of law at Harvard, wrote Freedom of Speech, printed in New York in 1920. The book grew out of the trials and fears of the First World War, when the United States jailed men for words against the war. Chafee dedicated it to Judge Learned Hand, who had held for free speech in the midst of that turmoil.

Chafee sorts out what the law may punish: words that urge violence stand apart from words that merely anger the crowd. He takes up radical meetings, the red flag, and the new laws against dissent, and argues that a free state must give the mind sea room. The book became a founding text of modern free-speech law.
7819-an-enquiry-into-an-origin-of-honour:
Bernard Mandeville, author of The Fable of the Bees, asks in An Enquiry into the Origin of Honour whether honor and virtue come from God or from human invention. His preface defends an earlier essay on moral virtue against charges of crime, and asks readers to hear his case with patience.

Mandeville holds that even heathen virtue was made by men, not heaven. Through dialogues on morals, manners, and war, he probes how pride, praise, and faith shape soldiers and citizens. It is a sharp, early work of moral philosophy, still keen on how praise steers conduct.
78389-moloch:
Beulah Marie Dix wrote Moloch, a play about war in a prologue, three acts, and an epilogue, issued by Knopf in New York in 1916. It stands as the second of the Borzoi Plays, beside works by Russian and German hands. The printed form was made for readers, and stage use calls for the author's leave and a fee.

The cast list shows one family at the core: a man, his wife, his son Roland, his mother, sister, and brother, plus kin and friends. Round them stand officers and troops of two lands at war. The name Moloch, an old god fed with human lives, tells the theme: war eats the young of both sides with the same hunger.
79064-those-about-trench:
Those About Trench is a novel by Edwin Herbert Lewis, printed by Macmillan in New York in 1916 and given to George Noble Carman after twenty years. Lewis opens with a prologue in which Trench fishes above Dixon mill in a wild of granite and cedar. The true start, he says, is a leaf of history.

He lists June the twenty eighth across the ages, from the death of Alexander of Macedon to the fall of Serbia at Kosovo. He runs the date through later years of kings, shows, and world strain. On that date in 1911, lady slipper flowers burst into bloom near home. Lewis binds one small place to the great sweep of time. Readers get a thoughtful tale where past and a quiet valley meet.
79120-figures-of-speech:
Tuttle wrote Figures of Speech as a string of comic letters to a friend named Hank. The narrator, Dobie Dalton, writes in tall western slang, mangling fine words as he goes, which is the joke of the title. His great news is a son and heir, about a month old, a humdinger with his father's mouth and nose. Dobie wanted to name the boy Hank, after his old friend.

That plan starts the fight. His wife Emmeline points out that Hank Peck is no friend of his at all, just a dish faced puncher, and a poor namesake. Uncle Gabe walks out on the argument, goat well and truly got. Threats of branding the child like a calf and naming him after a hated family round out the row. Tuttle's humour runs on voice: the letter writer hangs himself with every proud, wrong word.
8198-the-fourth-watch:
H. A. Cody, author of The Frontiersman and The Long Patrol, wrote The Fourth Watch for messengers, watchmen. And stewards of the Lord who have toiled through life's long night and now, in their fourth and last watch, behold a new life breaking. Dedicated by one still in the second watch, the novel's chapters move from an awakening and a vision, through Glendow Rectory. The warder of the night, the breath of slander, and an auction, to the Farringtons, the golden key, and guarding the flock.

Cody, a Canadian clergyman-novelist, writes a story of ministry, village life, and faith under trial. The night-watch image gives the book its structure and its comfort: darkness is long, but dawn comes. For readers of religious fiction, it is a earnest, old-fashioned novel of pastoral life and perseverance.
8425-caesar-a-sketch:
James Anthony Froude calls this work a sketch because, as his preface says, the materials do not exist for a portrait of Julius Caesar at once authentic and complete. The original authorities are thin, and Froude works from what survives to outline Caesar's life, character, and times, quoting Shakespeare's Henry V as his apology for daring so great an object.

Froude, the Victorian historian, writes with narrative force, and his Caesar is a statesman of genius in a republic falling apart. Readers get a readable, opinionated life, more sketch than scholarly biography, and a view of how Victorians judged Rome's fall. It pairs well with fuller modern lives, as a period portrait.
8433-the-vagabond-and-other-poems-from-p:
R. C. Lehmann gathers poems that first appeared in Punch, the London humorous weekly, with all but two pieces drawn from its pages. Published in 1918 by John Lane, the volume shows Lehmann, author of Anni Fugaces and Light and Shade, in his lightest vein: verses for a magazine audience, urbane, witty, and topical.

Punch verse was meant to amuse educated readers over breakfast, and Lehmann's pieces do that work with polish. The vagabond of the title sets the tone, a wanderer through modern life with a smile. Readers of light verse will find a period piece, charming and slight, and a reminder of how widely Punch once set the tone of English humor.
8574-racketty-packetty-house-as-told-by-:
Frances Hodgson Burnett tells this children's story through Queen Crosspatch, ruler of the doll world, who insists dolls get up to plenty when no one is watching. When backs are turned, they dance, sing, play the piano, and enjoy themselves; the moment someone looks, they freeze. The tale contrasts two doll families: one tidy and well liked, the other noisy and neglected.

Harrison Cady's pictures match the playful tone, and the story stays close to a child's logic about toys having secret lives. Burnett, already famous for Little Lord Fauntleroy, keeps the sentences simple and the humour gentle. Young readers get a short, funny fable about fairness and manners, while older readers can enjoy it as a small classic of nursery storytelling.
9454-orchesography-or-the-art-of-dancing:
John Weaver, a London dancing master, published Orchesography in 1706, a guide to the art of dance notation. It translates the French system of Monsieur Feuillet into English, with signs and figures for steps. Weaver claims any dancer who knows the craft can learn new dances from the page alone. The book also gives rules for the motions of the arms.

Tables set out all steps used in dancing, so a reader can read a dance as one reads music. The text notes that the work leans on diagrams, which is why this file holds no full text version. A reader gets a rare window on Baroque dance craft, and on how an age first tried to write motion down in print.
9479-the-boy-life-of-napoleon-afterwards:
Madame Eugénie Foa, a beloved French writer for children, wrote the boy life of Napoleon, here adapted for American boys and girls in 1895. Foa, famed for forty years in French homes, told history tales with pure tone and high morals. This book follows Napoleon from boyhood toward the throne he would one day seize. Vesper L. George drew the pictures.

Chapters trace the young Corsican's school days, pride, study, and early trials, with drama fit for young readers. Foa stresses truth to history as well as lively action. A reader gets a warm, old-style life of a great captain's youth, and a glimpse of how French children once learned their hero's tale.
9796-the-master-detective-being-some-fur:
Percy James Brebner wrote The Master Detective in 1916, further cases of Christopher Quarles, his consulting sleuth. Contents list the strange case of Sir Grenville Rusholm, the kidnapping of Eva Wilkison, and the Delverton affair. A house in Manleigh Road, a stolen aeroplane model, and a contessa's pearls follow. The crime in a yellow taxi and a jeweled chalice add color.

Quarles opens with Rusholm dead, blinds down, and obituaries in every paper. Each case tests his quiet reason against bold crime. A reader gets a classic Edwardian detective set, brisk and ingenious, with a sleuth of the Holmes school.
9957-the-personal-touch:
J. Wilbur Chapman, an American evangelist, wrote this book on personal Christian work, opening with his own testimony. He argues that faith spreads best not by crowds alone but by one person speaking plainly to another, and he states the general principle behind that claim.

Chapters offer a polished shaft, starting right, winning the young, and winning and holding converts, with practical illustrations and a final word on conversion as a miracle. Chapman's tone is direct and pastoral. Readers interested in evangelism a century ago will find its methods and motives set out clearly.
a-history-of-the-moravian-church:
J. E. Hutton writes a full history of the Moravian Church in this second edition, revised and enlarged, dated 1909 on its title page. Book one, The Bohemian Brethren, runs from 1457 to 1673 and opens with the rising storm in Bohemia and the burning of Hus in 1415. Persecuted brethren organize at Kunwald under Gregory the Patriarch.

Later books follow Luke of Prague, John Augusta's sufferings, the Brethren in Poland and exile, then Count Zinzendorf, the founding of Herrnhut, and the church's worldwide missions. Hutton writes as a sympathetic insider with a historian's care for dates and documents. The book remains a standard one-volume account of a small church with a vast missionary reach.
a-statement-on-the-future-of-this-church: John Haynes Holmes, minister of the Church of the Messiah in New York, states the future of his church in this sermon pamphlet, priced at five cents. He tells his people that on Sunday, November 24, he was invited by unanimous vote of All Souls Church, Chicago. The invitation was to carry on the work laid down by their late pastor, Jenkin Lloyd Jones. The statement weighs that call against his present charge, under a free platform where the preacher alone answers for his words.
an-enquiry-into-an-origin-of-honour-and-: Bernard Mandeville enquires into the origin of honour and the usefulness of Christianity in war. The preface and argument weigh how honour is made, and what faith can and cannot do for soldiers. Mandeville's sharp, sceptical prose challenges easy pieties about war and virtue. His dry wit keeps the hard points in view.
arcadian-adventures-with-the-idle-rich:
Stephen Leacock's Arcadian Adventures with the Idle Rich, his 1914 satire of a North American city's millionaires, opens at the Mausoleum Club on Plutoria Avenue. Infants in perambulators own distilleries and railway mergers while their fathers lunch downtown. The eight linked sketches follow Mr. Lucullus Fyshe's little dinner and the wizardry of finance that rules the avenue. Mrs. Rasselyer-Brown's oriental society and Mr. Tomlinson's arrested philanthropy come next in the contents.

Inside, the rival churches of St. Asaph and St. Osoph compete like department stores for rich souls. The Reverend Uttermust Dumfarthing ministers to congregations who prefer their gospel comfortable. A great fight for clean government ends, as Leacock's fights do, with the reformers absorbed by the machine. Readers get the Canadian humorist at his most surgical: a city where money has replaced every other faith, described in prose so smooth the victims would enjoy it.
aubin-histoire-diables-loudun-1694-frenc:
Nicolas Aubin published his Histoire des Diables de Loudun in French in 1694. Loudun was the town in France where Ursuline nuns claimed to be possessed in the 1630s. Aubin built his account from the first records of the case, close to sixty years after the events.

At the center stands Urbain Grandier, the priest accused of causing the possessions by sorcery. Grandier was tried and put to death in 1634, and Aubin follows that grim story step by step. The book became the base account of the most famous possession case of its century. Later writers on Loudun still lean on it.
back-to-methuselah-a-metabiological-pent:
Bernard Shaw published this cycle of five plays with a long preface in 1921, calling it a metabiological pentateuch. The preface, The Infidel Half Century, argues that Darwinism has left mankind without a saving faith. Shaw attacks the political inadequacy of the human animal, the flimsiness of civilisation, and technical education's diabolical efficiency, and answers with creative evolution and voluntary longevity.

Five linked plays then run from the Garden of Eden to a far future of long-lived ancients. Shaw holds that acquired habits can be inherited, Lamarck-fashion, and that longer lives would give wisdom time to grow up. A sample speech tots up an elixir ration for forty million people, five ounces a day, and loses the arithmetic mid-sentence. Doctrine and comedy share every page.
bavent-histoire-madeleine-bavent-1652-fr:
Madeleine Bavent was a nun at Louviers, in France, during the possessions said to grip her convent from 1642 to 1647. Her own story, told in the first person, was printed in French in 1652. The text here follows the 1878 reprint, which adds a life of Bavent and extra papers.

Bavent tells what she said she saw, feared, and confessed while priests and judges pressed the case. The added papers include her arrest and the formal record of her words. Few possession cases left so direct a voice from the accused woman herself. That closeness makes the book a key source on Louviers.
bayard-the-good-knight-without-fear-and-:
Christopher Hare retells the life of Pierre Terrail, the Chevalier Bayard, in this illustrated volume with coloured plates by Herbert Cole. Its source is the old loyal servant's history, the very joyful and delightful life of the good knight without fear and without reproach. Bayard was born at his family's castle in Dauphiné about 1474, under Louis XI, of a race whose privilege was shedding blood for France.

Plates mark the career: a fine exhibition of horsemanship, the battle of Fornovo, Bayard defending a bridge alone, the page presenting his prisoner, and his presentation to Henry VIII. A middle episode shows Venetians stealing Padua by hiding behind hay waggons from the second mowing, opening the gates at a signal. Hare writes chivalry for young readers, with the death of Bayard as its crown.
betty-gordon-at-boarding-school-or-the-t:
Alice B. Emerson wrote this girls' series volume in 1921, sending Betty Gordon from Bramble Farm to Shadyside School. New plans open the tale: Betty surprises Bob, says more good-byes, and meets Norma and Libbie at school. Contents promise a lost treasure, a mysterious four, the second degree, and the treasure of Indian Chasm itself as the final prize.

School discipline marks the hours. Girls who are good may go twice a month to Edentown, chaperoned, for shopping and moving pictures. Others are sentenced within bounds on the spacious grounds for sins of omission and commission. Bobby Littell, impulsive and heedless, is usually among the sentenced. Emerson — a Stratemeyer house name, also behind Ruth Fielding — writes boarding-school life as a round of pranks, secrets, and loyalty tests.
britannica-1911-abeken-heinrich:
Heinrich Abeken receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abeken, a German theologian and Prussian official born at Berlin in 1809, served as chaplain to the Prussian embassy in Rome from 1834. A Jerusalem mission for Frederick William the Fourth took him to England in 1841.

Foreign ministry work followed from 1848, with a privy councillor's rank by 1853. Bismarck used his pen for official despatches, and King William kept him at headquarters through the campaigns of 1866 and 1870. His widow's life of him prints letters from those headquarters. One anonymous book, Babylon und Jerusalem of 1851, lashed the Countess von Hahn-Hahn's views. Quiet service at the center of Prussian power fills the record.
britannica-1911-abel-karl-friedrich:
Karl Friedrich Abel receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abel, a German musician born at Köthen in 1725, was the great viola da gamba player of his day. Bach taught him at Leipzig, and Hasse's Dresden band held him ten years.

London took him in 1759 as chamber musician to Queen Charlotte. A concert of his own works showed off many instruments, the new pentachord among them. Johann Christian Bach's arrival in 1762 ripened into the famed Bach and Abel concerts from 1764. Fashion flocked to them under Mrs Cornelys, and Haydn's works first sounded in England there. Hard drinking hastened his end in 1787, the entry states. Gainsborough painted him twice.
britannica-1911-abimelech:
Abimelech receives a Bible entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, signed by Stanley Arthur Cook. The name, Hebrew for father of the king, covers two men. A king of Gerar dealt with Abraham and Isaac in Genesis, each time over a wife passed off as a sister.

Gideon's son by a Shechemite concubine takes the longer tale. Temple gold hired his band, and seventy brothers died at Ophrah, Jotham alone escaping to curse Shechem from Gerizim with his fable of the trees. Revolt under Gaal, Shechem destroyed, and a millstone from Thebez's wall ended him; his armour-bearer finished the blow to spare him a woman's kill. Cook reads the reign as Israel's first monarchy attempt, more petty-state rivalry than kingship.
britannica-1911-abyssinian-church:
Abyssinian Church covers the Christian church of Ethiopia, which tradition says adopted Christianity in the fourth century. About 330, Frumentius was made first bishop by Athanasius, patriarch of Alexandria. From then on the Metropolitan, or Abuna, was always appointed from Egypt and was always a foreigner. The Abyssinians rejected the council of Chalcedon and remained monophysites, holding one nature in Christ.

Portuguese missions in the sixteenth century pulled the church toward Rome, and Jesuit rule broke the Egyptian link for over a century. Church buildings get close attention: square churches in Tigre and circular ones in Amhara and Shoa, each with a central sanctuary, an outer court, and an altar slab called a tabut.
britannica-1911-adams-john-couch:
John Couch Adams (1819-1892) was a British astronomer. He was born at Laneast in Cornwall in June 1819. His father was a tenant farmer there. A village school and a Devonport school educated him. Mathematical promise sent him to Cambridge in 1839. He graduated as senior wrangler in 1843. He also took the first Smith's prize. Uranus had already caught his attention then. Its motion showed unexplained irregularities, he read.

Calculation found a new planet. Adams deduced an unseen body's mass and orbit. He gave Challis his solution in September 1845. Airy at Greenwich queried one point later. Adams, deeming it unessential, never replied. Leverrier reached the same planet independently in France. Neptune's discovery credit was shared uneasily between nations. Adams later directed the Cambridge Observatory for years.
britannica-1911-agricola-johann-friedric:
Johann Friedrich Agricola (1720-1774) was a German musician. He was born at Dobitschen in Saxe-Altenburg in 1720. Law at Leipzig was his ostensible study. Music under Johann Sebastian Bach claimed him there too. In 1741 he went to Berlin for composition study. Skilful organ playing won him general recognition. A comic opera at Potsdam pleased Frederick the Great. In 1751 the king made him court composer.

Direction of the royal orchestra followed. Graun's death in 1759 opened that post to him. Operas, instrumental pieces, and church music flowed from him. Reputation rests chiefly on his writings, though. Theoretical and critical works on music carry his name. He wrote them as Flavio Anicio Olibrio. That pseudonym disguised a court servant's criticism.
britannica-1911-aldegrever-heinrich:
Paintings by Heinrich Aldegrever (1502–1558) are so scarce that only one can be accepted without dispute: his 1551 portrait of Engelbert Therlaen, held at Berlin. Five pictures in galleries on the continent bear his name, but doubts hang over several. Born at Paderborn, the German artist settled young at Soest and died there.

Engraving, not painting, made his name. Most plates came from his own designs, worked in fine, close detail, though critics found the style somewhat hard. That skill put him at the front of the Little Masters, Germany's makers of small engraved plates. His closeness to Dürer's manner earned him the name Albert of Westphalia, and the British Museum keeps a strong group of his prints.
britannica-1911-alexius-mikhailovich:
Alexius Mikhailovich, tsar of Muscovy, who lived from 1629 to 1676, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Son of Tsar Michael Romanov, he was born in March 1629 and was still a youth when his father died in 1645. He was placed under Boris Morozov, a shrewd guardian open to Western ideas. Morozov kept a peaceful foreign policy and an equitable rule at home.

Trouble came through marriage. Morozov married the young tsar to Maria Miloslavskaya in 1648 and took her sister himself ten days later. The Miloslavski family's extortions made them detested, and Moscow rose against them that May, forcing the tsar to dismiss them and their patron. War with Poland followed over Ukraine and Lithuania, bringing Alexius large demands on Polish land. When tsar and Sweden quarrelled over the spoils, Alexius declared war on Sweden in 1656. Great things were expected, but multitudes were lost in vain before Riga.
britannica-1911-alexius-petrovich:
Alexius Petrovich (1690–1718), the Russian tsarevich, was the one son of Peter I who lived, born in February 1690 to Eudoxia Lopukhina. Peter had wed Eudoxia at his mother's command and soon found her company dull past bearing. A second son lived only briefly in 1691, and after that Peter all but left her.

The boy Alexius drew no notice from his father until he was nine. A son who loved his mother could feel small warmth for the man who plagued her most. Teachers such as the dry pedant Vyazemsky schooled him, and once his mother had been sent to a convent he passed into other hands. Peter grew to fear his heir would tear down the work of his life. Thoughts of pushing Alexius aside took hold, though in 1715 the tsar made one last try to win him back.
britannica-1911-antioch:
Antioch was the most famed of a host of towns that bore that name in the Greek age. It stood on the left bank of the Orontes, a short way from the sea and its port. Seleucus founded it as a Greek town in three hundred before Christ. It was set to match the great port of Egypt as chief town of the near east.

Its place made it the true hub of Syria for a west power. Roads from the sea, from the hills, and from the great east stream all met in its plain. One road south by the stream gorge was the sole way on. The tale of its first lay out fills the text.
britannica-1911-apraksin-thedor-matvyeev:
Thedor Matvyeevich Apraksin, a Russian soldier who lived from 1671 to 1728, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He began as a page to Tsar Theodore and then served the young Peter in the same post. That boyhood bond grew into a lifelong friendship. At age twenty one he became governor of Archangel.

At Archangel Apraksin built ships that could weather storms, to the tsars delight. He won his colonel rank at the siege of Azov in 1696. In 1700 he took charge of the admiralty and built fleets and forts while Peter fought Sweden. He led the defence of the new capital in 1708 and crushed the Swedes there. From 1710 he led descents on Sweden by sea that forced a peace. Russia gained the best of Swedens Baltic lands by that peace. He was made senator and admiral general for his service.
britannica-1911-arakcheev-aleksyei-andre:
Aleksei Arakcheev was a Russian officer who rebuilt his country's artillery arm. The text as hosted opens mid-career. In the first years of Alexander's reign he was out of favour. In April 1803 the tsar called him back to St Petersburg. He took the post of inspector-general of the artillery. His thorough overhaul of the whole arm won wide praise. Critics of the time call his years in charge its golden age.

His reforms split the artillery into separate, self-contained units. He also formed artillery brigades for the field. A school committee for the arm dates from 1808. An artillery journal began in those years as well. At Austerlitz he saw his reforms at work in a real battle. Scandals in the supply services after the peace of Tilsit raised him still higher. In 1808 he became war minister too. The war with Sweden in 1809 then tested his work.
britannica-1911-ashby-de-la-zouch:
Ashby de la Zouch, a market town in Leicestershire, England, is described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It stands north west of London on a branch rail line. In nineteen oh one its urban district had over four thousand folk. Wide coal mines lie in the district round it.

The church of Saint Helen is a fine late Gothic building, restored in eighteen eighty. It holds monuments of the Huntingdon family and an old finger pillory for bad conduct in church. Baths built in eighteen twenty six draw guests for their salt waters. The springs lie three miles west, at Moira. A canal runs south from Moira to join another canal. South of the town stand the large remains of Ashby Castle.
britannica-1911-auch:
Auch is the subject of a city entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is a city of south western France, capital of the department of Gers, west of Toulouse. The entry gives its population in nineteen hundred six. The city is built on the summit and sides of a hill above the Gers river.

An upper and a lower quarter are joined in places by flights of steps. The streets are in general steep and narrow, the entry says. A handsome promenade in the upper town was laid out in the eighteen hundreds. Three bridges cross the river to a suburb on the far bank. The entry then turns to its oldest quarters.
britannica-1911-auction-pitch:
Auction Pitch is the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a card game. The game is a well liked form of All Fours. Its name comes from one clear rule of play. The first card played, or pitched, sets the trump suit. The eldest hand may pitch that card. He may also sell the right to the highest bidder.

A full pack is used, and cards rank from ace down to two. Four to seven people may play, and each gets six cards. Players hold white counters and lose one for set feats. Points come from the highest trump played and the lowest trump dealt. The Jack of trumps and the most points also count. The aim is to shed all the white counters first.
britannica-1911-aurich: Aurich, a town of Germany in the Prussian province of Hanover, is described in this short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. Chief town of East Friesland, it stands on the Ems-Jade canal eighteen miles from Emden. Its people numbered 6,013 in 1900. It lies in a sandy but fertile plain, ringed by promenades. It has a palace of the former counts, three churches, a gymnasium, and four libraries. Close by is the Upstallsboom, where Frisian coast lands met at Whitsuntide.
britannica-1911-awe-loch:
Awe, Loch, is the longest freshwater lake in Scotland, lying in mid-Argyllshire 116 feet above the sea with an area of nearly sixteen square miles. It runs fully twenty-three miles from Kilchurn Castle to Ford, bending at its upper end into a crescent shape.

The two ends differ wholly: majestic scenery at the upper end, tame pastoral shores below. Among its many islands, Inishail holds ruins of a church and convent suppressed at the Reformation. Kilchurn Castle's imposing ruins, on an islet at the north-eastern end, draw landscape painters. The river Awe, leaving the loch's north-western horn, gives excellent trout and salmon fishing, and Dalmally village nearby draws summer visitors.
britannica-1911-bacharach:
Bacharach is a German town in the Prussian Rhine Province, set romantically on the Rhine's left bank above Coblenz on the Mainz railway, with about 2,000 people. A basilica church from the early 13th century and the ruins of a Gothic church mark its old core.

Above the town crowns the ruined castle of Stahleck, where Henry, eldest son of Henry the Lion, married Agnes of Hohenstaufen shortly before 1195, briefly reconciling the Welf and Hohenstaufen houses. Two more ruined castles, Fürstenberg and Stahlberg, belonged with it to the counts palatine. Bacharach wines were once held in the highest esteem, and the town remains a chief market of the Rhenish wine trade.
britannica-1911-bahraich:
Bahraich is a town and district of British India in the Fyzabad division of the United Provinces, the town standing on the river Sarju with 27,304 people in 1901. Since the railway opened, the place has begun to flourish, the entry reports.

The town holds Oudh's most popular pilgrimage spot, the tomb of Masaud, a champion of Islam killed by Rajput forces in 1033, visited by Muslims and Hindus alike. The district spreads over 2,647 square miles in three tracts: a raised plateau from the Himalaya foothills, the Gogra river plain, and the Rapti basin. Purely agricultural, with large estates held by taluqdars and trade in Nepal timber, it watered its fields only from wells, tanks, and rivers.
britannica-1911-bahrdt-karl-friedrich:
Bahrdt, Karl Friedrich (1741-1792), was a German theologian and adventurer born at Bischofswerda, son of a pastor later a Leipzig professor. Grossly neglected in training, he mixed pranks, even an attempt to raise spirits with a Faust spell book, with solid talent and perfect early orthodoxy.

Posts came fast: lecturer at Leipzig at twenty, professor at twenty-five, preaching with real eloquence. Scandal in his private life cost him that chair; Erfurt and inn-keeping followed, then a theology chair at Giessen. There his public view of religion changed, and his modernized New Testament version of 1773-1775, remembered through Goethe's scorn for its bad taste, got him expelled again. The entry follows a brilliant, coarse, restless man through repeated falls.
britannica-1911-balakirev-mili-alexeivic:
Balakirev, Mili Alexeivich (1836- ), was a Russian composer. Nijni-Novgorod was his birthplace in 1836. As a boy he lived with Oulibichev. That man wrote a Life of Mozart. He kept a private band too. Balakirev gained valuable musical schooling there.

At eighteen Balakirev went to St Petersburg. A mathematics course lay behind him. National ardour filled the young man. He made Glinka's acquaintance there. César Cui gathered around him with others. The Free School of Music opened in 1862. Balakirev's zeal drove that school's work. Modern Russian music owes it much. In 1869 he directed the imperial chapel. He also conducted the Imperial Musical Society. His own works are few in number. Songs and folk-song collections dominate them. A symphony and two symphonic poems stand out. Borodin and Rimsky-Korsakov were his disciples.
britannica-1911-baratynski-jewgenij-abra:
Jewgenij Abramovich Baratynski (1800-1844) was a Russian poet, recorded in a brief 1911 Britannica article. He was educated at the royal school at St Petersburg and then entered the army.

He served for eight years in Finland, where he composed his first poem, Eda. Through the help of friends he gained the tsar's leave to quit the army, and settled near Moscow in 1827. There he completed his chief work, The Gipsy, a poem in the style of Pushkin. He died in 1844 at Naples, where he had gone for the milder climate. A collected edition of his poems came out at St Petersburg in two volumes in 1835, with later editions at Moscow and Kazan.
britannica-1911-barth-heinrich:
Heinrich Barth (1821–1865), a German explorer born in Hamburg, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. Educated at Berlin University, where he graduated in 1844, he had already travelled in Italy and Sicily and planned wider Mediterranean journeys. After studying Arabic in London, he set out in 1845 and crossed North Africa. He visited ancient sites in Barbary and Cyrenaica, ascended the Nile, and was wounded by robbers in Egypt before reaching Berlin in 1847.

Africa made Barth's reputation. In 1850 he joined Richardson and Overweg on a British-backed mission to open trade with the Sudan states. Both companions died, leaving Barth to finish alone. By 1855 he had crossed the Sahara, reached Lake Chad, Bornu, Kano, Sokoto, and Timbuktu, and studied the lands closely. His five-volume Travels and Discoveries in North and Central Africa is praised as a standard authority.
britannica-1911-baruch:
Baruch, a Hebrew name meaning “blessed,” belongs in the Old Testament to Jeremiah's secretary and spokesman. The long 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article under this name covers the writings attached to him. First comes the Book of Baruch, a deuterocanonical book placed in the Greek Bible between Jeremiah and Lamentations. The entry stresses that its parts fit together so badly that more than one author must have written them.

Contents and doubts fill most of the article. The book holds a historical preface and two confessions of sin, one from the remnant in Jerusalem and one from the exiles in Babylon. It also praises wisdom, meaning the Law, as Israel's glory. Dates for the parts are called quite uncertain. A second large section treats the Apocalypse of Baruch, a lost work recovered from a Syriac manuscript found at Milan by Ceriani and published in the nineteenth century.
britannica-1911-beach:
Beach is a word of unknown origin, perhaps an old dialect term for shingle, the loose stones waves throw up. It can mean the material itself, the long ridge it forms, or the ground between high and low water. Storms can push that ground well above the usual tide line.

What a beach is made of depends on the rocks inshore, the currents and the force of the waves. On the Isle of Wight, chalk cliffs break down into flint shingle that drifts east and grinds finer toward Ventnor. Sandy stretches follow where greensand cliffs feed smooth sand instead, and the entry traces how undertow and tides keep sorting the shore.
britannica-1911-becker-heinrich:
Heinrich Becker is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Becker was a German actor, born at Berlin in 1770. His real name was Blumenthal. While still young he won a post at the court theatre at Weimar.

Weimar was then under the care of the poet Goethe. Goethe saw Becker's talent and made him stage-manager. He trusted him with leading roles in his own plays and asked his advice on staging. For years Becker was the favourite of the Weimar stage. He was at his best in comedy, yet he shone in grave parts too. The entry names his Vansen in Egmont and his roles in Schiller's plays. In 1809 he left Weimar, played at Hamburg and Breslau, and took to a wandering life. The article preserves the fame of an actor formed by Germany's greatest poet.
britannica-1911-beech:
Beech is a tree entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a well known tree of woods in the north temperate zone. The tree stands in the same plant order as the oak and chestnut. Its name in old tongues means both a book and the tree itself.

The entry links that odd double sense to carved boards of old times. Rune signs were cut on thin boards of beech wood in the north. Its nuts, once prized as food, gave a whole county its name in England. A grain crop takes its name from the likeness of its seeds to those nuts. The Latin name of the tree comes from a word that means to eat.
britannica-1911-bench:
Bench is an Old English form of a word common to the Teutonic tongues, kin to German Bank and English “bank.” At root it is a long, narrow wooden seat for several people, with or without a back. While the chair stayed a seat of rank, the bench served common folk, and schools, churches and theatres still use it.

In law the word took a second life. Bench, or Banc, first meant the seat judges sat on in court, then the court itself, as in King’s Bench or Common Bench. It now covers judges and magistrates as a body, and any official seat of a group, from the bench of aldermen to the front bench in the House of Commons.
britannica-1911-benedix-julius-roderich:
Julius Roderich Benedix (1811–1873) was a German dramatist and librettist born at Leipzig and schooled at the Thomasschule. He joined the stage in 1831 with a travelling company, sang tenor in Westphalian and Rhine theatres, and managed the theatre at Wesel. His comedy Das bemooste Haupt won great success there in 1841.

Benedix later ran the Elberfeld theatre, taught at Cologne’s Rhenish music school, and directed the Frankfurt municipal theatre from 1855 to 1861. His comedies, set mostly in comfortable middle-class life, kept their public: Dr Wespe, Die Hochzeitsreise and Das Gefängnis among them. Clear plots and bright, natural talk are their marks, and his gathered plays fill twenty-seven volumes.
britannica-1911-berghaus-heinrich:
Heinrich Berghaus (1797–1884) was a German geographer born at Kleve. Trained as a surveyor, he volunteered for war service in 1813 and joined the Prussian trigonometrical survey in 1816. At Potsdam he ran a geographical school with Lange, Petermann and others, and held a chair of applied mathematics at the Bauakademie.

Maps made Berghaus famous. His Physikalischer Atlas, issued at Gotha from 1838 to 1848 with his nephew Hermann’s help, was his greatest achievement. He also had a hand in the re-issue of Stieler’s great Handatlas. His books were many: surveys of lands and peoples, a five-book outline of geography, and in 1863 his letters with Alexander von Humboldt, printed for all to read.
britannica-1911-bertrich: Bertrich is a German village and watering place in the Prussian Rhine province. It sits in a narrow valley that runs down to the Mosel river, near Cochem. The whole 1911 Britannica entry runs to three short sentences. It gives the village a population of 500. No buildings, history, or dates are named. Its fame rests on its waters. The entry calls those waters efficacious, meaning they were held to work as a cure. They were used for gout, for rheumatism, and for biliary affections, disorders tied to the bile and liver.
britannica-1911-bezborodko-aleksander-an:
Aleksander Andreevich Bezborodko, Prince (1747-1799), was grand chancellor of Russia, and his rise is traced in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Gluchova and educated at home and at the Kiev academy, he entered service as a clerk under the governor-general of Little Russia. He followed him to the Turkish war of 1768.

The entry says the peace of 1774 brought him to Catherine II's notice, and in 1775 she made him her petition-secretary. His fine manners, vast memory, and clear style marked him out, and Catherine called him her factotum. In 1780 he drew up the first plan for sharing Turkey between Russia and Austria, later sent to Vienna almost unchanged.
britannica-1911-biberach:
Biberach is a town of Germany, in the kingdom of Württemberg, on the Riss, a small stream feeding the Danube, as this 1911 Britannica article describes it. It lies twenty-two miles south-south-west of Ulm and had 8,390 people in 1900. Old walls and towers still ring it, and its chief church dates from the 1100s, while its hospital is richly endowed.

Its main trades are cloth, bell casting, toys, and zinc wares, and its fruit markets are famed. Biberach appears as a village in the 700s and became a free imperial city in 1312. In the Thirty Years War it suffered many turns and was held for a while by the Swedes. The French captured and ransomed it in 1707 and later beat the Austrians nearby. In 1806 it passed to Württemberg, and it is the birthplace of the sculptor Johann Lorenz Natter.
britannica-1911-biekkich:
Biekkich is a German town in the Prussian province of Hesse-Nassau. It stands on the right bank of the Rhine, three miles south of Wiesbaden. It serves as Wiesbaden's river port. The Cologne to Frankfort railway main line passes through it. Population rose from 15,048 in 1900 to 20,137 in 1905. The palace of the former dukes of Nassau stands on the river bank. Its shady gardens draw many summer visitors.

The town is an important steamboat station for passengers and cargo alike. Its manufactures include cement, dyes, and soap. A large trade in the wines of the district also centres here. The 1911 Britannica entry is brief and factual throughout. It gives no history of the town beyond the ducal palace. The Rhine setting and the Wiesbaden link define the place in its account.
britannica-1911-birch:
Birch, in Latin Betula, is a genus of trees and shrubs kin to the alder. Both belong to the natural order Betulaceae. Most birches are trees of medium size, though several stay mere shrubs. They are hardy plants that thrive best in northern latitudes. Round, slender branches and toothed leaves that fall each year mark them. Barren and fertile catkins grow on the same tree, and the fruits carry wings.

The bark forms fine, soft layers that peel in thin white papery sheets. The common white or silver birch grows across most of Europe and into Asia and North America. The 1911 Britannica article follows the genus species by species. It closes with the tree's uses, from polished wood to birch wine from spring sap. Himalayan birch bark serves as wrapping and writing paper, and as roofing in Kashmir.
britannica-1911-bitsch:
Bitsch, in French Bitche, is a German town in Alsace-Lorraine, on the Horn river. It sits at the foot of the Vosges mountains' northern slope, between Hagenau and Saargemund. Its population in 1905 was 4,000. It holds a Catholic and a Protestant church, a classical school, and a forestry academy. Shoe-making and watch-making employ the town, with some trade in grain and timber. The town formed in the 17th century from the villages of Rohr and Kaltenhausen.

Its name comes from a stronghold on a rock 250 feet above the town, named in 1172. Vauban rebuilt that fort after the French took Bitsch in 1624. Restored and strengthened in 1740, it proved impregnable in later wars. Prussian attacks failed in 1793, and blockade alone was tried in 1815. In 1870 the town held out under close investment until the war's end. Much of the fortress is cut into red sandstone rock, proof against bombs.
britannica-1911-blass-friedrich:
Friedrich Blass (1843–1907) was a German scholar of Greek speech and prose rhythm. Born at Osnabrück, he studied at Göttingen and Bonn from 1860 to 1863 and taught at schools and at Königsberg. He became a professor at Kiel in 1876 and moved to Halle in 1892, where he died.

His reputation rests on Greek oratory. His Attic Oratory (1868–1880) is called his greatest work, and a study of Greek eloquence from Alexander to Augustus came before it. He edited many Teubner texts of the Attic orators, among them Andocides, Antiphon, Demosthenes, and Aeschines. Late works turned to the rhythms of Greek and Roman artistic prose. The entry also praises his open, kind dealings with British scholars, who gave him an honorary Dublin degree in 1892.
britannica-1911-bleek-friedrich:
Bleek, Friedrich is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a German biblical scholar. Born at Ahrensbök in Holstein on the fourth of July 1793, he went to the gymnasium at Lübeck at sixteen. There ancient languages gripped him so strongly that he gave up a planned legal career for theology. At Berlin he studied under De Wette, Neander and Schleiermacher.

The article tells of early promise and a strange setback. At Berlin he published sharp studies on the Sibylline Oracles and on the Book of Daniel. But when De Wette was dismissed in 1819, Bleek fell under suspicion as an extreme democrat, and his promised chair was withheld. The cause proved to be a mix-up: he had been confused with another man of a similar name. Cleared in 1823, he moved in 1829 to a chair at Bonn, where he taught for thirty years.
britannica-1911-boner-ulrich:
Ulrich Boner, who lived in the 1300s, was a Swiss-German writer of fables from Bern. He came of an old Bernese family. He seems to have taken minor orders, yet he later married. That fits a clerk who had received only the tonsure. Such a man could return to lay life. Records name him between 1324 and 1349, and not outside those years.

About 1349 he wrote Der Edelstein. It is a set of one hundred fables in Middle High German. They were drawn mainly from Avianus and the Anonymus collection. He dedicated the book to Johann von Rinkenberg, a Bernese patrician. Printed at Bamberg in 1461, it is claimed as the first book printed in German. The entry praises his free handling of his sources. It praises his clear plain style too. Humour lightens the teaching tone of the tales.
britannica-1911-breech:
Breech began as a word for a covering worn over the lower body and legs. It is kin to words across the early Teutonic tongues. It is also linked to the Latin braca, itself held to be Celtic. In strict use the word stays plural and means a garment that reaches only to the knees. Later senses grow out of that first one.

From clothing the term spread to the rear end of a gun and to gear built around the body, such as the breeches buoy used to rescue people at sea. Stage use gives a breeches part, played by a woman in male dress, while harness work gives breeching, a strap that lets a horse back a carriage. The Geneva Bible of 1560 even earned the name Breeches Bible from its wording in Genesis.
britannica-1911-breisach:
Breisach, or Altbreisach, is a German town in Baden perched on a basalt rock 250 feet above the left bank of the Rhine, 10 miles west of Freiburg. Its people numbered 3537 in 1900. Across the river, joined by a rail bridge, lie Neubreisach and the fort called Mortier.

The town church draws the eye: part Romanesque, part Gothic, built across the 10th to 15th centuries, with rich carving on its high altar and many old tombs and pictures. Trade rests on wine and farm goods rather than factories. In past ages Breisach ranked as a chief Rhine stronghold, held by a Gallic tribe, seized in Caesar's time, walled by the emperor Valentinian in 369. Praised as the cushion and key of the German empire.
britannica-1911-brockes-barthold-heinric:
Barthold Heinrich Brockes (1680–1747) was a German poet born at Hamburg on 22 September 1680. He studied law at Halle, travelled widely in Italy, France and Holland, and settled in his home town in 1704. In 1720 he joined the Hamburg senate with weighty offices, and from 1735 to 1741 served as magistrate at Ritzebuettell before dying at Hamburg on 16 January 1747.

His poems appeared in nine volumes under the fanciful title Earthly Pleasure in God, issued from 1721 to 1748, and he translated Marini, Pope's Essay on Man and Thomson's Seasons. The verse itself is judged of small worth. It marks a turn in German letters: Brockes was among the first to drop bombastic copying of Marini for clear, plain diction. A pioneer in turning German readers toward the new English poetry of nature. His lines voice reverence toward nature read as God's work.
britannica-1911-bullinger-heinrich:
Heinrich Bullinger, a Swiss reformer who lived from 1504 to 1575, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Bremgarten in Aargau on 18 July 1504, he was the son of the dean of that town. He studied at Emmerich and Cologne, where the teaching of Peter Lombard led him to first hand study of the Bible. 

In 1522 Bullinger was appointed teacher in the cloister school of Cappel. He heard Zwingli at Zurich in 1527 and went with him to the disputation at Berne in 1528. He was made pastor of Bremgarten in 1529 and married in that year. After the battle of Cappel in 1531, in which Zwingli fell, he left Bremgarten in haste. On 9 December 1531 he was chosen to succeed Zwingli as chief pastor of Zurich, a post he held for the rest of his long life.
britannica-1911-bulow-dietrich-heinrich:
Dietrich Heinrich von Bülow, a Prussian soldier and writer on war who lived from 1757 to 1807, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He entered the Prussian army in 1773, brother to a future field marshal. Routine duty bored him, and he fed instead on books. Folard and other theorists of war, and Rousseau, filled his reading.

After sixteen years he quit Prussia and failed to win an Austrian commission. He ran a theatre company, lost heavily, and crossed to America for a time. There he took up and preached the doctrines of Swedenborg. A glass venture with his brother failed utterly. Under those hardships he wrote his chief work on the modern system of war. It appeared at Hamburg in 1799, with a study of the campaign of 1800 after it.
britannica-1911-busching-anton-friedrich:
Anton Friedrich Busching, a German theologian and geographer who lived from 1724 to 1793, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Stadthagen, he became a tutor in 1748 in the family of an envoy bound for Saint Petersburg. On that journey he resolved to give his life to improving the science of geography.

Leaving the envoy's family, he settled at Copenhagen and gave himself wholly to the new pursuit. In 1752 he issued a description of two northern counties. He moved to Gottingen, where he became professor of philosophy in 1757. In 1761 he accepted a call to a German church at Saint Petersburg. There he set up a school that soon flourished as one of the best in northern Europe.
britannica-1911-chebichev-pafnutiy-lvovi:
Pafnutiy Lvovich Chebichev (1821–1894) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a Russian mathematician born at Borovsk. He was educated at the university of Moscow. In 1859 he became professor of mathematics at St Petersburg, a post he held until 1880. The Institute of France chose him a correspondent in 1860 and an associate in 1874. The entry ranks him, after Lobachevskiy, as the most distinguished mathematician Russia has produced.

His best known papers deal with prime numbers. In one of 1850 he fixed limits within which the sum of the logarithms of the primes below a given number must fall. He also worked hard on obtaining straight line motion by linkage. The parallel motion named for him comes very close to exact, but never quite reaches it. His pupil Lipkin, and Peaucellier before him, found the true linkage first. He also built an instrument for drawing large circles and a calculating machine.
britannica-1911-cilli-ulrich:
Cilli, Ulrich, Count of (1406–1456) was the son of Frederick II, count of Cilli, and Elizabeth Frangepan, and he married Catherine, daughter of the despot of Servia, about 1432. Emperor Sigismund made him and his father princes of the Empire in 1436, sparking feuds with the Habsburgs. He backed Albert II, then the widow Elizabeth and her infant son Ladislaus, crowned in 1440. A bitter feud with the Hunyadis followed over Bosnia and Serbia.

In 1452 he forced Emperor Frederick III to hand over the boy king Ladislaus, making himself practical ruler of Hungary. Succession to his father's vast wealth in 1454 raised his power further, and Ladislaus named him lieutenant in Hungary in 1456. The Hunyadis then conspired against him in earnest. On 8 November he entered Belgrade with the king despite warnings, and Laszlo Hunyadi and his friends killed him the next day.
britannica-1911-cockroach:
Cockroach names a family of insects in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Their marks are flattened bodies, long thread-like feelers, and shining leathery skins. They are creatures of the night by habit. By day they hide in chinks and cracks about houses.

When the lights go out, the cockroaches come forth with great speed. They hunt food and spoil whatever they touch with their foul smell. They eat, or at least damage, almost anything in their path. The common kind is not native to Europe, the article holds. It came from the Levant in the cargoes of trading ships. Its sixteen eggs are laid in a leathery capsule the female carries. The young hatch white and wingless from that case. A larger American kind haunts the seaports of Europe in grain cargoes.
britannica-1911-constantine-pavlovich:
Constantine Pavlovich, who lived from 1779 to 1831, was a grand duke and heir of Russia. The 1911 Britannica entry notes how closely he matched his father Paul in body and mind. His grandmother Catherine the Second took charge of his upbringing in full. She set each detail of his schooling and health by her own plan.

As with his elder brother Alexander, she left daily care to trusted men at court. Count Soltikov held the tutor post in name but passed the work to others. He stepped in in person only on rare and grave occasions, the entry says. The portrait is of a prince shaped by a strict court design from birth.
britannica-1911-credner-carl-friedrich-h:
Carl Friedrich Heinrich Credner (1809–1876) was a German geologist born at Waltershausen near Gotha on 13 March 1809. He studied the geology of the Thüringer Wald and published a map of it in 1846. A later work treated the upper Jurassic and Wealden formations of north-west Germany. He also made a geological map of Hanover in 1865. He died at Halle on 28 September 1876.

His son, Carl Hermann Credner, was born at Gotha on 1 October 1841 and studied at Breslau and Göttingen. He took his doctorate at Breslau in 1864. In 1870 he became professor of geology at Leipzig, and in 1872 he directed the Geological Survey of Saxony. His Elemente der Geologie ran to a seventh edition by 1891 and stood as the standard manual in Germany. He also wrote on the geology of Saxony and on fossil reptiles.
britannica-1911-creuzer-georg-friedrich:
Georg Friedrich Creuzer was a German scholar of old tongues and old art who lived from seventeen seventy-one to eighteen fifty-eight. He was born at Marburg, the son of a book binder. He taught at Marburg and then held a chair at Heidelberg for near forty-five years. He helped found a famed school for word study there.

His best known book dealt with signs and myths of old folk, most of all the Greeks. He held that Greek myth came from the east by an old race. That claim drew sharp fire from peers. The entry lists his work on Plotinus, Cicero, and Roman life as well.
britannica-1911-cutch:
Cutch is a place article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a native state of India, also spelled Kach. It lies in the Gujarat division of Bombay and covers 7,616 square miles. It is a tract of land shaped like a peninsula. The Indus bounds it to the west, the sea to the south, and a great salt marsh, the Runn, to the north.

Inside, hills rise across the land, and a range of mountains runs from east to west. Many of the rocks have wild, strange shapes. The article calls the general look of Cutch barren. Much of it is rock with no soil, cold and poor. The whole face of the land bears marks of past volcanic action. Its villages look ruined, worn down by years of harsh rule, raids, and earthquake shocks.
britannica-1911-czech:
Czech, in Bohemian Čech, is the name of an inhabitant of Čechy, the native name for Bohemia, as this 1911 Britannica article explains. The Czechs belong to the Slavic peoples. With the Poles and the Lusatians they form the group of the Western Slavs.

Czechs live across a large part of Bohemia, a still larger part of Moravia, parts of Silesia, and wide districts in northern Hungary. Beyond that core land there are many Czechs in Lower Austria, with Vienna holding a large and growing Czech population. Others live in Russia and in the United States, where many newspapers appear in Czech, and in London. Though the figures are unsure, the article puts the Czechs at about eight million in all.
britannica-1911-dahl-vladimir-ivanovich:
Vladimir Ivanovich Dahl, a Russian author and philologist who lived from 1802 to 1872, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born of Scandinavian parentage, he was educated at the naval cadets' institution at Saint Petersburg. He joined the Black Sea fleet in 1819, but later he entered the army and served in the Polish campaign of 1831.

Dahl was later appointed to a medical post in a government hospital, and in the end he was transferred to the civil service. His last years were spent at Moscow, where he died in 1872. Under the name Kossack Lugansky he won considerable fame by his stories of Russian life. His greatest work, though, was a dictionary of the living Russian tongue. It appeared in four volumes between 1861 and 1866. The entry calls it of the most essential service to students of the popular literature and folk lore of Russia.
britannica-1911-delitzsch:
Delitzsch is a town of Germany in the Prussian province of Saxony, and this short 1911 Britannica entry describes it. It stands on the Lober, a stream of the Mulde, twelve miles north of Leipzig at a railway junction. Its people numbered 10,479 in 1905. Its public buildings include a castle of the fourteenth century used as a women's prison, four churches, and a training college for teachers founded in 1873.

The town makes a peculiar kind of beer, tobacco, cigars, shoes, and hosiery, and coal is mined nearby. It was the birthplace of the naturalist Ehrenberg and of the economist Schulze-Delitzsch, who has a statue there. The town began as a settlement of the Sorbian Wends. It passed through the hands of bishops and electors before joining Electoral Saxony in 1738.
britannica-1911-emmerich:
Emmerich, the ancient Embrica, is a town of Germany in the Prussian Rhine province. It stands on the right bank of the Rhine, on the railway from Cologne to Amsterdam, five miles north-east of Cleves. Its population in 1905 was 12,578. The town has a large shipping trade. Its factories make tobacco and cigars, chocolate, margarine, oil, chemicals, brushes, vinegar, soap, guano, and perfumery. It also has iron foundries and machine works.

The old minster church, built in the middle of the 11th century, holds some fine choir stalls. Emmerich, first a Roman colony, is named in records as early as the 7th century, and St Willibrord founded a monastery and church there. The place came to the dukes of Gelderland in 1233 and gained town status in 1247. It fell to Cleves in 1371, joined the Hanseatic League in 1407, and passed to Prussia in 1815. The French bombarded it in 1794 under General Vandamme.
britannica-1911-enoch:
Enoch is a biblical name held by more than one figure in Genesis. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives the Hebrew sense as teaching or dedication. One Enoch was the eldest son of Cain, with a city named for him. A second, in the line of Seth, is the best known of the group.

That second Enoch walked with God, the text says, for 365 years. Then he was taken by God and was seen no more. Later Jewish tales made him a seer of the heavens and first author. Two books written in his name survive from old times. Short notes cover two clan names of the same form as well.
britannica-1911-eparch:
Eparch is an official, the governor of a province of Roman Greece, whose Greek title was held to match the Roman praefectus. The entry is a short word-and-office notice. The area under such an official was called an eparchy. Both words outlived the Roman world that made them.

The term survives, the entry says, as one of the governing units of modern Greece. There the country is divided into nomarchies, those into eparchies, and those again into demarchies, with a pointer to the article on Greek local government. “Eparch” and “eparchy” also live on in the Russian Orthodox Church. In that church they name a bishop and his diocese, in turn. The short entry thus follows one Greek office word through three worlds: a Roman province, a modern Greek county ladder, and the map of a great church.
britannica-1911-epoch:
Epoch is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a term for a point in time. The Greek root means a holding in suspense, a pause. The word names a date taken as a starting point. The birth of Christ is given as one such date. From that sense the word passes to a wider use. It names any period that marks a great change.

A great discovery or invention can mark such a period. Hence an event may be spoken of as epoch making. The word is also used, like period, for any span of time. Such a span is marked by a distinctive condition. In astronomy the word has a more exact sense. There it names the moment from which time is measured. A body's place in its orbit needs such a known moment.
britannica-1911-erbach:
Erbach is the subject of a town article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Erbach is a town in Germany, in the grand duchy of Hesse Darmstadt. It stands on the Mumling river, southeast of Darmstadt. Its people numbered about twenty eight hundred. The town has cloth mills and a trade in ivory turning, for which it holds a technical school. Wool and cattle fairs are held twice a year.

The article notes the castle, with its collection of weapons and pictures. In its chapel lie the coffins of Einhard, friend and biographer of Charlemagne, and his wife Emma. Erbach has long been the seat of the counts of Erbach, who trace their line to the twelve hundreds. In 1532 the emperor made their county a direct fief of the empire. Since 1717 the family has split into three lines. The county was absorbed into the duchy in 1806.
britannica-1911-erech:
Erech, called Uruk in Babylonian records, was an ancient city of Babylonia. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets it east of the Euphrates bed, south of Baghdad. Its famed temple E Anna honored the goddess Ishtar there. The city ranked among the oldest and greatest in the land.

Erech held sway in Babylonia before the time of Sargon, it says. Wars against Elam hurt it badly in early ages of strife. Tales of those wars live on in the Gilgamesh epic as passed down. Later it shone as a seat of learning and Ishtar worship. Ruins at Warka, dug in the eighteen fifties, show its vast walls.
britannica-1911-ericht-loch:
Ericht, Loch, is a lake lying partly in Inverness-shire and partly in Perthshire, Scotland, between the districts of Badenoch to the north and Rannoch to the south. It is a lonely lake in extremely wild country, 1153 feet above the sea. The entry calls it the loftiest lake of large size in the United Kingdom. It is over 14.5 miles long, with a mean breadth of half a mile.

The mean depth is 189 feet and the greatest depth 512 feet. The lake runs from north-east to south-west, its head a mile from Dalwhinnie station on the Highland railway. Salmon and trout give good fishing. The hills around are lofty and rugged, and Ben Alder, at 3757 feet on the west shore, is the chief height of the great Corrour deer forest.
britannica-1911-eschscholtz-johann-fried:
Johann Friedrich Eschscholtz (1793–1831) was a Russian traveller and naturalist, and a brief life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sums up his voyages. He was born at Dorpat in November 1793 and died there in May 1831. He sailed as naturalist and physician with Otto von Kotzebue on an exploring voyage from 1815 to 1818.

On his return, Eschscholtz became a professor of anatomy at Dorpat in 1819. In 1822 he took charge of the zoological museum of the university there. He sailed with Kotzebue again on a second voyage of discovery, from 1823 to 1826. In 1828 he rose to full professor of anatomy. His books include a system of the acalephs in 1829 and a zoological atlas. A botanical genus was named Eschscholtzia in his honour by his friend Chamisso.
britannica-1911-eunuch:
Eunuch means a man who has been castrated, and a 1911 Britannica entry traces the role across the old world. In the East such men guarded the women of great houses from early times. The Greek name points to charge of the bedchamber in a royal house. Trust in that post could grow into real sway over a prince.

In Egypt the term came to mean any court officer, castrated or not in fact. The entry rejects the claim that such men lack nerve or wit by nature. Herodotus says Persian kings prized them most for their proven faith. Narses, the great general under Justinian, is named as proof of their ability.
britannica-1911-exilarch:
The exilarch, in Jewish history, was the Chief or Prince of the Captivity, in Aramaic Resh Galutha. He headed the Babylonian Jews, the people of the Exile named by Jeremiah and Ezekiel. The office was hereditary and carried real power. Tradition made Jehoiachin, the last Davidic king, the first holder. Later exilarchs all claimed descent from Judah's royal house. The dignity continued under the Arsacid and Sassanid kings.

In the 6th century Mar Zutra led a bid for Jewish self-rule by force and was executed. The office lapsed, then revived under Arab rule. From the mid 7th to the 11th century the holders descended from Bostanai. David son of Zakkai was the last of real weight, and Hezekiah, about 1040, the last Babylonian exilarch. Installation was splendid: homage from the college heads, rich gifts, a canopy in the synagogue. The exilarch taxed his people and could excommunicate.
britannica-1911-fathers-of-the-church:
Fathers of the Church is the title borne by the leading early Christian writers. The entry traces the word father as a mark of respect in the Old Testament, applied to patriarchs, priests, prophets and ancestors. It then asks who counts as a father: all Christian writers of a period, or only orthodox writers on religion. Collections such as Migne's took in the wider body of ecclesiastical writers.
