The entry names the chief fathers by region and age. Ante-Nicene writers include Clement and Origen of Alexandria, Tertullian and Cyprian of Carthage, and Lactantius. Later names include Athanasius, Basil, the two Gregories, Chrysostom, Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome and Gregory the Great. It closes with their collected editions, English translations, and the question of what authority their teaching and Bible reading carry.
britannica-1911-feldkirch:
Feldkirch is a small town in the Austrian province of Vorarlberg, some 20 miles south of the southern end of Lake Constance. It sits in a green hollow on the Ill river, between two narrow rocky gorges where the river flows out to the broad Rhine valley. With only about 4,000 German-speaking, Roman Catholic inhabitants, its weight is military: it commands the western entrance into Tirol over the Arlberg Pass.

Battles were fought here often, last in 1799, when the French under Oudinot and Massena were driven back by Austrians under Hotze and Jellachich. The old castle of Schattenburg, built about 1200 by the count of Montfort, shadows the town. Other sights include the parish church of 1487, the Jesuit school Stella Matutina, and a Capuchin convent. Transit trade and factories add to its life.
britannica-1911-freytag-georg-wilhelm-fr:
Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Freytag (1788-1861), German scholar of oriental languages, was born at Lüneburg on 19 September 1788. He read philology and theology at Göttingen and served as a tutor. He then worked as sub-librarian at Königsberg. In 1815 he was a Prussian army chaplain who reached Paris. Peace let him return to Arabic, Persian, and Turkish studies under De Sacy.

In 1819 he took the professorship of oriental languages at Bonn. He held it until his death on 16 November 1861. He wrote a short Hebrew grammar and a treatise on Arabic verse. He edited two volumes of Arabic songs and three of Arabic proverbs. His chief fame rests on the Lexicon Arabico-latinum, published at Halle from 1830 to 1837. A shortened edition closed the work.
britannica-1911-fyne-loch:
Fyne, Loch, is a sea inlet of Argyllshire in Scotland, running some 44 miles from its head above Inveraray to its mouth on the Sound of Bute. Its width varies from about a mile and a quarter to six miles. The Fyne, Shira and Aray streams feed it, and side lochs branch off on the western shore, among them Loch Gilp with Ardrishaig and the Crinan Canal. All vessels using that canal pass through the loch.

The shores are picturesque and in many parts well wooded. Industries along the loch include granite quarrying, distilling and gunpowder-making, but fishing stands above all. Haddock, whiting and codling are taken, and the Loch Fyne herrings fetch the highest price in the market.
britannica-1911-gairloch: Gairloch is a sea loch, village and parish on the west coast of Ross and Cromarty in Scotland, its parish holding 3797 people in 1901. The parish reaches inland past Loch Maree, which lies wholly within it, and covers 200,646 acres including islands in Loch Gairloch and Loch Ewe. The Mackenzies have held Gairloch since the end of the 15th century. Flowerdale, an 18th-century house near the village, is the chief seat of the Gairloch Mackenzies, and the Gaelic poet William Ross lies in the old kirkyard.
britannica-1911-galt-sir-alexander-tillo:
Sir Alexander Tilloch Galt (1817-1893) was a Canadian statesman, youngest son of the novelist John Galt. The 1911 Britannica entry has him born in London on 6 September 1817 and emigrating to Canada in 1835. He worked for the British American Land Company at Sherbrooke, then helped extend the Grand Trunk railway westward from Toronto.

Galt entered parliament in 1849 and became the chief voice of English-speaking Protestants in Quebec. As finance minister he put Canada's finances in order, brought in decimal currency and protection for Canadian manufactures, and helped drive the federation of British North America. He held the finance post in the first Dominion ministry, then resigned in November 1867. Later he served on the Halifax fisheries commission and as high commissioner in London, dying on 19 September 1893.
britannica-1911-gauermann-friedrich:
Friedrich Gauermann (1807-1862) was an Austrian painter, born at Wiesenbach in Lower Austria on 20 September 1807. The 1911 Britannica entry makes him the son of the landscape painter Jacob Gauermann, who meant him for farming. The boy instead studied landscape under his father and copied the animal painters in Vienna's collections.

Animal pieces shown at Vienna in 1824 won him commissions from Prince Metternich and the French ambassador. His picture The Storm, shown in 1829, raised his name sharply, and his works sold for high prices. The entry puts him in the first rank of animal painters. His gift, it says, was showing men and animals within apt landscapes, above all the free life of animals in wild mountain country. He died at Vienna on 7 July 1862.
britannica-1911-gauss-karl-friedrich:
Karl Friedrich Gauss (1777-1855) was a German mathematician, born of humble parents at Brunswick on 30 April 1777. The 1911 Britannica entry says the reigning duke's notice of his talent won him a liberal education. His Disquisitiones arithmeticae of 1801, in his twenty-fifth year, made his name widely known.

In 1807 he became director of the Gottingen observatory, a post he held for life. His Theoria motus of 1809 reshaped how orbits were computed from observation. With Wilhelm Weber he built instruments to measure earth magnetism, set up an iron-free magnetic observatory in 1833, and sent telegraph signals to a nearby town. The entry then surveys his collected works volume by volume, including papers on curved surfaces. His notebooks held results that later made Abel and Jacobi famous.
britannica-1911-geffcken-friedrich-heinr:
Friedrich Heinrich Geffcken, a German envoy and jurist who lived from 1830 to 1896, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Hamburg, where his father was a senator. He studied law at Bonn, Gottingen, and Berlin. In 1854 he was attached to the Prussian legation at Paris.

For ten years Geffcken represented Hamburg in Berlin, then in a like post in London. In 1872 he became professor of constitutional history and public law at Strassburg university. In 1880 he joined the council of state of Alsace Lorraine. His nerves could not bear the strain, and he retired in 1882 to live mostly at Munich. He died there in 1896, suffocated by an accidental escape of gas. The entry praises his learning, his legal acumen, and his clear writing. He was a trusted adviser of the Prussian crown prince.
britannica-1911-gerstacker-friedrich:
Friedrich Gerstacker was a German writer of tales and trips who lived from eighteen sixteen to eighteen seventy-two. He was born at Hamburg, the son of a famed opera singer. He learned farm work, then sailed to America in eighteen thirty-seven for the sake of bold deeds. He roamed much of that land and lived by odd jobs.

Home in eighteen forty-three, he found he was famed as a writer. His mother had shown his home diary to a press chief, who had printed it. Books of hunts and tales then flowed from his pen each year. He went round the world and wrote of each land he saw.
britannica-1911-gladbach:
Gladbach is the name of two towns in Rhenish Prussia, and the 1911 Britannica entry treats them in turn. Bergisch-Gladbach, eight miles north-east of Cologne, held 13,410 people in 1905. It has four large paper mills, with paste-board, powder, percussion caps, nets and machinery beside, and ironstone, peat and lime nearby.

Munchen-Gladbach, 16 miles west-south-west of Dusseldorf, is the larger: 60,714 people in 1905. It ranks among the chief manufacturing places of Rhenish Prussia, spinning and weaving cotton, making silk, velvet and ribbon, and dyeing and bleaching. The entry notes its minster, with work from the 8th to the 13th century, and its Benedictine monastery founded in 793. Munchen means monks: the abbey's Gladbach was Monks' Gladbach, named to part it from the other town.
britannica-1911-glazunov-alexander-const:
Alexander Constantinovich Glazunov (born 1865) was a Russian composer, and his career to date fills an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Saint Petersburg, son of a publisher and bookseller, he showed an early gift for music and studied briefly with Rimsky-Korsakov. At sixteen he composed a symphony.

The entry tells how Liszt took him up in 1884, the year his first symphony was played at Weimar, and how he conducted at the Paris exhibition of 1889. In 1900 he became professor at the Saint Petersburg conservatoire. He is called a master of orchestration and a leading name of the modern Russian school, leaning toward classical form under the sway of Brahms.
britannica-1911-goch: Goch is a town of Germany in the Prussian Rhine province, on the river Niers. The short 1911 Britannica note sets it eight miles south of Cleves at a rail junction. Its count in 1905 was 10,232 people. The town has both a Protestant and a Roman Catholic church. Its works make brushes, plush goods, cigars, and margarine, and in the middle ages it held a large trade in linen.
britannica-1911-gogol-nikolai-vasilievic:
Nikolai Vasilievich Gogol was a Russian writer whose tales of Little-Russian life made his name. The hosted 1911 Britannica text opens in mid-course, at his first story collection. Evenings in a Farm near Dikanka, published in book form in 1831 under the name Rudy Panko, won immediate success for its light, colour and freshness.

The entry follows the Arabesques, Taras Bulba among the Cossack tales, and the novelettes that mark his move from romantic to realistic fiction. One is the tale of a poor clerk whose great aim in life is to secure a cloak. A St Petersburg professorship, won through his history plans, went badly and he resigned in 1835. The closing pages turn sombre: asceticism and mystical exaltation wore down his nerves and showed in his writing. He made a pilgrimage to Jerusalem in 1848, settled at Moscow, and died there on 3 March 1852.
britannica-1911-golitsuin-boris-aleksyee:
Boris Aleksyeevich Golitsuin was a Russian statesman of a princely family line. He lived from sixteen fifty four to seventeen fourteen. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. His house claimed descent from Prince Gedimin of Lithuania in old times.

Golitsuin became court chamberlain in sixteen seventy six at the Russian court. He chiefly backed the young tsar Peter against his sister Sophia in sixteen eighty nine. He urged refuge in the Troitsa monastery fort and won boyars over. In sixteen ninety he was made a boyar and shared home rule. He ruled Russia in a trio during Peter first foreign tour. A revolt at Astrakhan in seventeen o six shook Peter trust in him.
britannica-1911-golitsuin-dmitry-mikhail:
Dmitry Golitsuin was a Russian statesman sent as a young man to Italy to learn the art of war. He was then set to lead a help corps in Poland against a great Swedish king. For some years he served as governor of a border province of the realm.

He rose to head a new state board for funds and to sit in the senate, the 1911 Britannica entry says. A fall of a high court foe dragged him down: he lost all his posts and ranks at a stroke. The plea of an empress won them back for him. On the death of the great tsar who had reshaped Russia, Golitsuin stood as the known head of the old guard party. That party had never made peace with the tsars low born second wife, and its foes held sway while a famed upstart ruled.
britannica-1911-golitsuin-vasily-vasilev:
Vasily Vasilevich Golitsuin is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Golitsuin was a Russian statesman who lived from 1643 to 1714. He spent his early days at the court of Tsar Alexius and rose to the rank of boyar. In 1676 he was sent to the Ukraine against the Crimean Tatars. He helped end the old system of rank priority in army promotion.

The article tells how the revolt of 1682 placed him at the head of foreign affairs. During the regency of Sophia, sister of Peter the Great, he was chief minister of state. His peace with Poland in 1683 won Kiev back for Russia. His two campaigns against the Crimea failed and made him unpopular. When Sophia fell in 1689, he shared her ruin. His estates were taken, and he was banished to the far north, where he died.
britannica-1911-grabbe-christian-dietric:
Christian Dietrich Grabbe, a German dramatist who lived from 1801 to 1836, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Detmold, he went to Leipzig in 1819 to study law. He kept up wild habits there and let his studies slide. In literary circles he turned to the stage and wrote his first drama in 1822.

That play showed real talent but lacked form and was morally harsh. Ludwig Tieck praised the gift while he named the faults. Grabbe passed his law exams in 1824 and worked as a lawyer at home. Drink cost him his army law post in time, and his marriage broke down as well. He died at Detmold in 1836 from his excesses. The entry grants him true poetic gifts and bold ideas. His best works are histories and a play that joins Don Juan with Faust.
britannica-1911-graetz-heinrich:
Heinrich Graetz (1817–1891) is called the foremost Jewish historian of modern times, and his life opens a study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Posen in 1817 and died at Munich in 1891. His schooling was patchy, and he was largely self taught. One stage of his growth stood out from the rest.

For three years Graetz served at Oldenburg as aide and pupil to Hirsch. The enlightened orthodoxy of Hirsch drew him for a time. Later he went to Breslau and entered the university in 1842. Breslau was then a centre of Abraham Geiger, the leader of Jewish reform. Graetz was repelled by the stance of Geiger. Though he later took radical views of the Bible, he stayed a lifelong foe of reform as Geiger led it.
britannica-1911-graf-karl-heinrich:
Karl Heinrich Graf (1815–1869) was a German scholar of the Old Testament and of the East. He was born at Mülhausen in Alsace on 28 February 1815. He studied the reading of the Bible and the tongues of the East at Strassburg under E. Reuss. After posts as a teacher, he was made a teacher of French and Hebrew at the school of Meissen. In 1852 he gained the title of professor there, and he died on 16 July 1869.

Graf was one of the chief founders of the new study of the Old Testament. In his main work of 1866, he sought to show a bold claim. He held that the priestly laws of Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers are of a later date than the book of Deuteronomy. He still held the view of his day on one point, though.
britannica-1911-grafe-heinrich:
Heinrich Grafe, a German teacher and school reformer born at Buttstädt on 3 May 1802, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He studied maths and church studies at Jena. In 1823 he took a curacy at Weimar. Two years later he led the town school at Jena.

He rose to a chair in the science of schooling at Jena in 1840. At Cassel he ran the town schools and then a new Realschule from 1843. His push for reform in Hesse put him in the house of representatives in 1849. Part in the unrest of 1852 brought a prison term, later cut to twelve months. He ended his career at Bremen and died there in 1868. Many school books bear his name.
britannica-1911-greenfinch:
The Greenfinch, or Green Linnet, is a common European bird, the Fringilla chloris of Linnaeus. The 1911 Britannica entry, signed by Alfred Newton, weighs its place among the hawfinches. Many systematists rank it with one section of them, but it seems nearer another, and may fairly stand as the type of its own genus, Chloris or Ligurinus.

The cock's yellowish-green and yellow plumage makes him one of the most finely coloured of common English birds. He is heavily built, though, and his song is hardly commended. The hen is much duller. The species is plentiful all year through Britain, pervades almost all Europe, and reaches the river Ob in Asia. It visits Palestine but is unknown in Egypt. Bright birds from Mauritania were once split off as a separate species, a view now generally abandoned. Two allied species occur in north-east Asia.
britannica-1911-greenwich:
Greenwich is a borough of London on the south bank of the Thames. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it 95,770 people in 1901. A foot tunnel of 1902 links it to the Isle of Dogs. The Blackwall tunnel carries street traffic under the river. Watling Street, the old Roman road, runs through it as Shooter's Hill Road. Danes held a fleet station there in the days of Ethelred.

Its fame rests on the hospital and the observatory. The hospital, by 1911 a naval college, stands on a royal palace site. That palace was a loved royal home as early as 1300. Henry the Eighth was born there, as were Mary and Elizabeth. Edward the Sixth died under its roof. Humphrey of Gloucester had improved it and named it Placentia. The grand buildings strike a sharp contrast with the wharves beside them.
britannica-1911-hahnemann-samuel-christi:
Samuel Christian Friedrich Hahnemann was a German physician who founded homoeopathy. He lived from seventeen fifty five to eighteen forty three. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Meissen in Saxony, he studied medicine at Leipzig and Vienna.

Hahnemann took his medical degree at Erlangen in seventeen seventy nine. While he turned a Scots medical book into German, a fact struck him. Quinine caused in healthy men the same signs it was used to cure. From that he drew his law of similars for drug treatment. He claimed small doses held strong cure power in his system. His chief work Organon set out that system in eighteen ten.
britannica-1911-harlech:
Harlech, a town in Merionethshire, Wales, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It lies on the Cambrian railway, thirty eight miles from Aberystwyth and twenty nine from Carnarvon. Its population is given as nine hundred. Ruins of a fortress crown the rock of Harlech, about half a mile from the sea.

The entry traces a long past for the site. Roman coins found there suggest the Romans once held it. A tower named for Bronwen, daughter of Bran, is placed here in early Welsh tale. The present castle, square with towers, dates from the time of Edward the First. Old parts were kept in its building, the article notes, and its plan may match those of Carnarvon and Conway.
britannica-1911-hassenpflug-hans-daniel-:
Hans Daniel Ludwig Friedrich Hassenpflug, a German statesman, opens a hard rule life in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Hanau in Hesse in seventeen ninety four, he read law at Gottingen. He took his degree in eighteen sixteen and joined the state law board. His father sat on that same board at Cassel at the time. In eighteen thirty two he rose to chief for law and home rule.

From that post he set out to undo the free charter of eighteen thirty one. Press curbs, law tricks, and prince decrees were his tools for that work. His youth had held the pledge of a rebel student corps at school. That past made his turn seem black to the folk of his land. Hate and curse of Hesse was the name folk gave him.
britannica-1911-hebbel-christian-friedri:
Christian Friedrich Hebbel (1813–1863) was a German poet and dramatist. He was born at Wesselburen in Holstein on 18 March 1813. His father was a poor bricklayer. Verses sent to Amalie Schoppe won him patrons. Their kindness sent him to Hamburg for university preparation. Heidelberg law proved uncongenial, so Munich followed. Philosophy, history and literature claimed him there. He walked back to Hamburg in 1839.

His first tragedy, Judith, was performed in 1840 and made his name. Maria Magdalene (1844) is called a fine tragedy of common life. A Danish travelling studentship funded Paris and Italy. Vienna then claimed him for good. He married the actress Christine Enghaus in 1846. That marriage sacrificed Elise Lensing, who had sustained him. German sovereigns decorated him as Germany's greatest living dramatist. His Nibelungen trilogy (1862) won the Schiller prize. He died at Vienna in 1863. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; the Hebbel entry stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-heinecken-christian-hein:
Christian Heinrich Heinecken (1721–1725) was a child famous for precocity. He was born at Lübeck on 6 February 1721. His father was a painter there. He could speak at the age of ten months. By one year he knew the Pentateuch's principal incidents by heart. At two he had mastered sacred history. At three he knew history and geography, ancient and modern. French and Latin were also his by then.

His fourth year went to religion and church history. This was no mere feat of memory, contemporaries insisted. The child could reason about what he knew. Crowds flocked to Lübeck to see him. The king of Denmark summoned him to Copenhagen in 1724. On his return he began learning to write. His sickly constitution then gave way. He died on 22 June 1725, aged four. His tutor published his life the following year.
britannica-1911-hoe-richard-march:
Richard March Hoe (1812–1886) was an American inventor, born in New York City on the 12th of September 1812. His father Robert Hoe, an English-born mechanic, had founded a manufactory of printing presses in New York, using steam to run the machinery. Richard entered the works at fifteen and became head of the firm on his father's death. He had real inventive genius, and he set himself to win greater speed for printing presses.

Hoe dropped the old flat-bed model and set the type on a revolving cylinder. The model grew into the Hoe rotary, or lightning, press, patented in 1846. It was improved further as the Hoe web perfecting press. His nephew Robert Hoe carried the work on and wrote a short history of the press. Richard Hoe died at Florence, Italy, on the 7th of June 1886.
britannica-1911-holbeach:
Holbeach is a market town in the Holland or Spalding division of Lincolnshire, England, on the Midland and Great Northern joint railway. The urban district held 4,755 people in 1901. All Saints' church, with a lofty spire, is a fine specimen of late Decorated work. The grammar school was founded in 1669 and now occupies a building put up in 1877.

The town also has assembly rooms and a market house. Roman and Saxon remains have been found in the neighbourhood. Its market dates from the 13th century, so the little town's trading life runs back some six hundred years behind the railway age that now serves it.
britannica-1911-holderlin-johann-christi:
Johann Christian Friedrich Hölderlin, a German poet who lived from 1770 to 1843, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Lauffen on the Neckar river. His family meant him for the church, and he was trained in seminaries. At eighteen he entered Tübingen University to study theology, staying until 1793.

Schiller saw his gift early and printed his first writings in his journals. Hölderlin then worked as a tutor in great houses. In the Gontard home at Frankfurt he fell in love with the banker's wife, Susette. She became the Diotima of his novel Hyperion, and both his spur and his ruin. The first volume of Hyperion appeared in 1797, the second in 1799. He also began a tragedy on the death of Empedocles.
britannica-1911-horwich: Horwich is an urban district in the Westhoughton division of Lancashire, England, 4 m. W.N.W. of Bolton, on the Lancashire and Yorkshire railway. Its population was 15,084 in 1901. It lies below the high ground of Rivington Pike, where a great forest once stood. The town has extensive locomotive works, and large stone quarries work in the district. Bleaching and cotton-spinning are carried on, along with the making of fire-bricks and tiles. The entry is a short gazetteer note on the town and its trades.
britannica-1911-india-french:
French India is a territory article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name covers all the French possessions in India of that day. On the Coromandel coast lay Pondicherry, Karikal, and Yanaon. Mahe stood on the Malabar coast, and Chandernagore in Bengal.

A few small lodges elsewhere were mere remnants of old trading posts. The whole territory covered only 203 square miles. Pondicherry alone accounted for 113 of those miles. In 1901 the total population came to 273,185 people. A decree of 1879 gave French India an elected general council and local councils. The entry notes plainly that the results were not very good. Rules for the vote were changed more than once in response. Readers get the measure of a small empire held in scattered port towns.
britannica-1911-isaac-of-antioch:
Isaac of Antioch, a writer of verse sermons in the Syriac tongue, is the subject of a careful study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He is called one of the stars of Syriac letters. His sermons in verse are praised for fresh thought and sharp wit, rare among writers of his school. Yet who he was, and when he lived, is hard to pin down.

Old accounts place him in the days of Theodosius the Second, in the fifth century. Some make him a pupil of Saint Ephraim, others name a different master. He is said to have become abbot of a house near Antioch. His poems on the fall of Rome in 410 are lost. The study weighs a clash in the creed of the works that bear his name.
britannica-1911-jacobi-friedrich-heinric:
Friedrich Heinrich Jacobi, a German thinker born in seventeen forty three, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Dusseldorf, he was the second son of a rich sugar trade man of that town. He was bred for a life in trade. By bent he was a still man who loved to muse.

At Geneva he kept most with the set of men of letters and of science in that town. He read deep in the works of a famed Swiss thinker of nature. He read as well in the state views of two French men of the age. In seventeen sixty three he was called home. The next year he wed and took charge of his father trade. In a short time he gave up that life.
britannica-1911-jacobite-church:
Jacobite Church is a church history in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Syrian church that broke with the Greek church. The name was coined by hostile Greeks in a church decree of the year 787. It points to Jacob Baradaeus, who rebuilt the church and was made its bishop in 541 or 543.

The article tells how the church held to one nature in Christ. For that stand its clergy were hunted by the emperor Justinian. Jacob, dressed as a poor beggar, crossed Syria in secret. He preached and made new clergy by the thousand, it is said. His work lasted long past his death in 578. At its height the church counted 150 bishops under its patriarch. By 1842 its flock in Turkey had shrunk to about 100,000 souls.
britannica-1911-jung-johann-heinrich:
Johann Heinrich Jung (1740–1817), best known by his taken name Heinrich Stilling, was a German author born in the village of Grund in Westphalia on the 12th of September 1740. His father was a schoolmaster and tailor, and Jung followed both trades by his father's wish, finding each one wearisome. After several teaching posts he went in 1768 to study medicine at Strassburg.

At Strassburg he met Goethe, who brought him to Herder, and the meeting ripened into friendship. By Goethe's influence his first and best work, Heinrich Stillings Jugend, was written. In 1772 he settled at Elberfeld as a doctor and eye surgeon, winning fame for cataract work. In 1778 he took a lectureship at Kaiserslautern, and in 1787 a chair at Marburg. He gave up his chair in 1803, lived at Heidelberg, and from 1806 held a pension from the grand duke of Baden at Karlsruhe, where he died in 1817.
britannica-1911-karajich-vuk-stefanovich:
Vuk Stefanovich Karajich (1787–1864) was the father of modern Serbian literature. He was born on the 6th of November 1787 in the Serbian village of Trshich, on the border of Bosnia and Serbia. He learnt to read and write at the old monastery of Tronosha. At the start of the first Serbian rising in 1804 he was taken on as a writer of letters for a district commander.

Through the revolution he served mostly as a scribe to various voyvodes, and at times as a teacher. When the rising fell, he left Serbia and went, not to Russia with Karageorge and the other leaders, but to Vienna. There he met the Slavonic scholar Kopitar, who urged him to gather the poems and songs and to write a grammar and a dictionary. Karajich held to that plan all his life.
britannica-1911-karamzin-nikolai-mikhail:
Nikolai Mikhailovich Karamzin (1765–1826) was a Russian historian, critic, novelist, and poet. He was born at Mikhailovka in the government of Orenburg on the 1st of December 1765. He was not born at Simbirsk, as many life writers wrongly state. His father was an officer in the Russian army, of Tatar descent.

He was sent to Moscow to study under Professor Schaden, then moved to St Petersburg, where he met the poet Dmitriev and spent his time turning foreign essays into Russian. After a quiet spell at Simbirsk he came back to Moscow and its learned society. In 1789 he set out to travel and visited Germany, France, Switzerland, and England. On his return he published his Letters of a Russian Traveller, which met with great success. The letters first appeared in the Moscow Journal, which he edited, and were then gathered into a book.
britannica-1911-katkov-michael-nikiforov:
Michael Nikiforovich Katkov (1818–1887) was a Russian journalist, born in Moscow in 1818. On finishing his course at the university he gave himself to letters and philosophy. He showed so little marked character that through the reign of Nicholas I he never once fell foul of the authorities.

With the liberal reaction of the early years of Alexander II he felt warm sympathy. For a time he pressed for liberal institutions of the British type. But when the stir took on a socialist and nihilist tinge, and when some liberals showed softness toward Polish national hopes, his stance slowly changed. Liberals came to count him a renegade. At the start of 1863 he took the management and editorship of the Moscow Gazette. He held that post until his death in 1887. In those twenty four years he wielded a wide sway over Russian opinion.
britannica-1911-katrine-loch:
Loch Katrine is a fresh water lake of Scotland, lying almost wholly in Perthshire. The loch trends southeast, is about 8 miles long and at most a mile broad, and lies 364 feet above the sea. It covers some four and a third square miles and drains a basin of some thirty seven.

Its mean depth is 142 feet and its greatest depth 495. The yearly rainfall on it is 78 inches, and the water runs warm at the surface and cold at the bottom. Sir Walter Scott made its scenery deathless in The Lady of the Lake. The hills about it are of fair height, Ben A'an at 1750 feet and Ben Venue at 2393 among them. The Gyle and many burns feed it, and the Achray drains it to Loch Achray.
britannica-1911-kerch:
Kerch, or Kertch, is a seaport of southern Russia in the government of Taurida, on the Strait of Kerch or Yenikale, 60 miles east northeast of Theodosia. It held 31,702 people in 1897. It stands on the site of the old Greek city Panticapaeum, clustering round the foot and climbing the sides of the hill named after Mithradates, where the old citadel stood.

The church of St John the Baptist, founded in 717, is a good example of the early Byzantine style. That of Alexander Nevsky was once the Kerch museum of antiquities, founded in 1825. The finer pieces were later moved to the Hermitage at St Petersburg, while those left at Kerch were scattered in the English occupation during the Crimean War. What survives is a small collection in a private house. The entry goes on to the town's trade and to the rich burial mounds of the district.
britannica-1911-kiepert-heinrich:
Heinrich Kiepert, a German geographer who lived from 1818 to 1899, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Berlin in July 1818, he studied history, philology, and geography at the university there. From 1840 to 1846, with Karl Ritter, he issued an atlas of Greece and its colonies. That first work brought him instant standing in ancient historical map-making.

More atlases followed, and his Atlas antiquus of 1854 won wide recognition in many languages. In 1894 he began a larger atlas of the ancient world. His maps for the great collection of Latin inscriptions are also noted. He wrote textbooks of ancient geography, one of which appeared in English in 1881. His general atlas of all parts of the earth ran from 1855 on. Asia Minor drew his special interest, and he visited it four times.
britannica-1911-kirkintilloch:
Kirkintilloch is a municipal and police burgh of Dumbartonshire, Scotland, with 10,680 people in 1901. It stands 8 miles northeast of Glasgow by the North British railway, and part of its parish runs into Lanarkshire. It lies on the Forth and Clyde canal. The Kelvin, from which Lord Kelvin took the title of his barony, flows past the town.

There the Kelvin takes in the Glazert from the north and the Luggie from the south, the stream sung by David Gray. The Wall of Antoninus ran through the town's site. Its Gaelic name means the fort at the end of the ridge, the first word being caer, a fort, not kirk, a church. The town became a burgh of barony under the Comyns in 1170. Its cruciform parish church, with crow stepped gables, dates from 1644. The public buildings include the town hall with its clock tower and a convalescent home.
britannica-1911-klaproth-martin-heinrich:
Martin Heinrich Klaproth, German chemist who lived from 1743 to 1817, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Wernigerode on 1 December 1743. For a large part of his life he worked as an apothecary. He served as assistant in pharmacies at Quedlinburg, Hanover, Berlin, and Danzig in turn.

On the death of Valentin Rose in 1771 he came to Berlin to run that man shop. In 1780 he set up a place of his own in the same city. He became a judge of drugs for the top medical board in 1782. In 1787 he was picked to lecture on chemistry to the Royal Artillery. When the university was founded in 1810, he was chosen as its professor of chemistry. The entry calls him the leading chemist of his time in Germany.
britannica-1911-knigge-adolf-franz-fried:
Adolf Franz Friedrich, Freiherr von Knigge (1752–1796), was a German author born on the family estate of Bredenbeck, near Hanover, on the 16th of October 1752. He studied law at Göttingen and served at the courts of Hesse-Cassel and Weimar as a gentleman-in-waiting. He left court service in 1777 and lived a private life until 1791, when he became a civil administrator in Bremen, where he died on the 6th of May 1796.

As "Philo," Knigge was an active member of the Illuminati, the society founded by Adam Weishaupt at Ingolstadt. He wrote novels, among them Der Roman meines Lebens and the comic Die Reise nach Braunschweig. His best-known work is Über den Umgang mit Menschen (1788), which sets out rules for a peaceful, happy and useful life and was often reprinted. His collected writings filled 12 volumes (1804–1806).
britannica-1911-kriloff-ivan-andreevich:
Ivan Andreevich Kriloff (1768–1844) was the great national fabulist of Russia, born on the 14th of February 1768 at Moscow. His early years were spent at Orenburg and Tver. His father, an army officer, died in 1779, leaving the boy nothing but a chest of old books and his mother to raise him. The family moved to St Petersburg, where Kriloff took a civil service post, then gave it up when his mother died in 1788.

Kriloff found his true place as a writer of fables. The first set, 23 in number, came out in 1809. From 1812 to 1841 he worked at the Imperial Public Library, ending as head of its Russian books. Honours came thick: the Academy of Sciences took him in during 1811. About 77,000 copies of his Fables had sold before his death on the 21st of November 1844. His verse is praised for plain, idiomatic speech and for wisdom drawn from Russian life itself.
britannica-1911-kropotkin-peter-alexeivi:
Peter Alexeivich Kropotkin, Prince (1842– ), was a Russian geographer, author and revolutionary, born at Moscow in 1842. His father came of the old nobility, and his mother had strong literary and liberal tastes. At fifteen he entered the Corps of Pages at St Petersburg, and read widely on his own. In 1862 he chose a Siberian Cossack regiment in the Amur district, and served at Chita and Irkutsk.

In 1864 Kropotkin took charge of a survey expedition, and his Siberian work reshaped the map. He showed that the main lines of the land run from south-west to north-east, not as men had thought. In 1871 he studied the glacial deposits of Finland and Sweden for the Russian Geographical Society. Offered the secretaryship of that body, he refused it. He had resolved to spread the knowledge that exists among the people, rather than add new finds of his own.
britannica-1911-kuropatkin-alexei-nikola:
Alexei Nikolaievich Kuropatkin (1848– ) was a Russian general, born in 1848. He joined the army in 1864 and studied at the Nicholas staff college from 1872 to 1874. He served with French troops in Algiers, did diplomatic work in Kashgaria, and fought in Turkistan and Kokan. In the war of 1877–78 against Turkey he won a great name as chief of staff to the younger Skobelev. His detailed history of that war is still held the classic work on it.

In 1881 Kuropatkin marched 500 miles from Tashkent to Geok-Tepe and helped storm the place. He was a major-general at thirty-four, and men saw him as Skobelev's heir. He left the post of minister of war to command the Russian army in Manchuria against Japan. His failure in the war of 1904–5 is laid in part to the control of Admiral Alexeiev above him, and in part to friction among his generals.
britannica-1911-kurtz-johann-heinrich:
Johann Heinrich Kurtz (1809–1890) was a German Lutheran theologian, born at Montjoie near Aix la Chapelle on the 13th of December 1809. He was educated at Halle and Bonn. Giving up a planned career in trade, he turned to theology. He became a teacher of religion at the gymnasium of Mitau in 1835, then professor at Dorpat, in church history in 1850 and in exegesis in 1859. He gave up his chair in 1870, moved to Marburg, and died there on the 26th of April 1890.

Kurtz wrote a great deal, and many of his books won wide use. His Lehrbuch der heiligen Geschichte (1843) was much loved. In biblical study he wrote a history of the Old Covenant (1848–1855), a work on the Psalms and a commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews. His chief work lay in church history, with text-books and a general handbook (1853–1856). Several of his books were turned into English.
britannica-1911-kutusov-mikhail-larionov:
Mikhail Larionovich Kutusov, Prince of Smolensk (1745–1813), was a Russian field marshal, born at St Petersburg on the 16th of September 1745. He joined the army in 1759 or 1760, served in Poland and against the Turks, and lost an eye in action in 1774. He rose to major-general in 1784 and governor-general of the Crimea in 1787. Under Suvorov he won fame in the Turkish war of 1788–91.

In 1805 Kutusov led the Russian corps that faced Napoleon's advance on Vienna, and won the hard fight at Dürrenstein. Before Austerlitz he tried to stop the allied generals from giving battle, and was overruled. In 1811 he commanded against the Turks. Then the voice of army and people called him to lead the army falling back before Napoleon. He fought at Borodino, was beaten but not decisively, and by his retreat south-west of Moscow forced Napoleon to begin the great retreat.
britannica-1911-lambert-johann-heinrich:
Johann Heinrich Lambert (1728–1777), German physicist, mathematician and astronomer, was born at Mulhausen in Alsace on the 26th of August 1728, the son of a tailor. The little schooling of his town's free school he made up by private reading. He became a book-keeper at the Montbéliard ironworks, then in 1745 secretary to Professor Iselin, a Basel editor, who in 1748 recommended him as tutor to the family of Count A. von Salis at Coire. 

In 1759, after a two-year tour with his pupils through Göttingen, Utrecht, Paris, Marseilles and Turin, he resigned and settled at Augsburg. After brief stays in Munich, Erlangen, Coire and Leipzig he removed in 1764 to Berlin, where Frederick favoured him and he joined the Royal Academy of Sciences. In 1774 he edited the Berlin Ephemeris. He died of consumption on the 25th of September 1777, a man of original mind, gifted at applying mathematics to practice.
britannica-1911-lamech:
Lamech stands in the 1911 Britannica as a figure from the early lists in Genesis, placed before the Flood in two separate lines. One line makes him a descendant of Cain and father of Noah in the other, and the two accounts are treated as variant forms of an older list of early kings.

His Cainite sons carry the weight of the account. Jabal begins the life of herdsmen who move with their flocks, Jubal begins music, and Tubal-Cain works as the first smith. A short old poem in his voice boasts of harsh revenge, and the closing notes weigh the name itself, its doubtful sense, and a link put forward with a Babylonian moon title.
britannica-1911-landsberg-am-lech: Landsberg am Lech is a brief town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The town stands in Bavaria, on the river Lech, west of Munich by rail. In 1905 it held a little over six thousand five hundred people. It has eight Roman Catholic churches, one raised in 1498, and more than one house of monks. A fine town hall of the middle ages holds wall paintings by known artists. A grand old gate, the Bayer-Tor, also stands. Brewing, tanning, and farm machines are the chief trades.
britannica-1911-leech:
Leech is the common name for members of the Hirudinea, a worm group. Its animal entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Which kind first bore the name is in doubt in the entry text. The medicinal leech and the horse leech both have claims noted here.

Now the word covers every member of the Hirudinea group as a whole. Leeches occur in all parts of the world, in water and on land. Water forms haunt streams, ponds, marshes, and the sea near shores. All feed as flesh eaters or as parasites on other animals. Suckers at both ends of the body suit that parasitic life well.
britannica-1911-leo-heinrich:
Heinrich Leo (1799-1878) was a German historian born at Rudolstadt. His father served as garrison chaplain there. A strict home and a love of nature shaped his mind early. A school master, Karl Wilhelm Göttling, fed his taste for history. Study at Breslau, Jena, and Göttingen ran from 1816 to 1819.

Youth pulled him to the radical side. He joined gymnastic clubs and the Black Band at Jena. The murder of Kotzebue shocked him out of that course. From then on he moved step by step to the far right. His doctor's work in 1820 took up the free Lombard towns. A trip to Italy in 1823 fed that line of study. He taught at Erlangen, then at Halle, where he died in April 1878.
britannica-1911-lermontov-mikhail-yurevi:
Mikhail Yurevich Lermontov (1814-1841) was a Russian poet and novelist. Men called him the poet of the Caucasus. Born in Moscow of Scottish stock, he grew up at Tarkhanui under his grandmother's care. No cost was spared on his schooling. Moscow gymnasium and university came first.

A share in rowdy acts against a teacher cut his university time short. Cadet school at St Petersburg ran from 1830 to 1834. A guards officer's post followed. Pushkin's death in 1837 drew a fierce poem from him, sent to the tsar. Exile to the Caucasus was the reply. He had known those hills as a boy of ten. Their stern folk and high rocks matched his heart. In 1839 he wrote A Hero of Our Time. Poems such as The Demon spread his name abroad.
britannica-1911-leven-loch:
Loch Leven is a lake in Kinross-shire, Scotland, and this 1911 Britannica entry describes its shape, its fish, and its islands. The loch is oval, lying at 350 feet above the sea near the south and east edges of the shire. Drainage works in the years after 1826 cut its area by a quarter, yet it still covers over five square miles. It is one of the shallowest lakes in Scotland, less than fifteen feet deep on average.

The loch is famous for its trout, prized for size and quality. Seven islands dot the water. The largest, St Serf's, holds the ruins of the Priory of Portmoak, called the oldest Culdee house in Scotland. Castle Island holds a stronghold from the thirteenth century that was at times a royal home and stood a siege in 1335.
britannica-1911-limbach: Limbach is a town in the kingdom of Saxony, in the mill district of Chemnitz. It stands six miles north-west of that city. The count of 1905 gave 13,723 people. A public park serves the town. A stone there honours the composer Pache. Worsteds, cloth, and silk form the chief trades. Sewing-machine making stands beside them. Dyeing and bleaching round out the work of the place.
britannica-1911-lobachevskiy-nicolas-iva:
Nicolas Ivanovich Lobachevskiy (1793-1856) was a Russian mathematician born near Nizhniy Novgorod. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his move to Kazan as a boy in poor straits. He entered the new university there in 1807 as a student. By 1823 he held its full chair in mathematics for many years.

He was among the first to test the base rules of geometry with rigor. That work made him a pioneer of non Euclidean geometry in the field. A lecture at Kazan in 1826 gave his first results in public. Books in 1840 and a final summary in 1855 spread the work. He also rebuilt Kazan library, labs, and halls as an able manager.
britannica-1911-lobanov-rostovski-alexis:
Lobanov-Rostovski, Alexis Borisovich is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Russian statesman. Prince Alexis Borisovich was born on the thirtieth of December 1824 and died in 1896. He was schooled at the lyceum of Tsarskoe Selo, like so many leading Russians of his day. At twenty he entered the foreign service.

He became minister at Constantinople in 1859. A sad affair in his private life made him quit public work for a time in 1863. Four years later he came back and served ten years as aide to the minister of the interior. At the close of the war with Turkey in 1878 the emperor picked him as ambassador at Constantinople. There he worked, with skill, to calm the Eastern Question after the rash acts of his forerunner. Posts at London and Vienna followed.
britannica-1911-lomond-loch:
Loch Lomond is the largest of Scotland's lakes, set in Stirling and Dumbarton ground. Length runs near 23 miles. Width swings from five miles at the south end to a mile and a third at the narrows. Ground covered is 27 square miles and depth tops 630 feet. The loch sits just 23 feet over sea level.

Thirty islands dot its face. Inchmurrin, the largest, serves as a deer park for the duke of Montrose. Inch Cailliach held a nunnery once. Inchlonaig bears yews Bruce had planted for bow wood. Five streams feed it from the west, four from the east, and the Falloch from the north. The Leven drains it south to the Clyde. Ben Lomond, 3,192 feet, rules the view. Sea-trout, lake-trout, pike, and perch fill its waters.
britannica-1911-lomonosov-mikhail-vasili:
Mikhail Vasilievich Lomonosov (1711-1765) was a Russian poet and man of science, and this 1911 Britannica entry tells of his hunger for learning. He was born in the village of Denisovka, on an island near Kholmogori in the Archangel country. His father was a fisherman, and from the age of ten the boy worked beside him. Yet his thirst for knowledge had no bounds, and he learned the few books he could reach almost by heart.

Seeing no way to grow his stock of learning at home, he made for Moscow at seventeen and gained a place at the Zaikonospasski school. There he raced ahead, and in 1734 he was sent on to St Petersburg. He was sent abroad to finish his training and took up the study of metals at Marburg, where he also began to write poetry.
britannica-1911-long-branch:
Long Branch is a city in Monmouth county, New Jersey, on the Atlantic coast south of New York City. The 1911 Britannica article gives its count as 13,298 in 1910, up from 8,872 in 1900. Rail lines and steamboats link it with New York. The city stands on a bluff that rises twenty to thirty-five feet above the beach. It ranks among the oldest watering places in America.

Ocean Avenue runs for five miles along the bluff edge, with wide views of the sea. A bluff walk runs two miles above the water. The city has a hospital, a library, and parks by the sea and on the Shrewsbury river. Open-air operas are given in one park each summer. The south end, Elberon, holds grand summer houses. General Grant spent his summers in one, and President Garfield died in one in 1881.
britannica-1911-lucke-gottfried-christia:
Gottfried Christian Friedrich Lucke lived from 1791 to 1855 and was a German theologian. The 1911 Britannica life opens at Egeln near Magdeburg, his birth town. His father was a merchant in that small Saxon town. Lucke studied the study of God at Halle and at Gottingen. In 1813 he became a tutor at Gottingen in that field.

In 1814 Halle gave him the degree of doctor in philosophy. Two years later he moved to Berlin to teach and to write. There he grew close to Schleiermacher and to de Wette in work. In 1819 the three men joined to edit a journal of theology. His lectures and books soon won him a wide name in Germany.
britannica-1911-malstatt-burbach:
Malstatt-Burbach, a town of Germany in the Prussian Rhine province, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the right bank of the Saar, facing Saarbrücken across the river. The count in 1900 was 31195 people. The town lies in the midst of a rich coal and works district.

In form it is little more than a long narrow row of factories and homes for workmen. Its largest works make iron, steel, and cement. A large wharf on the river ships coal out in bulk. Malstatt gained town rights in 1321 but later gave them up to Saarbrücken. In 1818 the two villages held only about 800 people in all. Growth of mining and railways then swelled them fast, and they joined as one town in 1874.
britannica-1911-marko-kralyevich:
Marko Kralyevich, a Serbian hero, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In history he was the son of a Serbian king who died in 1371. Stung at not becoming king himself, he led a revolt against the new ruler. Later he passed into the service of the sultan of Turkey and was killed in battle about 1394.

The article says he is greater in legend than in history. The Serbian people see in him the image of their race, and tales of strength and wonder cling to his name. He is said to have lived for three hundred years and ridden a horse one hundred and fifty years old. He used his vast strength against oppressors, above all against the Turks. One tale says he quit the world when firearms came, since they made strength and valour count for nothing. Goethe set him beside Hercules.
britannica-1911-matvyeev-artamon-sergyee:
Artamon Matvyeev was a Russian state aide and reformer who died in the late sixteen hundreds. The 1911 Britannica entry calls him one of the great forerunners of Peter the Great. His birth and parentage are not sure, but he rose as a learned man, free of the worst narrow views of his age, and even wrote works of his own.

The entry traces his rise at the court of the tsar Alexius, whose chief aide he became. At his house, full of new things from the west, the tsar met the young bride he wed the next year. Matvyeev brought stage plays and other western ways into Moscow, backed the young Peter for the throne, and was then cast out by rival boyars.
britannica-1911-meletius-of-antioch:
Meletius of Antioch, a bishop and saint of the old church, fills a creed strife life in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Melitene of rich and high folk, he rose in the court church camp. Near three fifty seven he backed Acacius, chief of the soft creed camp. That camp sought a pact words to bridge two creed foes of the age. As a court man he took the see of Sebaste in that strife.

The clergy there spurned his post and drove him out to Beroea town. In three sixty he rose to the great see of Antioch in the east. Exile took him the next year on a claim of loose creed words. His flock kept a lone church in the old town while he was gone. A rival bishop of strict creed made the split worse in his lack.
britannica-1911-menshikov-alexander-serg:
Alexander Sergeievich Menshikov, a Russian prince who lived from 1787 to 1869, is the subject of a short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the great grandson of an earlier Menshikov and was born in September 1787. He entered Russian service as an attache at the embassy in Vienna. He joined the emperor on campaigns against Napoleon.

Menshikov left army service in 1823 and gave himself to naval matters. He became an admiral in 1834 and put the decayed Russian navy on a sound footing. At the start of the Crimean War he was made commander in chief by land and sea. He led the Russian army at the Alma and around Sevastopol. In March 1855 he was recalled, in name and perhaps in truth for failing health.
britannica-1911-merck-johann-heinrich:
Johann Heinrich Merck, who lived from 1741 to 1791, was a German author and critic born at Darmstadt. The 1911 Britannica entry notes his father, a chemist, died days before his birth. Law study at Giessen led to a pay office post at Darmstadt in 1767. A year later he himself became paymaster in that state service.

For years he swayed the literary movement in Germany from that modest base. He helped found a Frankfurt learned journal in 1772 with close allies. Work for Nicolai great review library kept his critical voice widely heard. Travel to Saint Petersburg and Weimar filled his later public years with honour.
britannica-1911-middlewich:
Middlewich is a town article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a town district in Cheshire, England. It lies 166 miles north west of London, on a main rail line. Its count in 1901 was 4,669.

The article sets the town in open country near the river Dane. Canals link it to a wide water network. The church of Saint Michael and All Angels shows work of many ages and holds many carved memorials. Old timber framed houses, a Cheshire mark, stand in and near the town. Salt works are the chief trade, shared with Northwich and Winsford near by. Chemical works and a plant that makes condensed milk add to the town's base.
britannica-1911-miloradovich-michael-and:
Michael Andrijevich Miloradovich was a Russian general and count of the Napoleonic wars. He lived from seventeen seventy to eighteen twenty five. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He served under Suvarov in wars against Turkey and Poland early on.

In the Italy and Switzerland campaign of seventeen ninety nine Miloradovich won high praise. He led advance troops with skill in that hard mountain campaign. In eighteen o five he served under Kutusov at Austerlitz battle field. His column held the Pratzen heights in that lost fight of December. At Borodino he led a corps, then beat Murat at Tarutino.
britannica-1911-neubreisach: Neubreisach is a town and fortress in Alsace Lorraine, described in a brief place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the Rhine Rhone canal, east of Colmar. The town is built in the shape of an eight sided figure. Louis the Fourteenth founded it in 1699, and Vauban built its walls. In 1870 the Germans bombarded it for eight days until it gave up.
britannica-1911-neumann-karl-friedrich:
Karl Friedrich Neumann, who lived from 1793 to 1870, was a German scholar of the east. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth name, Bamberger. He was born near Bamberg in December 1793. Studies at Heidelberg, Munich, and Göttingen came first. He turned Protestant and took the name Neumann. After teaching at Spires, he learned Armenian in Venice. In 1829 he sailed for China.

In China he studied the tongue and amassed a vast library. Some 12,000 books and manuscripts came home with him. He gave that hoard to the royal library at Munich. In 1831 he took a chair of Armenian and Chinese at Munich. Strong views in the revolt years cost him that chair in 1852. He spent his last years in Berlin on history. His books treat England's realm in Asia and the United States.
britannica-1911-offenbach:
Offenbach, a town in the German grand duchy of Hesse, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the left bank of the Main river, five miles from Frankfurt. Close to fifty nine thousand people lived there at the count in the entry. The old castle of the counts of Isenburg is named as its most notable building.

Work and trade take up most of the account. Offenbach was the chief factory town of the duchy, with goods of many kinds. Its best known trade was fine leather work, such as wallets, albums, and cases. The town is first named in a record from the year 970. French Protestant refugees who settled there helped it grow. Joining the German customs union in 1828 gave trade a further lift.
britannica-1911-orthodox-eastern-church:
Orthodox Eastern Church is the formal name for the church of the ancient East. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica also gives its common name as the Greek Church. Its full title is the Holy Orthodox Catholic Apostolic Eastern Church. Member churches accept the first seven general councils in full, it says.

Christian faith began in the East, with Greek as its first tongue. As Rome empire split, eastern and western churches grew apart in kind. Four eastern patriarch seats rose at Antioch, Alexandria, Jerusalem, and Constantinople. Rule in the east is shared among patriarchs, not held by one head. Each patriarch is supreme within his own diocese in that system.
britannica-1911-ostrovskiy-alexander-nik:
Alexander Nikolaivich Ostrovskiy, a Russian writer of plays who lived from 1823 to 1886, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Moscow, where his father was an officer of the senate. He read law at the university there but left with no degree. He then clerked in courts that heard the suits of merchants.

Those courts gave him the men and women of his first comedies. His plays show the raw, self-pleased merchants of Moscow with a sharp eye. One such play was banned for ten years, and he lost his post and lived under the eye of the police. A kindlier reign freed him and sent him up the Volga to report on the folk. That trip fed a run of plays drawn from the past of Russia.
britannica-1911-paskevich-ivan-fedorovic:
Paskevich, Ivan Fedorovich is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Russian field marshal of the nineteenth century. Born at Poltava in 1782 to an old family, he was schooled at the school for pages. In 1800 he took a Guards commission as aide-de-camp to the tsar. He fought at Austerlitz in 1805, then served against Turkey until 1812, winning a general's rank in his thirtieth year.

Command against Persia in 1826 brought swift triumphs, peace in 1828, and the title count of Erivan with rich gifts. Sent next against Turkey in Asia, he took fortress after fortress and was made field marshal at forty seven. In 1831 he crushed the Polish revolt, took Warsaw, and became prince of Warsaw and viceroy of Poland. Wounded at Silistria in 1854, he retired and died at Warsaw in 1856.
britannica-1911-passow-franz-ludwig-carl:
Franz Ludwig Carl Friedrich Passow, who lived from 1786 to 1833, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a German classical scholar and maker of word books. Born at Ludwigslust, he was named to a Greek chair at Weimar in 1807 by Goethe. In 1815 he moved to a chair of ancient letters at Breslau, where he stayed until his death.

His great work was a handbook dictionary of the Greek tongue, issued from 1819 to 1824. It began as a rework of an older lexicon by Schneider. By its fourth edition it stood as his own work alone. The article notes that it formed the basis of the famed Greek lexicon of Liddell and Scott. It also lists his editions of Persius, Longus, and other classic authors.
britannica-1911-peach:
Peach is a fruit tree classed by most botanists with the plum. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out its flower and fruit build. Some writers group it with the almond instead. Others give it a genus of its own called Persica.

The tree is of medium size with long narrow leaves. Blooms sit single or in small groups on last year shoots. Five sepals and five pink or white petals ring many stamens. The fruit is a drupe with skin, flesh, and stone. That build matches the plum and the apricot exactly. The almond differs only as its flesh turns dry and splits. Nectarine is a smooth skinned sport of the same tree. Peach seed can yield nectarines, and the reverse also holds. Both fruits can even share a single branch in rare cases.
britannica-1911-peesemsky-alexey-feofila:
Alexey Feofilactovich Peesemsky is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born on his father's estate in the province of Kostroma on the twenty second of March 1820, he was a Russian writer of tales. His forebears were of old noble stock but very poor.

The article tells of a boyhood spent reading Scott and Hugo in translation. He passed through Moscow University and took a post as a clerk in state service. His first tale was banned for its harsh view of the Russian nobles. His best known tale, of 1862, counts a thousand souls in its title. A play on the dark side of farm life won him a prize from the Russian Academy. He died at Moscow in February 1881.
britannica-1911-pertz-georg-heinrich:
Georg Heinrich Pertz was a German writer on the past who lived from seventeen ninety-five to eighteen seventy-six. He was born at Hanover and read at a chief school past a famed teacher. His first work on old palace chiefs caught the eye of a great lord. That lord set him to print old tales for a new group.

He roamed the stores of Germany and Italy for source texts. In time he took chief charge of a vast print of all chief writs on German deeds to the year fifteen hundred. That work, in scores of books, made new strict lore of the mid age past.
britannica-1911-pestalozzi-johann-heinri:
Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi, a Swiss reformer of schooling, was born at Zurich in seventeen forty six. His father died when he was young, and his mother raised him. At the university of Zurich he joined Lavater and the party of reform. His earliest years went to schemes for lifting the state of the people. The death of a friend turned him from politics to education.

Pestalozzi wed at twenty three and bought waste land at Neuhof in Aargau. He tried to farm madder there, but he knew nothing of business. The plan failed, and a school he opened in his farm house failed too. His first book, a set of short thoughts, came out in seventeen eighty. His great work Leonard and Gertrude followed a year later. That tale of a village reformed by a good woman was read with hunger in Germany.
britannica-1911-petermann-august-heinric:
August Heinrich Petermann, who lived from 1822 to 1878, was a German map maker. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth near Nordhausen. At seventeen he entered the school of map art at Potsdam. In 1845 he went to Edinburgh to aid an English atlas. In 1847 he settled in London and issued works there. One told of Barth's expedition to central Africa.

In 1854 he took charge of the Perthes institute at Gotha. There he edited the famed journal that bears his name. His work cleared up much of the map of inner Africa. The north polar regions owe him the same debt. Queen Victoria made him geographer royal at Bunsen's urging. He died by his own hand at Gotha in September 1878. The entry is brief, but it marks a hub of the age's map trade.
britannica-1911-petrarch:
Petrarch, born Francesco Petrarca in thirteen hundred and four, is the subject of a long life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry calls him the great Italian poet and the first true reviver of learning in medieval Europe. It opens with his birth at Arezzo and with his father Petracco, a notary who was driven out of Florence with Dante.

Readers follow the boy from Incisa on the Arno to Pisa and then to Avignon in thirteen thirteen. The text stresses how the move shaped the poet and scholar he became. It also notes the pure Tuscan speech he learned as a child and later used with great skill in ode and sonnet. The entry gives a full base for study of his life and work.
britannica-1911-pike-perch:
Pike perch are fresh water fish closely allied to the perch family. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes strong canine teeth set among smaller teeth in their jaws. Long bodies and heads make them look much like pike as well. They hunt other fresh water fish with great effect on stocks.

Fine flavor of their flesh offsets that harm in human eyes. Two species live in Europe, with the Zander the best known. That fish favors quiet large rivers and clear deep lakes. It can reach twenty five to thirty pounds in weight there. Two North American forms fill Canadian lakes and the upper Mississippi.
britannica-1911-piozzi-hester-lynch:
Hester Lynch Piozzi is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was an English writer who lived from 1741 to 1821. She is best known as Mrs Thrale, the friend of Samuel Johnson. Her father was John Salusbury of Carnarvonshire. She and her mother lived in London, and she gained a solid schooling. She knew Latin as well as French, Italian, and Spanish.

The article tells how she wed Henry Thrale, a rich Southwark brewer, in 1763. Their house at Streatham drew a famed circle of friends. She was introduced to Johnson in 1765, and he paid a long visit in 1766. From then on he was more or less at home with the Thrales. He spent the middle of each week at Streatham. He travelled with them in Wales and in France. When Thrale's business was hurt in 1772, her efforts saved the situation.
britannica-1911-pitch:
Pitch is the name of dark, sticky stuffs that grow soft and tenacious with heat, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica treats the word in a short entry with two branches. In the strict sense, pitch is the solid left over when wood tar is distilled. A like stuff from coal tar bears the name too, though it is not resinous.

The name also covers natural mineral stuffs, that is asphalt or bitumen. The word comes from an old English form of a Latin term, kin to Greek words for pine. The second branch of the entry turns to pitch as a verb and noun of place and slope. To pitch is first to thrust a pointed thing into the ground and fix it. From that come the senses of setting in order, of throwing, and of sloping. Its root is obscure, and may be a variant of pick.
britannica-1911-plehve-viatscheslaf-kons:
Viatscheslaf Konstantinovich Plehve is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a Russian statesman born in eighteen forty six. He was trained in law and rose fast in the courts and the civil service. By eighteen eighty one he ran the state police force.

The entry tells how his sharp work on a royal murder case won the trust of the tsar. He rose to run the home ministry in nineteen hundred and two. He pushed hard to force one tongue and faith on the lands of the empire. That course won him deep hate in Poland and Finland. He was killed by a bomb in nineteen hundred and four.
britannica-1911-plutarch:
Plutarch, a Greek biographer and wide ranging writer who lived from about 46 to 120, gets a long life entry in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Chaeronea in Boeotia, he studied at Athens and spent time at Rome, where he lectured and taught the young Hadrian. Trajan gave him consular rank, and Hadrian made him procurator of Greece. He died in his home town, where he served as archon and priest.

His fame rests chiefly on the forty-six Parallel Lives, thought to be work of his later years. In them he set a Greek and a Roman side by side in pairs, matched by their gifts or their lot. Theseus is paired with Romulus, and Alexander with Caesar. Long lists of sources mark the Lives as works of deep learning. The series ends with single lives, among them Galba and Otho.
britannica-1911-porch:
Porch names a covered frame that shelters the door of a large building. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows the form through the ages. The word comes through French from a Latin term for a colonnade. The first known cases stand at the Tower of the Winds in Athens.

Early Christian churches had a long arched porch called a narthex. Later church porches took two main forms in the West. Some spread wide across the west front with split doors. Others form a small roofed room on a side wall. Norman porches project only a little and bear rich carving. Later ones grow longer, with steep roofs and rooms above. Those upper rooms served as vestries or small chapels at times.
britannica-1911-repin-ilja-jefimovich:
Ilja Jefimovich Repin was a Russian painter who was born in eighteen forty-four at a town in the Charkov tract. His folk were poor. He learned the first steps of art from a painter of saints and lived by that craft for three years. In eighteen sixty-three he won a place at the chief art school.

Six years there brought a gold prize and a trip grant to France and Italy. Home once more, he chose themes of strong home mark. His works show firm line, deep feel, and sharp cast of face. His best known work shows a band of wild horse men in jest with a sultan.
britannica-1911-research:
Research is the act of search into a matter with close care, a hunt aimed at the find of truth. The 1911 Britannica entry draws the word from old French and late Latin roots that mean to go round in a ring, to roam and probe. In its strict sense it means trained probe of the laws and facts of a theme.

Such work, the entry says, rests on first hand study of sources or on trials in the lab. All probe built on first sources may bear the name. With no such work, no sound books have been writ, no finds in science made, and no views of worth put forth. In common use the word clings to the study of pure science more than to work science, to causes more than to craft use.
britannica-1911-reusch-franz-heinrich:
Franz Heinrich Reusch, an Old Catholic theologian who lived from 1823 to 1900, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Brilon in Westphalia, he studied at Paderborn and then theology at Bonn, Tubingen, and Munich. He was the friend and pupil of Dollinger, under whom he took his doctor's degree at Munich.

The entry says he was ordained priest in 1849 and became a chaplain at Cologne. From 1854 he taught the reading of the Old Testament at Bonn, rising to full professor in 1861. He also edited a Bonn theology review for eleven years. In the dispute over papal infallibility he sided with Dollinger. For that stand the archbishop barred him from teaching in 1871, and he was cast out of the church in 1872.
britannica-1911-rimsky-korsakov-nicolas-:
Nicolas Andreievich Rimsky-Korsakov, a Russian composer who lived from 1844 to 1908, gets a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Tikhvin in Novgorod, he was one of the young amateurs who gathered round Balakirev at St Petersburg. By 1865 his first symphony had been played under Balakirev, the first by a Russian composer. In 1873 he left the navy for a chair at the St Petersburg Conservatoire.

That year he wed a gifted pianist and brought out his first opera, Pskovitianka. Operas followed, from May Night to Sadko and The Tsar's Bride. Abroad, his fame rests more on his orchestral works, with their mastery of colour and fine use of Russian folk tunes. His Spanish Capriccio of 1887 is singled out, and he died at St Petersburg in 1908.
britannica-1911-roach: Roach is a small fish of the carp family, found across Europe in fresh waters. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives its Latin name as Leuciscus rutilus. Kin in the same genus include the rudd, the chub, and the dace. A roach can pass twelve inches long, but one of two pounds is rare. Its color is silvery, with reddish fins marking it well. Anglers value it for sport, though cooks rate it low. It does not occur in Ireland, the entry notes.
britannica-1911-roscher-wilhelm-georg-fr:
Wilhelm Georg Friedrich Roscher, a German economist who lived from 1817 to 1894, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Hanover and studied at Gottingen and Berlin. He became a professor at Gottingen in 1844 and then at Leipzig in 1848. The origin of the historical school of political economy may be traced to Roscher.

Its founding principles are dated to his short study of 1843 on lectures in political economy by the historical method. That study grew into his great System of Political Economy, in five volumes from 1854 to 1894. The volumes cover the foundations of the subject, farming, trade and industry, finance, and poor relief. His history of political economy in Germany, in 1874, is called a monumental work by the entry. He died at Leipzig in June 1894.
britannica-1911-rostoptschin-count-feodo:
Feodor Vassilievich Rostoptschin is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Rostoptschin was a Russian general who lived from 1763 to 1826. He was born in the government of Orel. He held great sway with Tsar Paul, who made him a top court officer and then minister of the interior. In 1799 he gained the title of count. He fell from favour in 1801 for opposing a French alliance.

The article tells how favour returned in 1810 and he became military governor of Moscow. He was charged with its defence against Napoleon. He used every means to rouse the town against the invader. He has often been charged with starting the burning of Moscow after the French entered. He denied the charge in print in 1823, but later made grave admissions. He died at Moscow in 1826.
britannica-1911-rubinstein-anton-grigoro:
Anton Grigorovich Rubinstein (1829–1894) was a Russian pianist, born on 28 November 1829 at Wechwotynetz in Podolia. He was the son of a maker of pencils who moved to Moscow. At the word of his grandfather, the whole family was baptized in 1830, when Anton was one year old. His one teacher, apart from his mother, was the piano master Alexander Villoing. Rubinstein said at the end of his life that he had never met a better teacher.

In July 1838 Rubinstein played in a theatre in Moscow, and the next year he went to Paris after Villoing. In 1840 he played before Liszt. He then went through Holland, Germany, and the north lands, and he reached England in 1842. There he played his first concert for the Choral Fund. In 1845 he went with his family, his brother Nikolaus with them, to Berlin.
britannica-1911-s-hertogenbosch:
's Hertogenbosch is chief town of North Brabant in Holland. French tongues call it Bois-le-Duc. It stands where the Dommel and Aa join to form the Dieze. Rail links run to Utrecht and Nijmwegen. The Zuid-Willem canal ties it to Maastricht. The count of 1900 gave 32,345 people.

St John's cathedral leads its sights. The choir rose in the mid-1400s on an older church's ground. Rare in Holland, its inner state is well kept. Font of the 1400s, pulpit of 1570, and organ of 1617 all draw note. A Lady chapel holds a prized Virgin image of the 1200s, borne through town each year. Its choir screen was sold to the South Kensington Museum for £900. Town hall panels paint the town's founding tale. Two museums hold Roman, German, and Frankish finds.
britannica-1911-saltykov-michael-evgrafo:
Michael Evgrafovich Saltykov, known as Stchedrin, a Russian satirist who lived from 1826 to 1889, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born on his father's estate in the province of Tula. His schooling was wholly neglected, and his youth was marked by harsh parents and domestic quarrels. Left to himself, he grew to love reading, though the Bible was the only book in the house.

At ten he entered the Moscow Institute for sons of the nobility, then the Lyceum at Saint Petersburg. There he published poems and translations of Byron and Heine. A clerkship in the Ministry of War followed. An early work of his led to banishment to Vyatka, where he spent eight years as a minor official. That time let him study provincial officials at close hand, the material of his famed Provincial Sketches.
britannica-1911-search:
Search, or visit and search, is a term of international law treated in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The entry says the phrase comes, in a confused way, from a French word meaning search. Some writers try to split visit from search, but that only breeds misunderstanding, it argues. Search is the exact English match for the French word.

The right of search belongs to fighting powers alone. Its aim is to check a ship's nationality and, if the ship is neutral, to see whether it carries contraband. Fighting back against search leads to capture and trial in a prize court. The entry quotes the Declaration of London of 1909 on this point. Force used against lawful search brings the loss of the ship in all cases, it states.
britannica-1911-sempach:
Sempach is a small town in the Swiss canton of Lucerne, described in this 1911 Britannica article. It is built above the east shore of the lake of the same name, north of its railway station. In 1900 it had 2,592 people, German speaking and Roman Catholic in faith.

The town keeps traces of its old look, above all its main gateway under a watch tower, reached by a bridge over the old moat. About half an hour to the north-east lies the site of the famed battle of Sempach of July 1386. There the Swiss beat the Austrians, and Duke Leopold lost his life, and the deed of Arnold of Winkelried is linked with that win. A battle chapel and a monument to Winkelried now mark the spot.
britannica-1911-spanish-reformed-church:
Spanish Reformed Church is a 1911 Britannica article on a small body of Protestants in Spain. The church is organized on the model of the Anglican Church. Its members may be called Spanish Episcopalians. The body had its origin in a single congregation.

That congregation met for the first time in June 1871. It met in the secularized church of San Basilio at Seville. Its leader was Francisco Palomares, a priest who had left the Roman communion. Lay people soon joined it in numbers. Several clergymen joined as well. Among them was Juan Cabrera, a former Roman priest. He had served for some time as a Presbyterian minister. In July 1878 a memorial went to the Lambeth Conference. Nine congregations in Spain and Portugal signed it. They asked for the episcopate for their church. The reply expressed sympathy, as the article goes on to tell.
britannica-1911-spiess-christian-heinric:
Christian Heinrich Spiess (1755-1799), a German writer of romances, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Freiberg in Saxony, he was for a time an actor. In 1788 he took a post as steward on the estate of a count in Bohemia. He died there in 1799, almost out of his mind, the entry says, as a result of his own weird fancies.

The article names him the founder of the German tale of horror. His books told of knights, robbers, and ghosts of the dark ages.
