He took the idea from works by Goethe and Schiller, and later writers kept the style going in a finer vein. Though his tales appealed to coarse taste, they made him one of the most read authors of his day. His most loved book was a ghost story of the thirteenth century, printed in 1793.
britannica-1911-spinach:
Spinach is an annual plant grown for its juicy leaves, and a practical entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells how to grow it through the year. It is probably of Persian origin and reached Europe about the fifteenth century. It wants good ground, well worked and well manured, with plenty of water for summer crops.

The entry gives a sowing calendar. Winter spinach goes in early and late in August, in rows eighteen inches apart, and the plants are thinned as they grow. The prickly-seeded and Flanders sorts are rated best for winter. Summer spinach is sown from February on, in small lots every fortnight, since it lasts only a short time.
britannica-1911-spinoza-baruch:
Baruch Spinoza is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a Dutch philosopher. He afterwards signed himself Benedict de Spinoza. He lived from 1632 to 1677. He was born at Amsterdam on the twenty fourth of November 1632. His parents belonged to the community of Jewish emigrants. Those emigrants had come from Portugal and from Spain. They fled Catholic persecution in the Peninsula. They sought refuge in the nearly free Netherlands.

The family name points to the province of Leon as a home. Five townships of that name lie near Burgos. His grandfather was head of the Amsterdam Jewish community in 1628. His father Michael was repeatedly warden of the synagogue. That service ran between 1630 and the year 1650. The father was a merchant in fair circumstances. He was thrice married and had six children in all. The entry roots the philosopher in a refugee merchant house.
britannica-1911-spitta-friedrich:
Spitta, Friedrich, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a German church scholar. Born at Wittingen on the 10th of January 1852, he was son of a famed hymn writer. He read at Gottingen and Erlangen. In 1887 he became a full chair holder and preacher at Strassburg.

From 1896 he helped edit a monthly journal on worship and church art. He was best known for a work on the Acts of the Apostles from 1891. The entry lists more of his books by name and year. They deal with the child Jesus, the Book of Revelation, and church worship reform. A three-part set on early church life and letters ran from 1893 to 1901.
britannica-1911-squinch:
Squinch is a 1911 Britannica article on a term used in building. A squinch is a way of corbelling out across the corners of a square tower. Arched rings of stone are thrown across each angle. Those rings then carry an eight-sided spire or a dome.

The earliest examples stand in palaces built by the Sassanian dynasty. Those at Serbittan and Firuzabad date from the years 350 to 450. In the mosque at Damascus, the squinch takes the form of a niche. Early French Romanesque work used a small niche with added rings above. Small shafts at the sides could give it more weight. Examples are named in the Coptic churches of Egypt. Others stand in France, at Le Puy cathedral and at Dijon. Builders and art readers get a small device with a long reach across East and West.
britannica-1911-starch:
Starch, a store food made by green plants, is set out in a plant and trade entry in the 1911 Britannica. It forms in live plant cells by the work of green leaf stuff in light. All plants that hold that green stuff hold starch in some part. In leaves it forms and shifts with great speed in the day. As fruit time nears, stores of it pile in set parts of the plant.

Roots, bulbs, and tubers hold vast stores of the food for the plant. Grain, beans, and fruits such as bananas hold it in bulk as well. Its grains are small, and each source gives grains of its own shape. Hot water makes it swell to a thick cloud paste. A blue flash with iodine forms a sure test for its trace.
britannica-1911-states-of-the-church:
States of the Church, also called the Papal States, were lands in central Italy ruled direct by the see of Rome. A 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry gives their shape before Italy was joined as one kingdom. Names for them in Italian, French, German, and church Latin are listed.

Apart from two small pockets, the lands formed one compact block. Lombardy and Venice lay to the north west, and the Adriatic to the north east. Naples lay to the south east, and the sea to the south west. Tuscany and Modena lay to the west. The coast ran a long way on each sea. A table lists each district, from the Comarca of Rome to Benevento, with its area in square miles.
britannica-1911-stellenbosch:
Stellenbosch is a town in the Cape province of South Africa, east of Cape Town by rail. A 1911 Britannica entry gives its people as 7573 in 1904, a third of them white. It lies in a pleasant upland valley on the slope of the coast range. Next to the capital it is the oldest settlement in the whole province.

Commandant Simon van der Stell founded it in 1681 and named it from himself and his wife. Great oaks line streets where thatched gable houses date from the 1600s. Church headquarters, a seminary, colleges, and a music school fill the town. The entry paints a place where schooling and faith anchor daily life.
britannica-1911-stomach:
Stomach is the subject of a medical article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The stomach is the bag like organ of digestion in the upper left part of the belly. Its name comes from a Greek word linked to the mouth. The article sends readers to other entries for its structure and its common diseases. It gives its own space to cancer of the stomach.

Cancer, the text says, is a common disease of the stomach. It strikes most often at or after middle life, in men and women alike. Its favoured site is the outlet, where a hard growth forms a narrowing ring. Signs can stay vague for weeks or months, as mere indigestion. Later come local pain, trouble in swallowing, and vomiting of large amounts of undigested food. Gas from fermenting food swells the organ and causes belching.
britannica-1911-strauss-david-friedrich:
David Friedrich Strauss (1808-1874) was a German theologian and man of letters. He was born at Ludwigsburg, near Stuttgart, on 27 January 1808. At thirteen he was sent to the seminary at Blaubeuren to be readied for the study of religion. His teachers there lit in their pupils a deep love of the old Greek and Latin classics above all. In 1825 Strauss went on to the university at Tubingen.

The philosophy teachers at Tubingen left Strauss cold. The works of Schleiermacher drew him strongly and freed him from the haze of romantic mysticism. In 1830 he became a helper to a country clergyman. He then taught Latin, history, and Hebrew at the high school at Maulbronn. In the autumn of 1831 he gave up that post to study in Berlin. Hegel died just as Strauss reached the city.
britannica-1911-suso-heinrich:
Heinrich Suso is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a German mystic born near Lake Constance near the year thirteen hundred. He took his mother name and was trained for the church at two towns. At Cologne he fell under the sway of a great mystic teacher.

The entry tells of the hard fasts and trials he laid on his own flesh. He then walked the land as a preacher and won hearts with soft speech. Nuns prized his song like words on the love of God. Two small books set out his thought, one on truth and one on wisdom. The second is called the finest fruit of German mystic writing.
britannica-1911-suvarov-alexander-vasili:
Alexander Suvarov was a Russian field marshal born at Moscow, of stock that traced to a Swede who had moved to Russia. He joined the army as a boy and served against the Swedes and in a great war against Prussia. He stood out in fight after fight, and rose to colonel while still a young man.

The 1911 Britannica entry tracks his wars in Poland, where he broke up rebel forces and stormed a great city. In first wars with the Turks he laid the base of his fame, above all in one great battle. He crushed a vast rising of peasants at home. Then came years of war in the Crimea and the hills of the Caucasus, with rank on rank won, and a fresh round of wins against the Turks.
britannica-1911-sylburg-friedrich:
Friedrich Sylburg is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was a German classical scholar from 1536 to 1596. He was born at Wetter near Marburg, son of a farmer. He studied at Marburg, Jena, Geneva, and Paris. At Paris his teacher was Henry Estienne, a famed scholar. He later gave much aid to that teacher great Greek word book. Back in Germany he held school posts in two towns.

At Lich he brought out a Greek tongue book in 1580. In 1583 he moved to Frankfort to edit Greek texts. A keen publisher there kept him at that work. Fine sets of Greek past writers came from his hand. A set of Aristotle works stands in that list. In 1591 he moved to Heidelberg as a book keeper. More sets for a new publisher followed that move.
britannica-1911-tchernaiev-mikhail-grego:
Tchernaiev, Mikhail Gregorjovich, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a Russian general. Born on the 24th of October 1828, he was of a noble house. He was schooled at the Nicholas Staff College and joined the army in 1847. He won note in the Crimean war and in the Caucasus.

In 1864 he led a famed march of 1,000 men across the Turkestan steppes. His force took Chimkent, then failed at Tashkent, eighty miles south. The next year he took Tashkent, though his orders said not to. The emperor gave him a sword of honour for the feat. Yet he was not used again in army service. He left the army in July 1874 and turned to the press.
britannica-1911-thatch:
Thatch, the plant stuff used for roofs in place of tiles or slates, is the topic of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word links to old tongues for roof and cover, and to the French word chaume. A good thatch uses wheat straw laid in layers. The depth runs from twelve to fourteen inches, and at times to eighteen.

Unthreshed straw is said to last twenty five to thirty years and is easy to mend. Marsh reeds in Norfolk last thirty to forty years or more. Such roofs are warm in winter and cool in summer. Town rules barred them in London, yet lime treatment was said to make thatch hard to burn.
britannica-1911-torch: Torch is a brief word entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes through Old French from a Latin term for a thing twisted. A torch is a light carried in the hand, made of twisted tow, hemp, or other stuff that burns well. The entry recalls the days before street lights were common. Then torches, also called links, were a need for all who walked or rode in towns at night. Many old houses in London kept iron stands by their doors for such lights.
britannica-1911-touch:
Touch, the sense of pressure, is worked through in a body study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word runs back through French to a root shared with tug. Touch is a sense of push felt at the skin's face. Light contact is still a gentle push, the entry reasons. More force gives a feel of push back from the skin.

Still more force wakes a sense of strain in the muscles. A weight held on the open palm shows that third step well. Push past that point and the feel turns into pain. Force can also pull, as when a hair is tugged or twirled. Touch in this way kin to hearing, the entry notes. Both senses answer to pushes laid on a sense organ.
britannica-1911-vetch:
Vetch is the subject of a plant entry in the 1911 Britannica. In botany the name is for a kind of legume herb. It is also known by the plain name of tare. Its stems trail or climb as it grows each year. Its leaves hold five or six pairs of leaflets. Its blooms are red purple and grow in the leaf joints. Its silky pod holds from four to ten smooth seeds. A wild form is common on dry soils of Britain.

Two races of the crop vetch are set out here. Winter vetch is hardy and can bear hard frost. Spring vetch is tender but grows fast and thick. The name vetch serves for more kinds than this one. Bitter vetch and wood vetch are British kin kinds. Vetches make a rich feed crop for farm stock. They grow well on poor soils with small care.
britannica-1911-watch:
Watch, in its chief sense a portable timepiece, is taken up at length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from an old English term for keeping guard or staying wakeful. From that root it names a guard or sentry, and the body of men who once patrolled the streets at night in place of a modern police.

The word also names a stretch of time. Greeks and Romans split the night into watches by the change of sentries. Ships still reckon time by watches, with the crew split into starboard and port sides on turn. From marking the hours, the word passed to the thing that shows them. Portable timepieces date from the end of the fourteen hundreds, and the first were made in Germany. They began as small clocks with mainsprings in boxes, too large for a pocket.
britannica-1911-wendt-hans-hinrich:
German Protestant church scholar Hans Hinrich Wendt, born in Hamburg in eighteen fifty three, is noted in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. He studied church doctrine at Leipzig, Gottingen, and Tubingen. In eighteen eighty five he became a full professor at Heidelberg. In eighteen ninety three he was called to Jena.

His work on the teaching of Jesus, put out in the late eighteen eighties, made him widely known. Part of it was rendered into English in eighteen ninety two. He also edited many editions of a noted commentary on the Acts of the Apostles. In nineteen oh four he gave two talks in London on how the divine is made known. Other works cover the Gospel of John and the proof of faith from experience.
britannica-1911-wenzel-karl-friedrich:
Karl Friedrich Wenzel, a German worker in metals, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Dresden in seventeen forty, he disliked his father's trade of bookbinding. He left home as a teen and took lessons in surgery and chemistry at Amsterdam. He then became a ship's surgeon in Dutch service.

Tired of sea life, he went to Leipzig to study chemistry in seventeen sixty six. He then gave himself to metal work and assaying at Dresden. His success won him a post as chemist to the Freiberg foundries in seventeen eighty. Later posts on the foundry board and at a porcelain works followed.
britannica-1911-wesleyan-methodist-churc:
Wesleyan Methodist Church is one of the chief branches of Methodism worldwide. Its church entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry opens with the note sent on the day John Wesley died. London preachers told country brethren that their aged father was no more.

Wesley death bed charge was that each preacher stay at his station. All were to hold place till the next Conference at Manchester met. Counts for seventeen ninety list preachers and members in Britain and America. Britain held two hundred ninety four preachers and over seventy one thousand members. A fast day and a prayer day were set before that Conference.
britannica-1911-wohler-friedrich:
Friedrich Wohler lived from 1800 to 1882 and was a German chemist of fame. The 1911 Britannica life opens at Eschersheim near Frankfurt on the Main. He was born there on the last day of July in 1800. In 1814 he began at the gymnasium at Frankfurt as a boy. There he ran tests in his science with a friend named Buch.

In 1820 he entered Marburg University to study for his degree. Next year he moved to Heidelberg to work in Gmelin's laboratory. He took his degree in medicine and surgery in the year 1823. Gmelin urged him to give his life to chemistry in its place. He then studied in Stockholm in the laboratory of Berzelius the Swede.
britannica-1911-zwingli-huldreich:
Huldreich Zwingli is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a Swiss church reformer born in a high valley in fourteen eighty four. He came from free farm stock, and his father led the village. A love of books and music marked him for the church from youth.

The entry follows his school years in three towns and his love of the classics. His father kept him from life as a monk and sent him to a university. He then taught classics and took a degree at Basel. The entry sets his calm school path beside the fierce soul trials of Luther. That contrast frames his own road to reform in Zurich.
bunch-grass-a-chronicle-of-life-on-a-cat:
Horace Annesley Vachell wrote a chronicle of ranch life, dated 1913. Twenty tales line the contents page, each a sketch of folk on one spread. Alethea-Belle opens the set. The Dumbles, Pap Spooner, and Gloriana follow. Bumblepuppy and Jasperson's Best Girl keep the light tone.

Fat steers, a trial scheme, and a poisoned spring turn the run. The Baron, Jim's Pup, and Mary mark the heart of the book. One Who Died gives the set its grave note. A Ragamuffin of the Foothills and Dennis close the list. The frame tale starts in the early 1880s, with the author and his brother Ajax raising cattle in south California foothills. Teamsters used their house as a stop on the Coast Range haul. Boom days then forced board on all who came. The book is given to the author's brother Arthur.
catherine-booth-a-sketch:
Mildred Duff's Catherine Booth: A Sketch, reprinted from The Warriors' Library, tells the life of the Salvation Army's co-founder. General Bramwell Booth, her son, supplies a preface, praising Duff's interesting and touching account of his dear mother.

Bramwell Booth answers the natural question: was Mrs. Booth not exceptional, with great gifts and special training? He replies that she walked with God, from her days as a timid girl helping her mother at home to her fame among multitudes. Readers interested in the Salvation Army, or in Victorian women preachers, will find Duff's sketch short, affectionate and inspiring.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-echt:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Echternach describes a Benedictine house in Luxemburg, founded in 698 by St. Willibrord. Willibrord, an English monk of Ripon, was apostle of Friesland and first bishop of Utrecht. He ruled the house as abbot until his death in 739, on land given by St. Irmine, Abbess of Oeren.

Kings, including Pepin and Charlemagne, heaped gifts on Echternach. After secular canons displaced the monks in 859, Emperor Otto the First brought back Benedictine life in 971 with forty monks from St. Maximin at Trier. The house became one of northern Europe's most famed, flourishing until the French Revolution closed it and scattered its monks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-achimelech:
Achimelech is a name borne by several men in scripture, and this entry separates them. First is the priest of Nobe who sheltered David during his flight from Saul. For that hospitality he was put to death with all the priests of Nobe, except his son Abiathar, who escaped and joined David. Second is a Hethite companion of the outlawed David.

Third is an Achimelech called son of Abiathar and associate of Sadoc in the priesthood, though that post is usually given to Abiathar, son of Achimelech. The entry judges the son of Abiathar reading an accidental transposition in Kings that also affected Paralipomenon. Fourth, Psalm 33's title gives Achis, King of Geth, the name Achimelech, where some texts read Abimelech.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adrian-and-pe:
Adrian and Peter von Walenburch were Cologne auxiliary bishops and celebrated controversial theologians, born at Rotterdam early in the seventeenth century, with exact birth dates unknown. Adrian died at Mainz or Wiesbaden in September 1669, and Peter died at Cologne in December 1675. Early accounts disagree over whether the brothers were Protestants or Catholics in youth.

They studied law in France and took doctorates in civil and canon law, then studied Catholic theology after returning to Rotterdam. Religious turmoil in Holland drove them to Germany, and in 1647 Cologne's archbishop made Adrian auxiliary bishop and vicar-general. Peter became canon at Mainz, titular Bishop of Mysia in 1658, and later auxiliary bishop of Cologne. Peter aided Leibniz's theological studies for church reunion, and their Tractatus de controversiis fidei of 1671 holds seventeen treatises.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aldersbach:
Aldersbach was once a Cistercian abbey in Lower Bavaria's Vils valley. St. Otto, Bishop of Bamberg, founded it in 1127, first as a house of canons regular. In 1146 his successor Egilbert gave the foundation to the Cistercians, with Abbot Sefried and monks from Ebrach taking possession. Under Cistercian rule the abbey flourished, kept strict discipline, and sent out daughter houses at Fürstenfeld, Fürstenzell, and Gotteszell.

The monks farmed the soil, served neighbouring churches, and pursued learning. The first abbot founded a library that later abbots enlarged, and monks studied at Paris, Vienna, Padua, Heidelberg, and Ingolstadt. War ravaged the house, above all in the Thirty Years' War, when it was pillaged and nearly abandoned, though the library survived. Suppressed on 1 April 1803 with forty monks, its church became a parish church and its library passed to the National Library at Munich.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambo-in-the-r:
The ambo has practically disappeared from the Roman Rite, its only reminder the pulpit or reading desk. Two ambos sometimes served, one for Epistle and one for Gospel, as at Rome's St. Clement and Venice's St. Mark. In the Russian Orthodox Church the ambo now means two or three semicircular steps from the soleas to the floor, directly before the royal doors.

Russian cathedrals add another mid-nave ambo, where the bishop stands during parts of the pontifical service. Greek Orthodox usage keeps the ambo's ancient style, though moved from middle to sides. The closing prayer behind the ambo is said before the royal doors outside the iconostasis. In the Greek Catholic Church, Slavic and American, the ambo is a table before the royal doors holding crucifix and two candles. Baptisms, confirmations, and marriages are performed there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amorbach:
A Benedictine abbey in Lower Franconia, Bavaria, stands about twenty-five miles south of Aschaffenburg. The town that grew around its walls shares its name. Saint Pirmin founded the house early in the eighth century. Count Ruthard had called him to preach in the region, and the abbey church was consecrated in 734.

Its monks carried Christianity through the Oden forest and into northern Germany. There they helped convert the Saxons, and several early bishops of Verden had served as abbots here. Gifts from Charles Martel and his sons enriched the house. Yet Huns, Peasants' War fighters, and Swedish troops each damaged it in turn. Rebuilt in the seventeenth century, with a church long famed for its organ, the abbey was suppressed in 1803 and passed to Bavaria in 1816.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-dioce:
Norwich took its present name only in the eleventh century. Its history runs five hundred years further back, to the conversion of East Anglia by Saint Felix in the reign of King Sigeberht. Felix fixed his see at Dunwich, a coastal town since swallowed by the sea in Southwold Bay, and from there he preached across Norfolk, Suffolk, and Cambridgeshire.

Thomas followed him in 647, then Beorhtgils, then Bisi. On Bisi's death in 673 Archbishop Theodore of Canterbury split the see in two, with cathedrals at Dunwich and Elmham. The article lists both successions in full, with dates where research allows. Elmham came to an end about 870, with the murder of King Edmund of the East Angles and Bishop Hunbeorht. The Dunwich line ran on toward the later Norwich see.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antioch:
Antioch of Syria: modern Antakieh holds the once famous Queen of the East. With over half a million people, beautiful site, trade, culture, and military position, it rivalled Alexandria, the empire's second city. Founded in 300 B.C. by Seleucus I, Antioch stood on the Orontes, at the Lebanon and Taurus ranges' junction. Its harbour, fifteen miles distant, was Seleucia.

Unknown disciples, dispersed by Stephen's persecution, brought Christianity to Antioch. There the new Faith was preached to Greeks with such success that Christianity received its name here, perhaps as a nickname by witty Antiochenes. Acknowledged by Jerusalem's mother-church, the new community soon showed vitality and faith intelligence by spontaneous generosity to Jerusalem's brethren. Antioch, the Apostle of the Gentiles' apprenticeship place, became headquarters of Paul and Barnabas, first together, later Paul alone. Starting thence on Apostolic journeys, they brought back their work's report.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antiphon-in-t:
In the Greek Church, the antiphon goes back to Saint Ignatius of Antioch, third from Saint Peter in that see. Socrates says Ignatius saw angels singing the Trinity's praises in alternating hymns and gave that singing to Antioch, whence it spread to all other Churches. The Greek Church made it an integral part of Mass and of morning and evening services. It is best known as a Greek Mass portion, in first, second, and third antiphons.

While the choir sings the antiphons' versicles in turn, the priest quietly says each antiphon's prayer. These antiphons come early in Mass, after the opening Great Synapte litany, and change with the feast celebrated. Usually they have three versicles and three responses, each closing with Glory be to the Father and As it is now. The Greek Horologion, an Office book like the Roman Breviary, gives the antiphons for the year's feast-days.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anton-ulrich:
Anton Ulrich, duke of Brunswick-Wolfenbuttel, was born in 1633 and ruled as the most scholarly prince of his age. With his brother he became co-regent in 1685 and sole ruler in 1704. A pioneer of the German historical romance, he also wrote plays and hymns, yet his deepest study was the Fathers and the differences between Catholics and Lutherans.

He entered the Catholic Church secretly in 1710 and soon declared his conversion in public, publishing a learned apology called Fifty Motives. The book was suppressed and became rare, but his sons later secured free Catholic worship in his state. Two of his daughters followed him into the church, and the entry presents a prince whose faith cost him standing and won him a cause.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arch:
An arch is a structure of separate pieces, such as stone or brick, shaped as truncated wedges. They are set on a curved line so that mutual pressure holds them in place. This arcuated method contrasts with the trabeated style of Greek architecture, where lintels, or horizontal beams, spanned gaps between columns or between column and wall. The stones forming the arch's curve are called voussoirs, or arch stones, with the lowest being springers, whose joints are usually horizontal.

The upper face of the springer, where the first true arch stone starts, is skewbacked. The topmost central stone is the keystone. The concave underside is the intrados or soffit, and the convex upper side is the extrados. Piers and abutments give the arch its resting and resisting points. The entry is a builder's lexicon, defining each part before moving to arch forms and uses in church building.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-auch:
Auch, anciently Augusta Auscorum, is an archdiocese covering the Gers department in France. Before the Revolution it held ten suffragan sees, small bishoprics under its care, including Dax, Aire, Lectoure, and Tarbes, most of which were later merged elsewhere. Its archbishops bore the title of Aquitaine until 1789, long after any Aquitaine had ceased to exist. Re-established in 1882, the archdiocese joined the old see with Lectoure, Condom, and Lombez.

Local tradition holds that Taurinus, fifth Bishop of Eauze, moved his see to Auch. Vandals had destroyed his city, though Eauze likely stayed a metropolitan see until the Northmen invasions of the 800s. The first known Bishop of Auch is the poet St Orientius, of the early 400s, honored by a famous seventh-century abbey. Later landmarks include a council in 1276 defending church jurisdiction, and a provincial council in 1851 on faith, worship, and clerical study.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-auzias-march:
Auzias March was a Catalan poet, born in the last quarter of the fourteenth century at Valencia, who died there in 1458. He stands as the greatest lyric poet of older Catalan literature. Among foreigners he best captures Petrarch's love lyric, and Dante's work also shows in his imagery. His images rise above the troubadour verse his contemporaries still wrote.

Report calls him a famed soldier in Alfonso V's Naples expedition, though that report needs proof. He came of noble stock and seems to have married twice. His surviving poems hold ninety-three love songs, eight death songs, moral songs, a long spiritual song, and a brief demand to Lady Tecla. His love lady was Teresa Bou of Valencia, met, like Petrarch's Laura, in church on Good Friday. He sings her in life and in death. His work was twice turned into Castilian, first in 1539, and shaped Boscan, Garcilaso, and Mendoza.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baruch:
Baruch, Hebrew for blessed, was Jeremiah's disciple and the traditional author of the deutero-canonical book bearing his name. Son of Nerias and probably brother to Saraias, chamberlain to King Sedecias, he served the prophet through crisis. After Nebuchadnezzar plundered Jerusalem's temple in 599 BC, Baruch wrote Jeremiah's oracle at dictation and read it publicly at risk of his life. When King Joachim burned the first prophecies, Baruch wrote a second, enlarged edition.

He stayed true to Jeremiah's teachings despite bouts of despondence and perhaps personal ambition. He witnessed Jeremiah's purchase of ancestral land at Anathoth during the last siege and lived with him at Masphath after Jerusalem's fall. Tradition says both died in Egypt's path before Nebuchadnezzar invaded, though Baruch's own book complicates that account. Trent defined the Book of Baruch as sacred and canonical, and its Vulgate Latin follows the Greek fairly literally.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-hadewych: Blessed Hadewych, prioress of the Premonstratensian convent of Meer near Büderich, was born about 1150 and died about 1200. Hildegundis's daughter, she helped her mother found the convent about 1165, she succeeded her mother as prioress in 1183. Her brother Herman was provost of Kappenberg monastery from 1171 to 1210, and mother, daughter, and brother are all counted among the Blessed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caesarius-of-:
Caesarius of Heisterbach, born about 1170 near Cologne, was a learned Cistercian monk of the house near Bonn. He studied the Fathers, Boethius, and the Latin poets Virgil, Ovid, Seneca, and Claudian, and mastered a refined, fluent Latin style. On Abbot Gevard's advice he entered Heisterbach in 1199 and became master of novices, teaching new monks the austere Cistercian spirit and theology.

At Abbot Henry's request he wrote an abstract of his teaching, the famous Dialogue, and in 1228 he became prior, traveling with the abbot on visits through Germany and Friesland. His best known work is the Dialogue of Visions and Miracles in twelve books, which became likely the most popular book in Germany of its day. By 1238 he had listed thirty-six of his own works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-care-of-the-p:
Care of the poor by the Church treats charity as a branch of mercy rooted in love of God. The poor are those who cannot gain the means to live. Christ's command makes their care the duty of every Christian, yet the entry argues that organized cooperation works best, so church provision supplements rather than replaces private giving. Three grades of poverty, sorted by degree of need, frame the discussion.

After objects, history, and organization, the entry surveys national scenes, with sections on Canada, Great Britain and Ireland, and the United States. Reports of Catholic charities conferences and of the Society of St. Vincent de Paul anchor the modern picture, from a 1910 Washington conference to gatherings at St. Louis, Richmond, and Boston. The whole forms a reference survey of how an ancient duty took institutional shape.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carl-von-reis:
Carl von Reisach was a Bavarian churchman born at Roth in July 1800. He died in a Redemptorist monastery at Contamine in December 1869. After philosophy at Munich, he studied law at Heidelberg, Göttingen, and Landshut, taking a doctorate in both laws in 1821. He then turned to theology and was ordained in 1828 after study at the German College in Rome. Pius VII put him in charge of studies at the Propaganda College, bringing him close to the future Gregory XVI.

At Gregory's urging he attacked anti-church views in Germany, above all on mixed marriages, in an 1835 Mainz work as Athanasius Sincerus Philalethes. He became Bishop of Eichstätt in 1836, founding a boys' seminary in 1838 and a lyceum in 1843. Later he held Roman offices, from the Congregation of Ecclesiastical Affairs and the Propaganda to minister of education for the Papal States. In 1868 he became Cardinal-Bishop of Ostia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christchurch:
Christchurch, in New Zealand, centres a diocese covering Canterbury and Westland, part of Nelson, and the Chatham Islands. The French corvette Aube sailed in July 1840 for Akaroa to land settlers and claim the South Island for France. Lieutenant-Governor Hobson raced her there in the Britomart and proclaimed the island British four days before the French arrived.

The Canterbury Pilgrims landed at Lyttelton in December 1850 under the Canterbury Association, a High Church body whose scheme critics called a Puseyite invasion. Only 136 Catholics lived in all Canterbury in 1851, served by Marist fathers. Christchurch gained its first resident priest in 1860. Gold brought missions to the West Coast in 1864, and the diocese itself was erected in May 1887, with 35 churches, 16 schools, and 17 priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-wol:
An entry on Christian Wolfgang Herdtrich, an Austrian Jesuit missionary to China, born at Graz in June 1625. He joined the Austrian Jesuits in October 1641, was chosen for the China mission in 1656, laboured two years on Celebes, then worked in Shanxi and Henan after 1660. In 1671 he was called to Peking as court mathematician, joining the scholarly Jesuits around the great emperor Kangxi.

Herdtrich knew Chinese language and literature deeply and helped write Confucius Sinarum Philosophus, published at Paris, the first translation and exposition to give European scholars real insight into the Chinese sage. He also wrote a large Chinese-Latin dictionary. His last nine years passed as superior of the Jiangzhou mission in Shanxi, and Kangxi himself composed his epitaph after his death in July 1684.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-church-of-ant:
An entry on the Church of Antioch and the city that mothered it, founded about 300 before Christ by Seleucus Nicator on the lower Orontes. Named for his father Antiochus, the city was meant as capital of his realm, stretched from Mount Silpius to the river, and grew into four walled towns under one rampart. Made a Roman province by Pompey in 64 before Christ, it stayed metropolis of the East, third city of the empire after Rome and Alexandria, with over half a million people.

Seleucids and Romans adorned Antioch with statues, theatres, temples, aqueducts, baths, gardens, and a colonnaded avenue miles long, while the grove of Daphne offered its famed pleasure resort and Apollo temple. Into this great city came the Gospel, and Antioch became a mother church of the East. The entry traces city and church together, from foundation to later centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-classical-lat:
Classical literature, chiefly Latin, shaped Catholic schooling from Roman times onward. When Christianity first appeared in Rome, schooling meant poets and historians, above all Horace and Virgil. New converts carried pagan learning into the Faith, using mythology and rhetoric against paganism. Tertullian forbade Christians to teach, yet allowed pupils to attend school, and his rigour was not followed: Arnobius taught rhetoric, and his pupil Lactantius became professor at Nicomedia.

In the fourth century opposition grew between profane letters and the Bible, hardened by Jerome's psalm translation and by Julian's persecution. Gregory the Great condemned literary study for bishops, Isidore of Seville compressed ancient culture into his Origines, and only Cassiodorus planned a broad union of secular and sacred science. Cluny and Clairvaux reforms later discouraged study, manuscript copying became a secular trade, and in recent times practical men and declared enemies of the Church have attacked Latin training itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-commandments-:
John Melody's entry treats the Commandments of the Church under three heads: their nature, their history, and their classification. Lawmaking power over all the faithful belongs to the Church by her very constitution. She holds the deposit of Christian revelation and interprets it for all time. Her universal laws may define doctrine, condemn error, or fix times and manners for keeping divine law. Such laws, binding all the faithful, truly count as commandments of the Church.

History shows the form and number of the precepts shifting across ages and lands. Spanish America kept five, following Aspilcueta in the sixteenth century. French catechisms after Bossuet dropped the last two yet kept Bellarmine's count. The Baltimore council list of 1886 for the United States covers Easter duty, support of pastors, and marriage rules on kindred and forbidden times. Melody thus gives both the theory and the local variety.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-communion-ben:
Patrick Morrisroe's entry explains the Communion bench as an adaptation of the sanctuary guard, or altar rail. Before this barrier, in a space called the chancel, the faithful once received Holy Communion standing. Men took the consecrated Bread in their hands. Women received it on a white cloth called the domenical. Deacons gave the Precious Blood, which each person took through a reed of gold or silver.

About the twelfth century, receiving under one kind only became the custom. Priests then laid the small Hosts on communicants' tongues at the rail. Kneeling reception came in about the fifteenth century, and the rail slowly took its modern form. For great crowds, rows of prie-Dieu or benches with Communion cloths and a candle at each row's end may ring the chancel, by decree of the Congregation of Rites.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conrad-of-ura:
Michael Ott's entry follows Conrad of Urach, Cardinal-Bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina, born about 1180, died in 1227. Young, he became canon of Saint Lambert's church, Liège cathedral. In 1199 he entered Belgium's Cistercian monastery of Villers, soon becoming prior and in 1209 abbot. In 1214 he was chosen Abbot of Clairvaux, and in 1217 Abbot of Cîteaux and general of his order. Honorius III created him cardinal on 8 January 1219 and charged him with two important legations.

France claimed the first, from 1220 to 1223, to suppress the Albigenses. Germany claimed the second, from 1224 to 1226, to preach and arrange the crusade Frederick II had vowed. After Honorius III died, cardinals agreed to elect Conrad pope, but he refused the dignity. Cistercians venerate him as Blessed, his feast falling on 30 September. A career spanning abbacies, generalship, cardinalate, and refused papacy marks him among the order's leading thirteenth-century figures.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-david-paul-dr:
A biographical entry follows David Paul Drach, a convert from Judaism born at Strasbourg in 1791 and dead at Rome in early 1868. Rosenthal called his conversion one of the century's most important in France. It moved earnest minds to serious study, and drew many fellow Jews toward the Church. Drach's father, a renowned Hebraist and Talmud scholar, gave him his first teaching.

At twelve he entered Talmud school at Edendorf, finishing a three-year course in one year. He then graduated at Bischheim in eighteen months. Teaching at sixteen, he pursued rabbinic learning until his conversion redirected his scholarship. His writings sought to lead fellow Jews to acknowledge Jesus as Messiah. His later work included a great French Bible commentary, with his own contributions on the Pauline and Catholic Epistles and the Apocalypse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diptych:
A diptych is a notebook made of two tablets laid together and joined by rings or a hinge. The tablets were cut from wood, ivory, bone, or metal, and their inner faces were framed and coated with wax. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that Greeks knew such books from the sixth century before Christ. They served as copybooks, for letters, and for many daily uses, and Roman army discharge papers took the same form.

Adding leaves made a triptych or polyptych, and the finest diptychs were richly carved. In church use the diptychs held names read aloud at Mass, the living and the dead. The entry traces that liturgical use to the Memento of the Mass today, where the old reading of names still lives on in prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-doctors-of-th:
Doctors of the Church are writers honored because the whole Church gained from their teaching. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry names the four great Western fathers of the early Middle Ages, Gregory the Great, Ambrose, Augustine, and Jerome. Their feasts were ordered as doubles through the whole Church by Boniface the Eighth in 1298. The four became a byword among the schoolmen.

In the East, three doctors stood foremost, John Chrysostom, Basil, and Gregory Nazianzen, whose feasts Leo the Wise made binding through the empire. The entry then follows later additions to the roll and the rules for the honor. It offers a clear guide to a title that marks the Church's most trusted teachers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-early-african:
The Early African Church is the name for the Christian communities of Roman Africa, a coastal strip from Cyrenaica in the east to the river Ampsaga in the west. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry adds Mauretania, the Atlantic-facing part, and notes that the communities seem to have reached only toward Tangiers. The spread of the faith followed the lines of Roman civilization, starting from Carthage across Proconsular Africa and Numidia, thinning toward Mauretania.

Fixing the church's bounds is hard, since Roman political lines shifted again and again. The entry follows bishops, councils, and writers of a church that gave the West Tertullian, Cyprian, and Augustine. It notes that native Libyan speech lived on only among nomad tribes, while Latin and Punic carried the faith of the cities.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecclesiasticu:
Ecclesiasticus, also called the Book of Sirach, is the longest of the deuterocanonical books and the last wisdom writing in the Vulgate Old Testament. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry gives its Greek title, the Wisdom of Jesus son of Sirach. A subscription at the end of newly found Hebrew fragments names the author more fully, Simeon son of Yeshua son of Eleazar son of Sira.

The full Hebrew heading would read Wisdom of Yeshua son of Sira, though Saint Jerome's prologue complicates the picture. The entry surveys the book's text, versions, and commentators, from Cornely and Konig to Gigot, with studies of the Hebrew fragments by Touzard and Knabenbauer. For readers of the wisdom books, it maps a work long prized and long debated.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-emmanuel-henr:
Emmanuel-Henri-Dieudonne Domenech was a French missionary priest and writer, born at Lyons in 1826 and dead in France in 1886. In the spring of 1846, not yet twenty and still short of finishing seminary, he answered an urgent call for missionaries in Texas, then filling fast with American and European settlers. He spent two years at Saint Louis finishing theology and learning English and German.

In May 1848 he was sent to the new German settlement of Castroville, then to Brownsville. The Mexican war had just ended, raiders and outlaws ranged both banks of the Rio Grande, hostile Indians hovered near, and cholera added its horrors. Yet the young priest worked with such energy that he became a power for good across south Texas. His health broke, he returned to France as canon of Montpellier, served as army chaplain in Mexico under Maximilian, and spent his last years in travel and writing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ephraim-of-an:
Ephraim of Antioch was a defender of the faith of Chalcedon against the Monophysites, born at Amida in Mesopotamia and dead in 545. Under Justinian I he served as Count of the East, and in 527 he succeeded Euphrasius as Patriarch of Antioch. Most of his works are lost, though their titles survive through Anastasius Sinaita, the Sacra Parallela, and Photius.

Anastasius quotes his work against Severus, the Monophysite Patriarch of Antioch from 512 to 519. The Parallela give a passage from his work on John the Grammarian and the synod. Photius describes four books: sermons and letters, a treatise against Severus in three parts, and an answer to five questions on Genesis from a monk, Anatolius. Those fragments are nearly all that remains. Krumbacher holds that, had more survived, Ephraim would rank with Leontius of Byzantium, for his wide knowledge of the Greek Fathers and his following of Cyril of Alexandria.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-erwin-of-stei:
Erwin of Steinbach was one of the architects of the Strasburg cathedral, date of birth unknown, dead at Strasburg on 17 January 1318. Later tradition calls him Erwin of Steinbach, and Steinbach village near Baden-Baden holds a monument to him. Two of his sons, Erwin and Johannes, his grandson Gerlach from 1341 to 1371, and another scion named Kuntze up to 1382 were also superintending architects.

Hence they were heads of the Strasburg guild of stone-masons, whose influence extended as far as Bavaria, Austria, and the borders of Italy. He must already have proved himself a master-builder elsewhere before taking charge of the Strasburg cathedral façade about 1277. His work on the cathedral shows the influence of the French Gothic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-evangelical-c:
The Evangelical Church in Prussia was the united Protestant church formed in 1817 by King Frederick William III from the Lutheran and Reformed churches. The Reformers had called themselves Evangelicals, followers of the pure Gospel, against Roman tradition. By the early nineteenth century, rationalism and indifference had sapped religious life in Germany, and the king sought one church to match his army, schools, and trade.

On 27 September 1817 he declared his wish to unite the two confessions in his lands into one Evangelical Christian Church, setting the example at Potsdam. Berlin's synod and most clergy answered warmly, and other German states followed, though Saxony, Hanover, and Bavaria held back. The union kept each side's doctrines but gave them one government and one liturgy, the royal Agenda, which met sharp opposition as oppressive and leaning toward Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-exarch:
Exarch is a title used in several senses, civil and churchly. In the Roman Empire it meant the governor of a large province. The best known was the Exarch of Italy, who ruled from Ravenna from 552 to 751. In church speech it first meant a metropolitan ruling over other metropolitans.

At Chalcedon in 451 the patriarchs were still called exarchs. Later the name stayed with the metropolitans of Asia, Cappadocia and Pontus, and Thrace. In the East an exarch ranks between patriarch and ordinary metropolitan. Cyprus won the title in 431, Bulgaria took it in 1870, and Georgia's primate bears it still.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fathers-of-th:
The Fathers of the Church are the early teachers who handed on apostolic teaching. The name first meant bishops and holy predecessors of each local church. Its limits run from the apostolic age to Gregory the Great in the West. In the East the line reaches John Damascene, who died about 754.

Appeals to the Fathers form one branch of the appeal to tradition. Irenaeus cited the succession of bishops, and Tertullian the agreement of churches. Later teachers like Origen, though priests, shaped doctrine without the title. The article surveys centuries, regions, writings, and schools of patristic study.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-filial-church:
A filial church is a daughter church dependent on an older mother church. Usually it arises when an older parish is divided. Its rector holds a priest's rights but defers in certain accidental matters. He fetches baptismal water and makes a moderate money offering yearly to the mother church.

Some filial churches stand inside an extensive parish without any division. Their pastors act as curates, removable at will by the mother priest. The mother priest may keep baptisms, marriages, and similar offices to himself. In practice curates act as parish priests for their districts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-pet:
Francesco Petrarch, born at Arezzo on 20 July 1304 and dead at Arqua on 19 July 1374, was the Italian poet and humanist who helped revive classical learning in Europe. His father, a Florentine court clerk banished with the White Guelphs in 1302, meant him for law, sending him to Montpellier and Bologna. Francesco gave himself to letters, and his father once burned his favourite ancient authors in anger. After his father's death he took minor orders at Avignon, which let him live on church benefices.

There on Good Friday 1327 he first saw Laura, the beloved of his poems. He entered the gay court life of Avignon while building his fame as a Latin scholar and poet. His Italian lyrics, his Latin epic Africa, and his letters shaped the Renaissance idea of the scholar-poet. His search for lost manuscripts of Livy and Cicero made him a founder of humanism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-ittenba:
Franz Ittenbach, born at Konigswinter at the foot of the Drachenfels in 1813 and died at Dusseldorf in 1879, was a German historical painter of deep religion. At nineteen he entered the Dusseldorf Academy, taking private lessons from its president Schadow. With three friends and fellow students, Karl and Andreas Muller and Ernst Deger, he travelled Germany studying and painting. Exceedingly religious, he persistently refused commissions for mythological or pagan subjects and gave his energies almost entirely to church decoration, preparing his greatest works by confession and communion.

His finest paintings stand at Bonn in St. Remigius church and at Breslau in a church of the same saint, with a remarkable Holy Family of 1861 for Prince Liechtenstein's private chapel near Vienna. He also painted many works in Catholic churches across Germany. His sole important fresco was painted in 1844 at Remagen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-geography-and:
Geography and the Church argues that the science of the earth's surface owes its greatest debt to Catholic explorers and scholars. Humboldt, Ritter, and Peschel all confessed it. Priests and scholars were once one calling. While greed and conquest pushed discovery, a nobler motive, spreading the faith, sent the bravest, steadiest men into unknown lands through the Middle Ages and beyond.

The survey runs in three parts. First, how church activity opened new lands and peoples in the Middle Ages. Second, what medieval theologians thought of the world. Third, how missionaries and Catholic scholars mapped foreign shores from the age of discovery to the present. Ptolemy's world bounds the start, and Copernicus, himself a churchman, crowns the proof that clerical minds chased the Creator's order in nature.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-von-pe:
George von Peuerbach, an Austrian astronomer born near Linz in 1423, led Western astronomy based on watching the sky and on maths. Master of arts at Vienna about 1440, he traveled to Italy in 1448, where Bianchini and Cardinal Cusa had him lecture at Ferrara. Refusing Bologna, Padua, and Hungary's court post, he returned to Vienna in 1450 to teach philology and classics. Science he taught chiefly in private.

His most famous pupil was Regiomontanus. Peuerbach reworked Ptolemy's Almagest, replacing chords with sines and tabulating sines for every minute of arc. This was a first step from base-twelve to base-ten counting, done with simple tools like a plumb line. His New Theories of the Planets, first printed at Nuremberg in 1460, joined homocentric spheres with epicycles and grounded school astronomy until years after Copernicus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-greek-church:
The Greek Church is a subject treated under terms, the Orthodox Church and its divisions, and the Uniat churches. Its history runs from the first five centuries through the schism and the Crusades to 1453 and the present. A Catholic Encyclopedia article begins by insisting that race, speech, rite, and belief be kept distinct.

Eastern Churches, in the usual sense, means all churches with a rite differing from the Latin. Whether they accept or reject the pope, they cover the Byzantine, Armenian, Syrian, Chaldean, Maronite, and Coptic rites. The Greek Church ordinarily means all churches using the Byzantine Rite, separated or in communion with Rome, whatever their race and speech. Confusion arises precisely when these distinctions are not observed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gregor-reisch:
Gregor Reisch was born at Balingen in Wurtemberg about 1467 and died at Freiburg on 9 May 1525. He entered the Carthusian Order after taking his magister at Freiburg in 1489, served as prior at Klein-Basel and then at Freiburg, and visited for the Rhenish province. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a scholar called an oracle.

His chief work, Margarita philosophica of 1503, is an encyclopedia of knowledge in twelve books. It runs from Latin grammar and rhetoric to arithmetic, music, geometry, astronomy, physics, natural history, physiology, psychology, and ethics. Cast as questions from the scholar answered by the teacher, with woodcuts and a full index, it became a customary textbook of the higher schools. Alexander von Humboldt said it aided the spread of knowledge for a half-century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heisterbach:
Rhineland Cistercian house Heisterbach in the Siebengebirge began with the hermit Walther on the Petersberg, whose disciples built a monastery in 1134 under Augustine's rule. After Walther's death they moved to Reussrath, and in 1189 Archbishop Philip of Cologne had Himmerod's abbot repeople the empty Petersberg with twelve Cistercians under Abbot Hermann.

Three or four years later the monks moved downhill to Petersthal, called Heisterbach, and raised a basilica begun under Abbot Gerard and consecrated in 1237, blending Romanesque round arches with Gothic points. Rich and flourishing until suppression in 1803, it lost library and archives to Düsseldorf. Church and monastery were sold and torn down in 1809, leaving only its apse and choir ruins, with a monument to its monk Caesarius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henoch:
Henoch, Greek for Enoch, names four biblical figures, of whom the patriarch son of Jared and father of Methuselah is by far the most famous. At sixty-five Henoch fathered Methuselah, and his whole life ran 365 years. Where other patriarchs' sketches close with and he died, his says he walked with God and was taken, seen no more.

Hebrews adds that by faith Henoch was translated not to see death, Sirach agrees. Jude shows him as a prophet announcing God's judgment on the ungodly. Whether Jude quoted the apocryphal Book of Henoch or that book borrowed from Jude is weighed here. The entry favours Jewish tradition as Jude's source and interpolation into the apocryphal book as the likelier path.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hermann-of-al:
Hermann of Altach was a thirteenth-century Benedictine abbot and historian at Niederaltaich in Bavaria. Born around 1200, he was schooled in the monastery, became keeper of its church, and carried out missions to the emperor at Verona and to the Roman Curia. Elected abbot in 1242, he ruled thirty-one years, improving both monastic discipline and the house finances before resigning in 1273.

His chief work, the Annales Hermanni, runs from 1137 to 1273. Its early part leans on older chronicles, but from 1146 onward it is his own work and counts as a key source for Bavaria, Bohemia, and Austria. He also wrote short accounts of building work at Niederaltaich, the founding of the house, and its patrons, the dukes of Bogen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hermann-von-k:
Hermann von Kerssenbroch was a sixteenth-century German teacher and historian, born near Barntrup about 1520 and dead at Osnabrück in 1585. Schooled at Paderborn, Münster, and Cologne, he taught at Düsseldorf and served as rector at Hamm. He then led the Pauline Gymnasium at Münster for twenty-five fruitful years before moving on to schools at Düsseldorf, Werl, and Osnabrück.

Kerssenbroch is praised above all as a school reformer. He worked to put poorly paid teachers on a firmer financial footing. He also stressed thorough grounding in Latin learning, as his surviving 1551 programme of studies for the Münster school shows. The entry follows a wandering schoolmaster whose steady work helped revive the failing school system of Westphalia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hexateuch: Hexateuch is a name used by critics for the six books opening the Old Testament: the Pentateuch's five books plus the book of Josue. The name marks those six books as forming one literary whole. It does not mean, the entry stresses, that the sources behind these books are found only within the six books themselves.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hierarchy-of-:
This vast article treats the hierarchy of the early church, the ordered grades by which the church was governed. Hierarchy here first means the three grades of bishop, priest, and deacon, which Catholic doctrine, following the Council of Trent, traces to divine institution. Because those grades match the grades of the sacrament of Holy Orders, this is called the hierarchy of order.

The word stretches wider, however. Add the bishop of Rome, head of the church, plus offices of merely church origin, such as cardinals and patriarchs, and you have the hierarchy of jurisdiction. It is marked by real power rather than orders alone. In its widest sense the word covers clergy and laity together as members of the church. The entry traces each grade from its scriptural and early roots.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-michae:
Johann Michael Raich was a Catholic theologian and writer who spent his career at Mainz in Germany. Born in Bavaria in 1832, he studied at the Collegium Germanicum in Rome. Ordained there in 1858, he became secretary to Bishop von Ketteler. He went with the bishop to Rome during the Vatican Council. He rose through the Mainz cathedral chapter, becoming canon in 1890 and dean in 1900.

His own books took on Dollinger's break with the Church. They also dealt with the age of first communicants, Shakespeare's stance toward Catholicism, and what he saw as the inner falsehood of Freemasonry. He also edited older theological works and Ketteler's sermons and letters. From 1891 until his death in 1907 he edited the journal Der Katholik, through the Kulturkampf years and after.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-lynch:
John Lynch was an Irish historian whose Cambrensis Eversus answered Gerald of Wales's calumnies against Ireland. Born at Galway in 1599, son of a schoolmaster whose classical school held twelve hundred students until Ussher closed it in 1615, he studied under the Jesuits in France. He was ordained and returned to Galway in 1622 to open his own school.

Penal laws forced him to minister in secret until 1642, when churches opened again. Loyal to England despite his sufferings, he condemned the rebellion of 1641, viewed the Catholic Confederation coldly, and disapproved of the nuncio and Owen Roe O'Neill. Driven into French exile after Galway fell to the Puritans in 1652, he wrote a life of his uncle Bishop Kirwan and the Alithonologia on the Anglo-Irish. In 1662 came his great work, vigorous in Latin and rich in learning, vindicating Ireland against Gerald Barry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-of-antio:
John of Antioch is a name shared by four persons, and this entry sorts them out, beginning with the patriarch at the Council of Ephesus. John, Patriarch of Antioch from 428 to 441, had been a fellow student and friend of Nestorius. When trouble over the title Theotokos began, he warned Nestorius not to stir a disturbance, noting that orthodox Fathers had constantly used it.

Summoned to Ephesus in 430, he arrived six days after the council opened and refused to join it. He opened a rival synod defending Nestorius and condemning Cyril of Alexandria. In schism with Alexandria and Rome, he later sent Paul of Emesa to Alexandria with an orthodox profession in 433. He signed Cyril's formula condemning Nestorius that April, and saw peace restored between the patriarchates, though many Syrian bishops broke communion with him for it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-ruysch:
John Ruysch was a Dutch Benedictine astronomer, cartographer, and painter of the age of discovery. Born at Utrecht about 1460, he became a secular priest, joined the Benedictines at St. Martin's in Cologne in 1492, and devoted himself to astronomy and painting, decorating his monastery's refectory with the lunar month and signs of the zodiac.

Going to Rome about 1508, he took a post in the pontifical palace. He published his famous world map, the New and More Universal Table of the Known World, showing Spain's and Portugal's new discoveries in America. He assisted Raphael in the Vatican paintings, then went to Portugal, where the king, esteeming his astronomy and cosmography, made him astronomer to the fleet. Returning to Cologne, he spent his last years in his monastery, making astronomical instruments and writing on spiritual counsel and the mixing of colors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-fesch:
Joseph Fesch was a Corsican cardinal and the uncle of Napoleon Bonaparte. Born at Ajaccio in 1763, he was the half-brother of Napoleon's mother, Letizia. After serving in the army's supply service under Bonaparte, he returned to church life, helped negotiate the Concordat of 1801, and became Archbishop of Lyons in 1802 and cardinal in 1803.

As ambassador to Rome he persuaded Pius VII to travel to Paris and crown Napoleon, his greatest feat. He blessed Napoleon's marriage to Josephine and later refused the emperor's offer of Paris, since he could not gain canonical institution. He died at Rome in 1839, still Archbishop of Lyons in title.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-fuhric:
Joseph Führich was a Bohemian religious painter of the Nazarene school. Born in 1800, the son of a poor painter at Kratzau, he learned drawing in his father's shop and practiced while herding his flock. At sixteen he went to the painter Bergler in Prague, and patrons soon funded his academy studies. Reading Romantic poets made him a Romanticist.

In Rome from 1826 he joined the Nazarenes, learned fresco technique, and finished the Tasso cycle in the Villa Massimi. Settled in Vienna from 1834, he held that church art must teach the faith through the senses, not merely decorate. His Jacob and Rachel and Mary's Journey over the Mountains soon sold for five times their first price.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-ritter:
Joseph, Ritter von Aschbach was a German historian of Spain, the Visigoths, and Vienna University. Born at Höchst in 1801, he began in theology and philosophy at Heidelberg, then turned to history under Schlosser. He taught at Frankfurt, became professor at Bonn in 1842, and moved to Vienna in 1853.

Aschbach wrote histories of the Visigoths, the Umayyads in Spain, and Emperor Sigismund, and edited a four-volume General Church Lexicon. At Vienna he wrote a three-volume history of the university for its fifth centenary. His bold claim that a poem ascribed to the nun Roswitha was really by Conrad Celtes drew wide attention.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juliana-of-no:
Juliana of Norwich was an English mystic and author of the Revelations of Divine Love. Probably a Benedictine recluse at St. Julian's church in Norwich, she received her showings on 8 or 14 May 1373, when she was thirty and a half, placing her birth near the end of 1342. She wrote the book only after twenty years of inward teaching, so not before 1393.

Calling herself a simple, unlettered creature, Juliana yet learned theological language and shows the influence of Walter Hilton and the Cloud of Unknowing. Her sixteen showings, called the finest fruit of later English medieval mysticism, dwell on Christ's love and a place in his side for all who shall be saved. A manuscript notes her alive in 1413.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-laibach:
Laibach is an Austrian bishopric, suffragan of Gorz, covering the crownland of Carniola. From the Avars' overthrow in 811 until its founding, the region belonged to the Patriarchate of Aquileia, whose patriarchs also claimed the margravate of Krain.

Frederick III, seeking to detach the province from Aquileia, founded the see in 1461, confirmed by Pius II in 1462 as directly subject to Rome. Sigismund von Lamberg became first bishop in 1463. Lutheran teaching took hold under later bishops, and by mid-sixteenth century most nobles and nearly half the middle class had turned Protestant. Bishop Johann Tautscher fought its advance from 1580, and his successor Thomas Chroen, called the Apostle of Krain, pressed the Catholic restoration harder still.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-latin-church:
The Latin Church is the vast part of the Catholic body that obeys the Latin patriarch, submitting to the pope in papal and patriarchal matters alike. It stands apart from the Eastern Churches, Catholic or schismatic, which represent the other four patriarchates: Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem.

The article reaches that sense through the word Church itself. In its first sense it means the whole congregation united in one faith under one hierarchy, as in Matthew and Ephesians. In a second sense it names parts: dioceses like Paris or Milan, provinces and nations like Gaul or Spain, and patriarchates. Church of Rome, strictly, names only Rome's local diocese or province, mother and mistress of all Churches, not the whole Catholic body.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-low-church:
Low Church names one of three parties in the Church of England, beside High Church and Broad Church. High and Low came into use together at the start of the eighteenth century, during pamphlet wars over William III's bid to soften the Act of Uniformity for Dissenters.

Burnet records that Low Churchmen, who treated Dissenters with temper and backed steady parish residence, were smeared as secret Presbyterians ready to quit the Church when profit failed. They resented the slur, yet the label stuck. The root split endures: High Churchmen hold the threefold ministry as Christ's fixed order, while Low Churchmen treat it as apostolic precedent that may bend without losing church standing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lucian-of-ant:
Lucian of Antioch was a priest and martyr, killed on 7 January 312 under Maximinus Daza. Tradition from Suidas makes him a Samosata native schooled at Edessa, though the entry warns that tale may mix him with Lucian the pagan satirist, a century earlier.

At Antioch he headed the theological school and championed a literal reading of Scripture against Alexandrine allegory, a method that ruled the East for ages. Suspected after Paul of Samosata's fall, he broke with the orthodox party for years, then returned. Most writers blame his Christology, a middle path between Modalism and Subordinationism, as the seedbed of later Arian views.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-macarius-of-a:
Macarius of Antioch was a patriarch deposed in 681, whose dignity was largely honorary, for his see lay under Saracen rule and he himself lived at Constantinople. His life before the Sixth General Council, which removed him for Monothelitism, is a blank, and after it he vanished into a Roman monastery.

Yet he left a mark by bringing about the condemnation of Honorius. When Roman legates spoke of patriarchs who disturbed the peace with new expressions, Macarius answered that he published only what synods and fathers had received, adding Honorius to their names. Forged documents and garbled testimonies sealed his fall, and he vowed death by dismemberment and drowning sooner than accept two wills.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maria-laach:
Maria-Laach was a Benedictine abbey on the south-west bank of Lake Laach, near Andernach in the Rhineland. Count Palatine Henry II of Lorraine founded it in 1093. Cluniac Benedictines from Afflighem in Belgium took it over, and its first abbot, Gilbert, arrived in 1127, making it independent.

In the fourteenth century Benedictine fervour faded across Germany, and under Abbot Johannes I it showed at Laach too. Only in the later fifteenth century, through alliance with Bursfeld, did monastic spirit revive, as Abbot Johannes V of Deidesheim beat down monks who resisted reform and fresh literary life followed. Until dissolution in 1802 it stayed a centre of religion and letters. The house passed to France, then Prussia in 1815, then private hands, and Jesuits later made it a seat of learning. Beuron Benedictines returned in 1892, the abbey was restored in 1893, and by 1910 it held 41 monks and 74 lay brothers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mateo-aimeric:
Mateo Aimerich was a learned philologist, born at Bordil, Spain, in 1715 and dead at Ferrara in 1799. He joined the Jesuits at eighteen, finished studies, and taught philosophy and theology in several order colleges. He later served as rector of Barcelona and Cervera and chancellor of Gandia University.

Settling at Ferrara in exile, he wrote the works that won him a distinguished place among eighteenth-century philologists and critics. Remarkably, his only help was the public library, and infirmities often barred even that. He died at eighty-four in great piety. Gifted with fine, judicious mind and vast erudition, he wrote Latin with great eloquence and purity. Besides scholastic philosophy, ascetical works, and discourses, he left a Barcelona bishops' monograph and a rare Censorinus paradox work, with a defence of it. He also left a specimen of lost Roman literature and his famed Novum Lexicon of ancient Roman literature.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-melchisedech:
Melchisedech, whose Hebrew name means King of Righteousness, was King of Salem in Genesis 14. When Abraham returned with spoil from the four kings, Melchisedech brought out bread and wine, for he was priest of the most high God, blessed Abraham, and received tithes of all. Josephus identifies Salem with Jerusalem and adds that he fed Abraham's army lavishly and accepted the tenth of the prey.

Cheyne calls him a plausible fiction, a guess Kaufmann rightly rejects. Rabbis identified him with Sem, son of Noah, more from polemic than history, since they resisted his portrait as a type of Christ without father, mother, or genealogy in Hebrews 7. There the Epistle unfolds his Messianic meaning: Christ is a priest forever after the order of Melchisedech, not Aaron's line, by virtue of his twofold dignity as priest and king.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-meletius-of-a:
Meletius of Antioch, a bishop born at Melitene in Lesser Armenia, died at Antioch in 381. Before Antioch he held Sebaste, capital of Armenia Prima, perhaps from 358 or 359, though his stay was short and troubled by loyalty to his predecessor Eustathius. Asia Minor and Syria then seethed with Arian and semi-Arian disputes. Under Eustathius from 324 to 330, Antioch had been a centre of Nicene orthodoxy.

Eustathius was set aside, and Paulinus and Eulalius held the see briefly in 330-332. Weaker successors followed, and schism tore the church in two. The Eustathians stayed a fierce, unruly minority in the orthodox camp. Under Leontius from 344 to 358, open Arian sympathy ruled, and his disciple Aetius preached pure Arianism yet was ordained deacon. Orthodox leaders Flavius and Diodorus forced Aetius out. On Leontius's death, the Arian Eudoxius of Germanicia seized the see by intrigue, held it briefly, and was banished to Armenia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moloch:
Moloch was a god worshipped by idolatrous Israelites. His name most likely began as Melech, meaning king. Mocking vowels from the word for shame were later folded into it. That makes some Old Testament passages hard to read. The word can mean either the deity himself or simply a king.

His worship centred on child sacrifice, described as making children pass through fire. The main site was Tophet in the valley of Gehenna, just outside Jerusalem. Solomon is blamed for building him a shrine. The cult spread through both kingdoms, encouraged by kings such as Ahaz and Manasseh. Josiah stamped it out and defiled Tophet, though it may have revived before the Babylonian Captivity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mystical-body:
The Church, like any society of men, resembles an organism. Its members unite for a common end, and the parts they play match the functions of bodily organs. They form a moral unity. The Church, however, has a unity of a higher order. It is not merely a moral body but a mystical body.

That truth, that the Church is the mystical body of Christ, comes chiefly from Saint Paul, above all Ephesians 4. Christ the head guides and directs all members. They share a supernatural life given through the sacraments. He endows each with gifts fitting his place in the body. Those graces knit the parts together like ligaments and joints, and through them the Church grows outward across the world and inward in each Christian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-fren:
Nicholas French, Bishop of Ferns, Ireland, was born at Ballytory, County Wexford, in 1604 to John French and Christina Rosseter, and died at Ghent on 23 August 1678. He studied at Louvain, apparently presiding over one of its colleges, and returned to Ireland in 1640 as Wexford's parish priest. In the Confederation War he sided with the Confederates and played an active role in the Kilkenny Assembly's debates.

Consecrated Bishop of Ferns in November 1645, he opposed Preston's party, favoured the 1648 peace against Nuncio Rinuccini, yet bitterly opposed the Ormond faction at Jamestown's 1650 synod. In 1651 he joined a deputation to the Duke of Lorraine seeking aid against Cromwell and offering Ireland's protectorship, but the mission failed and he stayed on the Continent. He retired to Santiago in Spain, assisting its archbishop and writing his Lucubrations of the Bishop of Ferns in Spain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolaus-van-:
Dutch mystical writer Nicolaus van Esch, known as Eschius, guided souls at Cologne and Diest in the sixteenth century. Born near 's-Hertogenbosch in 1507, he read philosophy, theology, and canon law at Louvain, refused a doctorate, and was ordained in 1530.

Settling at Cologne, he tutored students including Peter Canisius and Lawrence Surius, lived beside the Carthusians, and followed their rule as far as his frail health allowed. As pastor of the Diest beguinage from 1538, he founded seminaries on Trent's model and wrote on the inward life until his death in 1578.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oriental-stud:
Oriental study, the scientific investigation of the East, spans languages, archaeology, ethnology, and religion across a field too vast for one scholar. China and the Far East form one great division, Sanskrit and ancient Hindu lore another, shedding light on European tongues and peoples.

From a religious view the richest gains came from Semitic languages and digs in Bible lands: Assyria, Babylonia, Syria, Palestine, Arabia, and Egypt. Those finds lit up Old Testament writings and recovered forgotten histories, and the entry maps the field's departments and methods. The field divides by necessity into many departments, each with specialized branches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orthodox-chur:
Orthodox Church is the name explained here for Christians who follow the Byzantine Rite in many tongues. They stand in union with the Patriarch of Constantinople, while out of communion with the Pope of Rome. Orthodox means right believer, a title claimed by many faiths. The entry shows how the word shifted from a mark set against Eastern heretics to the proper name of the Eastern Church.

Sixteen churches make up the communion. They range from the four old eastern patriarchates of Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem to national churches in Russia, Greece, Serbia, Romania, and Bulgaria. No single head rules them all. Their shared guide is Christ and the seven Ecumenical Councils, from Nicaea I in 325 to Nicaea II in 787. World numbers are put at ninety-five to one hundred million.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patriarch:
Patriarch, as applied to Bible figures, comes from the Septuagint, where it covers religious and civil officials in a broad sense. In common use it marks the antediluvian fathers of mankind, and above all the three great forebears of Israel, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The New Testament extends it to Jacob's sons and to King David, whose stories stand in their own entries.

Earlier patriarchs fall in two groups: those before the Flood and those between Flood and Abraham. Genesis gives two lists. The first, from Cain, runs Henoch, Irad, Mehujael, Methusael, and Lamech. The second, far fuller and dated, runs from Seth through Enos, Cainan, Mahalaleel, Jared, Henoch, and Methuselah to Lamech again. Since both end at Lamech, the second likely amplifies the first with added matter.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peace-of-the-:
The Peace of the Church names the Church's condition after Constantine's Milan edict of toleration in 313, granting Christians full liberty to practise their religion without molestation. Freedom of conscience demanded by Christianity clashed with theocratic or absolutist views of State and religion that had ruled before Christ. That basic difference over civil power's reach, with religious, social, and economic reasons, led to prescribing Christ's followers in the Roman Empire.

Civil attitudes shifted as Christians grew in numbers and weight. First seen as mere Jewish schismatics, Christians were later persecuted as foes of State and established order. A new stage came in the mid-third century, when the Church itself became the attack's object. Decius opened that attitude, making the issue plain: the Christian Church and pagan Rome could not coexist, so only Christianity's destruction or Rome's conversion remained possible. For half a century the outcome hung in doubt.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pentateuch:
The Pentateuch is the name for the first five books of the Old Testament. This vast Catholic Encyclopedia study begins with the word itself, Greek for five cases or scroll-boxes. It then gives the older Jewish names: the Law, the Book of the Law, and the Law of Moses. It traces how the fivefold division was known to Philo and Josephus, though its exact origin remains unsettled.

From names the study moves to contents, authorship, and credibility.
