Genesis through Deuteronomy unfold creation, patriarchs, exodus, and lawgiving, and the entry weighs in full the question of Moses as author or mediator of the legislation. Later sections test the books against history and archaeology, defending their standing as law, narrative, and revelation against the critical theories of the nineteenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-ambarac:
Peter Ambarach was a Maronite Orientalist, also called Benedictus or Benedetti from the Arabic word for blessed. Born at Gusta in Syria in 1663, he was schooled by Jesuits at the Maronite College in Rome from 1672 to 1685, then ordained on his return home. Sent back to Rome on Maronite business, he was asked by Cosimo III de' Medici to build an Oriental press at Florence and took the Hebrew chair at Pisa.

He joined the Society of Jesus in 1708, and Clement XI named him to the commission preparing a corrected Septuagint. His chief labour was an edition of St. Ephrem's Syriac works with a Latin translation. Death at Rome in 1742 cut it short at two volumes, and Stephen Assemani finished the third.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-van-der:
Peter van der Bosch was a Brussels Bollandist, born in 1686. He studied humanities at Brussels College from 1698 to 1705, entered the Jesuit novitiate at Mechlin, studied philosophy at Antwerp, and spent a year in Italy perfecting his letters. Recalled to Antwerp in 1710, he taught for six years, then took theology at Louvain from 1716 to 1720 and was ordained there in 1719.

Public defences of theses in 1719 and a defence of universal theology in 1720 marked him as a scholar. In 1721, at the end of his third probation year, he joined the Bollandists as an assistant and stayed with that body for the rest of his life. His lives of saints appear in the July volumes four to six and the August volumes one to three of the Acta Sanctorum. He died in 1736.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prince-von-me:
Metternich, statesman, was born at Coblenz on 15 May 1773 and died at Vienna on 11 June 1859. His father was Count Georg, Austrian envoy at Coblenz; his mother Maria Beatrix, née Countess von Kageneck. He read philosophy at Strasburg and law and diplomacy at Mainz, and a trip to England crowned his schooling. He began public life in 1801 at Dresden as Austrian ambassador. Two years later he moved to Berlin. There the emperor prized a minister who could win the court's favour and wed keen observation to a mild, pleasing manner. Metternich had already shown those gifts.

With Napoleon at his zenith, Emperor Francis needed his ablest envoy at Napoleon's court, and in May 1806 sent Metternich to Paris. There he met Napoleon's threats and plans with dignity and firmness; his report of the weighty 15 August 1808 audience with Napoleon shows it. The year 1809 brought the great war between Austria and France.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-procopius-div:
Procopius Divisch, Premonstratensian, was born at Senftenberg, Bohemia, on 26 March 1698, and died at Prenditz, Moravia, on 25 December 1765. Christened Wenceslaus, he took the name Procopius as a religious. He studied at Znaym, then entered Bruck's Premonstratensian cloister school in Styria. Ordained in 1726, he soon became the school's philosophy professor.

In 1736 Prenditz's little parish near Znaym came under his charge. There he had leisure for work in hydraulics and electricity, building his own instruments. His fame spread, and Vienna called him to repeat his electrical experiments ere Emperor Francis and Empress Maria Theresa. He was among the first to use electricity in treating disease. Ere the French rendering of Franklin's letters appeared in 1751, he knew the discharging power of pointed rods. The first lightning rod rose by Divisch's hand at Prenditz in 1754, ere Franklin's hints were known or carried out elsewhere.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ruggiero-gius:
Ruggiero Giuseppe Boscovich was a Dalmatian Jesuit and man of science, born at Ragusa in 1711 and died at Milan in 1787. Youngest of six brothers, he was schooled at his native city's Jesuit college. Impressed by his masters, he entered the Jesuit novitiate at Rome in 1725, aged fourteen. At the Roman College he discovered for himself the proof of Pythagoras's theorem.

His teacher, Father Borgondi, trained him so well that he replaced his former teacher before finishing theology. Appointed teacher of maths there, he served with honour for a generation, publishing Latin papers nearly every year. These included Sunspots in 1736, Mercury's transit in 1737, and Aurora Borealis in 1738. The earth's shape, gravity's effects, and star shifts followed. Pure maths and theories of matter also engaged him, and academies at Bologna, Paris, and London took him in.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sanctity-mark:
Sanctity as a mark of the Church is the subject of this doctrinal entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. The word shifts meaning with its subject: in God it means absolute moral perfection by nature, and in people a close union with God with the moral goodness that follows. Creatures hold holiness only by sharing in God's gift, never by essence. Applied to a society, the word means something testable.

A holy society aims to make its members holy and owns means able to do so. Its members' lives match that aim at least in part, with real rather than merely nominal holiness. The Church claims sanctity in a surpassing degree as one of four notes, with unity, catholicity, and apostolicity, by which Christ's society can be told apart from every human body. The entry defends that claim against objections.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saxe-weimar-e:
Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach, a grand duchy in Thuringia also called the Grand Duchy of Saxony, covers 1,397 square miles in three detached parts: Weimar at 678, Eisenach at 465, and Neustadt at 254. In 1910 it held 417,166 people, with 18,049 Catholics, about five per cent, in 1905. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia traces a state pieced together by Wettin partitions.

The Wettins split in 1485 into Ernestine and Albertine lines. John Frederick the Magnanimous, of the Ernestine line, lost his electoral dignity and most estates in the Wittenberg Capitulation of 1547, keeping only Thuringia. Even under his sons Thuringia began splitting into principalities. Since the division of 1672 the Ernestine line has run in two main branches, the Weimar line, now grand ducal, and its Eisenach kin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-science-and-t:
Science and the Church, in this long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia, takes science in Aristotle's and Aquinas's broad sense, not merely natural science. Aristotle calls science sure and evident knowledge gained by demonstration, and Aquinas calls it knowledge of things through their causes. In that sense science covers the whole university curriculum. Church means in theory any doctrinal authority, in practice the Catholic Church.

The relation is treated under two heads, science and Church. Science is viewed from three angles: contact with faith, legitimate freedom, and unlimited freedom. Contacts with faith lie mainly in philosophy and history. The entry defends the scientist's rightful freedom within his field while marking where faith and reason meet, a classic statement of the Catholic position before modern science's later battles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-berach:
St. Berach of Termonbarry, who died in 595, learned from St. Kevin and remains a celebrated Irish saint, his memory still fresh in County Roscommon. This entry follows a man of the tribe of Cinel Dobtha, or O'Hanley of Doohey Hanley, to which the MacCoilidh family also belongs. Most of his long life was spent in the diocese of Elphin, where he built his church at Cluain Coirpthe, now Termonbarry or Kilbarry.

His sister, St. Midabaria, was abbess of a nunnery at Bumlin, or Strokestown, of which she is venerated as patroness on 22 February. Her ancient church and graveyard are still to be seen. Under the title Berach of Cluain Coirpthe, Berach is honoured in several martyrologies, and his holy life drew pilgrims to Kilbarry from all Ireland. The MacCoilidh family, whose name became Cox in the early seventeenth century, were hereditary custodians of his crosier.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-brenach:
St. Brenach was an Irish missionary in Wales, a contemporary of St. Patrick, and among the earliest Irish saints who laboured among the Celts of that country. This entry follows a pilgrim who about 418 journeyed to Rome and Brittany, then on to Milford Haven. He put up various oratories by the Cleddau, Gwain, and Caman rivers, and at the foot of Carn Engyli, or Mountain of the Angels, his most famous foundation.

Among his converts was Brecan, an Irish chief and ruler of South Wales about 425. The Triads reckon Brecan as a saint who founded numerous churches in Brecknockshire, Carmarthenshire, Pembrokeshire, Denbighshire, and Anglesey. From the Welsh Lives we learn that Brenach died on 7 April, the day his feast is celebrated. His church, overhanging the Severn, stands as a lasting memorial to the Irish pilgrim through whom, under God, a great part of Wales was converted.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-edmund-ric:
Edmund Rich, archbishop of Canterbury, grew from a pious Abingdon household into a reformer whose discipline began at home. Born about 1180 to Reinald and Mabel Rich, he was trained by his mother in fasting, hair shirts, and night prayer. Sent to Oxford, he knew a vision of the Child Christ in the fields and thereafter signed his forehead nightly with the words Jesus of Nazareth. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 follows him to his death at Soissy on 16 November 1240.

His sisters became nuns at Catesby, and his father entered Eynsham monastery even during his mother's lifetime. That family austerity shaped an archbishop who prized purity of mind and body above comfort. The entry reads as a study in formation: a household of penance producing a pastor who carried its habits into high office.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-eustathius:
Eustathius of Antioch, bishop from about 323, was deposed and exiled for fighting Arianism too fearlessly. Born at Side in Pamphylia about 270, he first held Beroea in Syria before transfer to Antioch. At Nicaea in 325 he stood among the most prominent opponents of Arian teaching, then waged almost continuous literary warfare against it until 330. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death in exile at Trajanopolis, most probably in 360.

Arian leaders headed by the two Eusebii convened a synod at Antioch in 331. Suborned witnesses charged him with Sabellianism, incontinence, cruelty, and other crimes. Deposed by the synod and banished by Constantine, who believed the scandal, he left a people ready to take up arms for him. The entry closes on an injustice: a learned patriarch removed by rigged testimony.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ignatius-o:
Ignatius of Antioch, called God-bearer, wrote his way to martyrdom in letters that still shape the early church. Born in Syria around the year 50, third bishop of Antioch after Peter and Evodius, he was, with Polycarp, likely a hearer of the apostle John. Legend made him the child Christ took in his arms in Mark's gospel, a tale the entry notes without good reason. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates his death at Rome between 98 and 117.

Chained and bound for Rome to feed wild beasts as a public spectacle, he called his guards ten leopards, growing worse when kindly treated. His overland road ran through Philadelphia and Sardis to Smyrna, where Polycarp was bishop, and his stay there lengthened into a triumph of visits and letters. The entry follows a pastor-soldier whose chains became correspondence, and whose death became testimony.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-roch:
Roch, a pilgrim saint of Montpellier, gave his fortune to the poor and spent himself tending plague victims. Born toward 1295 to the governor of Montpellier, he was said to bear a red cross on his breast from birth. Orphaned about twenty, he divided his wealth among the poor, left the city's government to his uncle, and set out for Italy as a mendicant pilgrim.

At Aquapendente, stricken by plague, he nursed the sick and cured them with the sign of the cross. He worked the same ministry at Cesena, Rome, Mantua, Modena, and Parma. At Piacenza he caught the plague himself, recovered in a forest hut supplied by Gothard, and returned to France. Taken for a spy at Montpellier, he died in prison in 1327, unrecognised by his own uncle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-tassach:
Tassach, an Irish saint of the fifth century, gave Patrick his last Communion. Born in the first decade of the fifth century, he was one of Patrick's artificers, craftsmen who built and equipped the apostle's churches. When Patrick founded the church of Raholp, a couple of miles north-east of Saul in County Down, he placed Tassach over it.

Tassach's rule is memorable for one act: Patrick chose him to stand by in his last moments and administer the Holy Viaticum. The Martyrology of Donegal records it plainly: Tassach of Raholp gave the Body of Christ to Patrick before his death in the monastery of Saul. Tassach died about 497, and his feast is kept on 14 April.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ulrich:
Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg, ruled his diocese for fifty years through Hungarian invasions and church reform. Born at Kyburg near Zurich in 890, he was son of Count Hucpald and Thetbirga. His kin included the Alamannian dukes and the Ottonian emperors. A sickly child, he was sent to St Gall's monastic school, where he proved an excellent scholar.

Unsure between Benedictine life and secular priesthood, he trained under Adalbero of Augsburg, who made him chamberlain. After Adalbero's death and Bishop Hiltine's in 923, his uncle Duke Burchard secured his appointment, and he was consecrated on 28 December 923. Uniting severity with gentleness, he reformed clergy morals by regular visitations, rebuilt churches, and defended Augsburg against the Magyars. He died on 4 July 973.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-william-of:
William of Norwich, a tanner's apprentice found dead in 1144, became the centre of a cult built on an accusation against Jews. On Holy Saturday 1144 a boy's corpse, showing signs of violent death, was found in Thorpe Wood near Norwich. It lay untouched until Easter Monday, when it was buried where it lay. The body was recognised as William, who frequented houses of certain Jews with his master.

His uncle, the priest Godwin Stuart, accused Norwich's Jews of murder before a diocesan synod and offered proof by ordeal. The sheriff objected that the Jews, as the king's men, lay outside the bishop's jurisdiction, and no conviction followed. Thomas of Monmouth later wrote a life promoting the cult and the charge. The entry presents the episode as accusation and cult history, not as established fact.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-state-and-chu:
Church and State, both perfect societies in this article's terms, claim a common good and the means to pursue it. The State is shown such by ethics, the Church by the theology of revelation. Sharing subjects, territory, and some means of action, they inevitably stand in mutual juridical relations, which the article states from an ethical viewpoint.

Five heads organise the argument: the basis of their respective rights, the range of their jurisdictions, their mutual corporate relation, the union of Church and State, and counter theories. All earthly rights and duties, it argues, come from God through divine law, natural or positive, shaped by the Creator's purpose for human nature. The entry offers a compact Thomistic framework for judging concordats, establishments, and separations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-states-of-the:
The States of the Church, the pope's civil territory for over a thousand years, from 754 to 1870, began as private property. Patrimonium Sancti Petri first meant the landed possessions and revenues of St Peter's Church at Rome. Constantine's law of 321, qualifying the Christian Church to hold and transmit property, gave those possessions legal ground, and donations swelled them, the Lateran Palace most probably among Constantine's own gifts.

Later the term covered the States themselves, above all the Duchy of Rome. The article traces the patrimony to Charlemagne, then narrates the States' history: Pepin's donation, imperial contests, Renaissance popes, Napoleon, and the Risorgimento's end. It closes with the territory's loss in 1870 and the pope's consequent position. Readers get a millennium of temporal power in one reference sweep.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tancred-princ:
Tancred, Prince of Antioch, was born about 1072. He was the son of Marquess Odo and Emma, probably daughter of Robert Guiscard. He took the Cross in 1096 with Norman lords of southern Italy, serving his uncle Bohemund. He won notice for bravery, restless zeal, and kindness to the defenceless. Crossing the Vardar in February 1097, he routed a Byzantine force and became a bitter enemy of the Greeks.

Alone among the leaders, he refused the oath of fidelity Alexis demanded. He helped take Nicaea, seized Tarsus ahead of Baldwin, and took Cilician towns. He led the vanguard into Jerusalem on 15 July 1099. He failed to save three hundred Muslims sheltering in the Mosque of Omar. He looted its treasures, then later ruled Antioch after Bohemund's capture in 1100. He widened its borders at Turkish and Greek expense.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-anglo-sax:
Britain between the Roman withdrawal and the Norman Conquest fills this long survey, covering the Teutonic settlers who became the foundation stock of the English people. Jutes, Saxons, and Angles arrived from the mid fifth century onward, pushing Celtic inhabitants westward and holding the land until 1066. Their tribal origins, settlements, and kings form the opening ground.

Missionaries then enter the story, above all Augustine's mission from Rome and the older Celtic missions from Ireland and Iona. Conversion, monastic life, church organisation, and the slow growth of dioceses and parishes follow in turn, with law, learning, and art woven through. It is a full history of faith taking root in a new people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-book-of-e:
Henoch, the patriarch who walked with God and vanished, lends his name to a body of apocalyptic writing examined here. Mystery around his departure, joined to hints of special revelations, made him a natural figurehead for visionary authors. Their books shaped later Jewish apocrypha and left marks on the New Testament and the early Fathers.

Jude's epistle quotes Enoch outright, in verses 14 and 15, and the citation survives in the Ethiopic version. Barnabas cites him as Scripture, while Clement, Tertullian, Origen, and even Augustine show his influence. Surviving versions, contents, and the book's fall from favour in the West round out an entry on a text that hovered at Scripture's edge.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-church:
Society founded by Christ, called church in Teutonic tongues, is the subject of this vast doctrinal entry. Greek ekklesia, the New Testament word for that society, reaches English through kyriakon or Lord's house, a term used from the third century for a Christian place of worship. Northern tribes, pillaging imperial churches ere their own conversion, already owned words for Christian externals.

Sections follow in order: the term ecclesia, the Church in prophecy, its founding by Christ, life after the Ascension, organisation by the Apostles, marks, constitution, and mission. Scripture, tradition, councils, and theologians all contribute to a full account of what Catholics mean when they say Church, one, holy, catholic, and apostolic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tilman-pesch:
Tilman Pesch, a Jesuit philosopher, was born at Cologne in 1836 and died at Valkenburg, Holland, in 1899. He joined the Society in October 1852, studied classics at Paderborn and philosophy at Bonn, taught at Feldkirch, and studied theology at Paderborn and Maria-Laach. He taught philosophy at Maria-Laach from 1867 to 1869 and at Blyenbeck from 1876 to 1884.

His writing began in 1876 with Latin textbooks on natural philosophy, logic and psychology. In German he published works on the world as phenomenon, the riddle of the world, soul and love, and Christian philosophy of life. Under the pen name Gottlieb he wrote popular articles against common charges facing the Church, later gathered as Letters from Hamburg and The Crash of Wittenberg.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-unity-as-a-ma:
Unity as a mark of the church means one of the unmistakable signs by which the true church can be recognized and told apart from every other religious society. Such outward signs must exist, the entry argues, because Christ founded a church to guard and expound revealed truths, and made it binding on all to know and hear it. A church meant to stand in Christ's place and carry on his work cannot hide itself from those it summons.

The entry then shows how Catholic unity appears in one faith, one worship, and one government under the pope, despite the spread of peoples and tongues within the fold. It answers objections drawn from schisms and heresies, and contrasts this visible oneness with the divisions of separated bodies. Readers seeking the theological case for unity as a note of the church will find it argued here in full.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-use-of-number:
No attentive reader of the Old Testament can miss the sacredness that clings to certain numbers, such as seven, forty, and twelve. It is not mere recurrence that matters, but ritual and ceremonial use. Abraham's oath in Genesis 21, after setting apart seven ewe lambs for sacrifice, gains point from the link between the Hebrew word for swearing, nishba, and sheba, seven. The same mystical use of numbers runs through the New Testament, above all in the Apocalypse.

Even so early a writer as St Irenaeus explains the beast's number 666 by the word Lateinos, whose letters add up to that sum. The entry follows seven, twelve, forty, and other numbers through Scripture and liturgy, weighing what is symbol and what is fancy. It gives readers a sober guide to number lore in worship, neither credulous nor dismissive.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-veit-amerbach:
Veit Amerbach was born at Wembdingen in 1503 and died at Ingolstadt on 13 September 1557, a humanist and convert from Lutheranism to the Catholic Church. After schooling at Eichstätt and Wittenberg, he taught philosophy, law, Oriental tongues, and Lutheran theology at Wittenberg, meeting Luther, Melanchthon, and other new-movement leaders daily. There he came to see Lutheran doctrines as novel and false, and the church's teaching as true.

After long controversial letters with Melanchthon, he departed Wittenberg in 1543 and entered the Catholic Church together with his wife and children. Prince-Bishop Maurice von Hutten named him professor of rhetoric at Eichstätt. A year later he moved to Ingolstadt as professor of philosophy, where he stayed until his death. The entry counts him among the converts who shaped Catholic learning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-anne-cath:
Anne Catherine Emmerich was an Augustinian nun, stigmatic, and ecstatic, born on 8 September 1774 at Flamsche near Coesfeld in Westphalia, who died at Dülmen on 9 February 1824. Her parents, both peasants, were poor and deeply pious. At twelve she was bound to a farmer, and later she worked as a seamstress for several years. Always delicate, she was sent to learn music, yet found the organist's family very poor and handed them her small savings toward convent entry.

She actually served that family for several years, and at times went so short of food that her mother brought her bread, part of which went to her master's family. In her twenty-eighth year, in 1802, she entered the Augustinian convent at Agnetenberg in Dülmen. There she was content to rank lowest in the house, and the entry follows her visions, her stigmata, and her fame as a mystic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-john-finc:
John Finch was a martyr born about 1548 who died on 20 April 1584. A yeoman of Eccleston in Lancashire from a well-known old Catholic family, he seems to have been raised in schism. At twenty he went to London and spent nearly a year with cousins at the Inner Temple. There the contrast between Protestant and Catholic practice struck him forcibly, and he resolved to live as a Catholic.

Finding no advancement in London, he returned to Lancashire and was reconciled to the church. He married and settled down, his house becoming a centre of missionary work, sheltering priests, aiding them in every way, and serving as catechist himself. His zeal drew official hostility, and at Christmas 1581 he was trapped into bringing a priest, George Ostcliffe, to his house, leading to his arrest and execution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vestibule-por:
A vestibule, or porch, is the hall projecting before a church's façade, found from the fifth century in both East and West.

In the East, especially Syria, it gained a fine façade flanked by two towers, often closed in front, entered by one or three doors, and sometimes two storeys high. Medieval Italy kept the simple open chamber. North of the Alps the porch grew into a projecting structure joined to the main building, recalling Syrian churches. Charlemagne's palace church at Aachen, with a multi-storey ante-structure between two western round towers, set a pattern adopted in the early Romanesque period, above all by Cluniac monks. Speyer cathedral first used the covered west-front ante-structure on a large scale, with three storeys.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vich:
Vich is a Catalan diocese, suffragan to Tarragona, lying mostly in the province of Barcelona and bounded by Gerona, Barcelona, Tarragona, and Lérida. Its capital, of about 9,500 people, is of very ancient origin: Roman Ausa, Iberian coins bearing that name have been found there, Gothic Ausona, then.

Moorish destruction, only one quarter rebuilt, Vicus Ausonensis, whence Vich. Christianity there is undoubtedly remote, with martyrs of Ausa recorded under Decius and the bishop of Vich among the first named in Tarragona's earliest records. No bishop is named until Cinidius in 516. Successors attended the great councils of Toledo, and the see's pre-Saracen history ends with Wisefredus, before reconquest under Louis the Pious entrusted civil rule to Borrell, Count of Ausona.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-welsh-church:
The Welsh Church is treated here as one continuous subject, following the practice of English historical writers and Haddan and Stubbs's Councils and Ecclesiastical Documents. The entry questions their sharp divisions between the British Church in the Roman period, 200 to 450, during the Saxon conquest, 450 to 681. The Church of Wales proper, 681 to 1295.

In the Roman period both Tertullian about 208 and Origen about 240 use language implying the Gospel had reached Britain, Tertullian speaking of regions inaccessible to Romans but subdued to Christ. Origen of the Lord's power among those separated from the world in Britain. Though somewhat rhetorical, those passages gain support from Constantius's Life of St Germanus and Gildas's account of St Alban's martyrdom in the Roman period. Later sections follow Saxon conquest, the age of saints, whose dates remain uncertain, the supposed synods against Pelagianism at Llandewi-Brefi and Lucus Victoriae, and the spread of monasticism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-bened:
William Benedict Fytch, born Filch, was an English Capuchin friar famed for miracles and prophecy. Born at Canfield in Essex in 1563, he died in 1610. His parents stood with the Puritan party, and he himself held Calvinist views until study in London brought him into the Catholic Church. He crossed to Paris and joined the Capuchins. In 1599 he asked to be sent to England, but he had barely landed when officers seized him and threw him into prison.

Three years in jail gave him room for debates with his captors on the true faith. Freed through the French ambassador, he returned to France as master of novices. Court and common folk alike revered him for his wonder-working and foresight. His best-known devotional work, The Will of God, written in English, spread swiftly into other tongues, and the order's minister general had it turned into Latin in 1625.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wolfram-von-e:
Wolfram von Eschenbach is counted the greatest Middle High German epic poet. His birth date is unknown; he died soon after 1216. All we know of him comes from his works. A poor Bavarian noble, perhaps a younger son, he owned only Wildenberg estate near Ansbach, and took his name from Eschenbach town southeast of Ansbach. He called the Count of Wertheim my lord, which may mean vassalage or mere courtesy.

Wolfram wandered and after 1203 stayed often at Eisenach with Landgrave Hermann, where parts of Parzival took shape. He outlived Hermann, dead in 1217, and died after, leaving works unfinished, buried at Eschenbach's Frauenkirche, his tomb visible into the seventeenth century. Parzival itself, twenty-five thousand verses from 1200 to 1216, tells how a simpleton passes struggle and temptation to win joy and the Grail kingship. Wolfram, who says he could neither read nor write, dictated it from French sources and a shadowy Kyot.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zurich:
Zurich is the capital of the Swiss canton of the same name, second largest and richest of Switzerland's twenty-five cantons, and the country's largest city with 200,000 inhabitants. It commands the outlet of Lake Zurich, flanked by the wooded Uetliberg and Zurichberg heights, with a ring of lofty Glarus, Schwyz, and Uri mountains behind.

Historically the city first appears as Turicum under Roman rule at the Christian era's start, when Christianity probably arrived, brought by legend's Theban Legion members Felix, Regula, and Exuperantius, the city's patrons. After the Alamanni conquered northern Switzerland in the fourth and fifth centuries, Zurich became capital of its districts. Ruled in the early Middle Ages by Fraumünster's abbess, the great lady of Zurich, it later became a free imperial city and joined the Swiss Confederation in 1351. At the sixteenth century's start it became German Switzerland's Reformation cradle under pastor Huldreich Zwingli.
doe-osti-2997285-abbreviated-report-for-:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory abbreviated report LLNL-TR-2011960, by Marcus Hill and Geoff Sanders, dated September 2025, summarizes project 25-FS-011, called Switch and Stitch. Security analysts who hunt malicious code need to know which parts of a program a similarity model found suspicious. The project studied automated explanations for graph neural network models that compare the control flow graphs of compiled programs.

A reinforcement learning method was built to pick out the subgraph that best explains a match between two program graphs. Given a pair, the learner updates its chosen set of explanatory points step by step. The aim is to point analysts at the code regions worth human review, rather than handing them a bare score. The filing is a brief project summary, with method and purpose stated and fuller results held in project records.
doe-osti-3013031-laser-driven-inertial-f:
General Atomics Electromagnetic Systems' final scientific report, dated November 10, 2025, covers its ARPA-E award DE-AR0001744 on laser driven inertial fusion energy, with Michael Perry as principal investigator. The reporting period ran May 2023 to August 2024. The project developed laser direct drive fusion, in which many laser beams strike a fuel target evenly from all sides to compress and ignite it.

The team surveyed the point design parameter space for a direct drive power plant concept, covering target design, required laser energy, beam count and focusing, and suitable bandwidth formats. Laser material options were analyzed with detailed performance modeling to guide the diode-pumped solid-state laser design. A separate appendix holds controlled information and is not part of the public report.
doe-osti-3013451-additive-manufactured-c:
Oak Ridge CRADA final report ORNL/TM-2025/4388, dated December 2025, models a 3D-printed composite phase-change material for thermal energy storage. Balasubramaniam Radhakrishnan led the author team. Co-authors came from Siemens Energy, Carnegie Mellon University, the University of Alabama, and Oak Ridge. Phase-change materials soak up heat as they melt. They release it as they freeze. Printing them into a metal composite could shape storage blocks for industry.

The work is computational. Phase-field models simulate how the material's internal structure evolves. One model family used is the Kim-Kim-Suzuki formulation. Test cases varied droplet size and grain boundary diffusivity. That is the speed atoms move along crystal seams. Doubling that diffusivity in one test did not make the liquid phase spread along the boundaries. The results guide how printed composites should be structured before anyone prints them.
doe-osti-3020944-strategic-petroleum-res:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2026-17546, by Todd R. Zeitler and Hannah Maurer, monitors how the Strategic Petroleum Reserve's salt caverns changed during calendar year 2024. The reserve stores crude oil in 60 caverns inside salt domes at four Louisiana and Texas sites, with capacity above 700 million barrels. Since 2016, congressionally mandated oil sales have required injecting unsaturated water to push oil out, and that water slowly dissolves the cavern walls.

Only two caverns received substantial raw water in 2024, totaling 1.2 million barrels, while seven more caverns were surveyed by sonar to check earlier leaching. The team modeled dissolution with the SANSMIC solution mining code, including a new Python version built during the year. Sonar surveys give direct shape measurements but are costly across many caverns; modeling flags which caverns need closer attention.
doe-osti-3399434-considerations-for-mari:
Considerations for Maritime Nuclear Technologies, Economic Viability and Public Acceptance, Idaho National Laboratory report INL/RPT-24-80343, dated May 2025, comes from the Maritime Nuclear Applications Group. The group was convened by the National Reactor Innovation Center. The American Bureau of Shipping and the law firm Morgan, Lewis, and Bockius joined it. That mix signals the subject: reactors at sea raise engineering, classification, and legal questions together.

Two use cases structure the examination. The first is the maritime nuclear power plant, floating or shore-sited plants serving ports and coastal industry. The report reviews their history. The second is nuclear propulsion and ship power for commercial civilian vessels. Economic viability and public acceptance get full chapters. A reactor ship must pencil out against diesel and ammonia rivals. It must also be welcome in the ports it visits.
doe-osti-3402220-wyoming-trails-carbon-h:
Final report for award DE-FE0032347 covers the Wyoming Trails Carbon Hub, known as WyoTCH. Richard Middleton led a team from the University of Wyoming, INTERA, Glenrock Energy, and other partners. The project ran from October 1, 2023 to March 31, 2026.

Engineers finished a front-end design study for a shared carbon dioxide pipeline in Wyoming. The line would serve many sources and many storage sites, not just one plant. That shared design aims to lower the cost bar for new capture projects. Later pages give build details such as coating systems for steel, vessels, and piping.
doe-osti-3685179-progress-towards-synthe:
Argonne report ANL/CFCT-26/21 tracks progress on making uranium chloride fuel salts with zinc chloride. Stephanie Dulovic, Christian K. Nilles, and Krista L. Hawthorne are the printed authors. Molten salt reactors will need actinide chloride salts in lots over one hundred kilograms. Older routes used cadmium or lead chlorides, both toxic and costly to dispose of.

Zinc chloride reacts the same way and leaves a zinc metal layer that parts from the salt. A bench unit was built, installed, and run at high heat. It made a lithium-potassium chloride salt holding about a quarter uranium by weight, in steps. Heat drove off the zinc formed during the reaction. Electrical tests found no leftover zinc metal in the salt. Lab checks of exact makeup and impurities were still to come. The rig can now test other salts and cleanup routes for scale-up.
doe-osti-3740851-strategic-petroleum-res:
Sandia report SAND2026-26070, printed September 2026, tracks salt cavern growth at the Strategic Petroleum Reserve during calendar year 2025. Todd Zeitler and Hannah Maurer are the printed authors. The reserve stores oil in caverns washed out of salt domes. Each drawdown lets raw water dissolve more salt, slowly reshaping the walls. Staff watch that growth so caverns never creep too close together.

The SANSMIC code models each wash from water flow records. Runs cover four sites: Bayou Choctaw, Bryan Mound, West Hackberry, and Big Hill. At Bryan Mound, about half a million barrels of raw water entered two caverns that year. Model shapes are checked against sonar surveys, and gaps between cavern walls are tallied site by site. Three Bryan Mound caverns stay on a watch list. The team also reports a bug found in the current code and its effect on past runs. Python notebooks now drive each run.
doe-osti-3904547-ldrd-lw-fy26-abbreviate: Livermore short-form final report LLNL-TR-2024732, dated September 2026, sums up a project on drying-tolerant biofertilizer bacteria. Jennifer Chlebek led the work, with Joshua White and Sean Leonard. The text is the programme's abbreviated close-out: one overview plus findings. Nitrogen-fixing microbes offer a greener route than chemical fertilizer but die back when dried for storage. The team edited genes tied to surviving drying, then let lab evolution expose the microbes' own fixes. Genes for clumping and holding water stood out.
elsie-inglis-the-woman-with-the-torch:
Eva Shaw McLaren tells the life of Dr. Elsie Inglis in Elsie Inglis: The Woman with the Torch, from the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge in 1920, in the Pioneers of Progress series on women. Lena Ashwell supplies a preface and a poem of tribute. A frontispiece shows Inglis after her return from Serbia in 1916.

The chapter syllabus runs from an Indian childhood and Edinburgh schooldays to medical study and a practice begun in 1894. War made her famous: she raised the Scottish Women's Hospitals and served in Serbia. A letter of October 4, 1914, printed here, says she can think of nothing except those units, and can hardly sit still at the awful need. McLaren writes of a leader whose make-weight helpers steadied brilliant work. The book is warm, brief, and meant to inspire women entering medicine.
govdocs-archive_org-jors195320fppng_v03_:
Vannevar Bush ran American science during the Second World War, heading the office that put radar, the proximity fuze, and the atomic bomb program into motion. Research and the War Effort, his piece in the Operational Research Society's journal, looks back at that mobilization.

Bush describes how thousands of scientists were drawn into war work and what their research changed on the battlefield and at sea. He writes as the administrator who built the system, plain about both its triumphs and its friction with the military. The piece is a primary source on wartime science policy by the man who directed it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HochPaulHSCANot:
Paul L. Hoch drafted a commentary on the House Select Committee on Assassinations hearings in October and November 1978. The piece was a first draft prepared for Inquiry magazine. Hoch followed the hearings as a researcher who knew the files, grading the committee's work as it unfolded in public.

A first draft is a mind not yet polished for print. Hoch's comments show what an informed skeptic made of the testimony day by day. Prepared for a magazine of inquiry, the draft preserves the research community's running verdict on the second great assassination investigation.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p:
Vladimir Putin first won election as president of Russia in March 2000, after Boris Yeltsin handed him power at the end of 1999. Twenty-four years later, in March 2024, the National Security Archive published declassified American records looking back at that vote and at how United States officials judged it at the time.

One declassified record quoted in the posting calls the 2000 election reasonably free and fair. That judgment sits at the heart of the release, since Putin's later elections drew far harsher charges from Western governments. Readers get the early American view in the officials' own words, from a moment when ties between Washington and Moscow were warmer and the new Russian leader was still an open question.
grand-grimoire-french:
Le Grand Grimoire, the Grand Grimoire, is the most famous black book of the French tradition. This French text belongs to the nineteenth century, when printed copies spread widely. Its other name, the Red Dragon, comes from the title under which many copies traveled through France.

At its center stands a pact with Lucifuge Rofocale, a chief spirit of hell. The magician signs away his soul and names his price, in the book's own chilling bargain. That scene defined the grimoire tradition for popular imagination. Treasure hunting, spirit service, and dire warnings fill the pages. No French grimoire has cast a longer shadow, for better or worse.
grimorium-verum-french:
The Grimorium Verum, the True Grimoire, survives here in its classic French text of about 1817. It claims descent from Solomon, like most books of its kind. The French version became the standard one, a concise manual of spirits, seals, and pacts that working magicians actually used.

Its pages teach the conjurer how to prepare, which spirits to call, and what seals to draw. The tone is practical, brief, and dark. The book anchored the eighteenth-century French grimoire trade that peddlers carried across Europe. Unlike the vast learned tomes, the Grimorium Verum fits a pocket and a purpose. Generations of magicians passed it from hand to hand.
hilgers-die-bucherverbote-in-papstbriefe:
Joseph Hilgers wrote this German study of book bans in papal letters, issued in 1907. He works as a canon lawyer and a book scholar at once. His subject is how popes, by formal briefs, barred set books by name. Each ban is traced in the Vatican records and old lists.

Hilgers prints and sorts dozens of papal letters with care. One case treats a brief of Clement the Eleventh from the year 1709. Names, dates, shelf marks, and charges fill the pages. The work is in German, with Latin texts quoted. Scholars of church censorship will find a strict, source-bound survey here.
how-to-teach:
George Drayton Strayer and Naomi Norsworthy wrote this teacher's manual, dated February 1917. Education, they open, is a group enterprise. Schools exist for the group, not first for the single child, they argue. The teacher's work heads a fifteen-chapter course.

Original nature is the capital teachers work with, in their phrase. Attention, habit, memory, and imagination each get a chapter. Play's meaning and single differences among children follow. Moral social conduct and transfer of training close the list. Measuring children's achievements ends the book. Normal-school students of the day got progressive doctrine in a plain, ordered form.
impressions-of-theophrastus-such:
George Eliot issued Impressions of Theophrastus Such in a second edition in London and Edinburgh in 1879. The speaker, Theophrastus, gives an account of himself and of the folk he meets. Chapter heads name his themes, from looking inward to moral swindlers and small authorship.

Essays probe vanity, false praise, and the wish to seem original. One piece asks how we give ourselves false testimonials and then believe them. Another treats the wasp credited with the honeycomb. Eliot uses the mask to judge literary and social folly with sharp, calm humor.
indian-frontier-policy-an-historical-ske:
General Sir John Adye's Indian Frontier Policy is a historical sketch of Britain's policy on India's north-west frontier. Adye writes while military operations on a considerable scale are under way against a combination of independent tribes along the frontier.

He insists that the troubles are no sudden outbreak, but the consequence of events in bygone years, and he offers a short summary of their varying phases. Contents begin with events before and including the first Afghan war of 1839 to 1841, and the proposed invasion of India by Napoleon. Adye hopes his summary will help the public understand the bearings of policy and judge what should be pursued. Readers of imperial history will find it concise and soldierly.
indian-games-an-historical-research:
Andrew McFarland Davis's Indian Games is a historical research into the games of North America's native peoples. Davis begins with Father Brebeuf's 1636 account of the Hurons, who prized three games above others: cross, platter and straw.

Brebeuf marvelled that a sick man, hot with fever, might be ordered a game of cross as his only cooling remedy. Villages would array themselves against each other in a beautiful field, wagering beaver skins to raise the excitement. Davis traces these games and their meanings through the early accounts, treating play as medicine, ritual and social contest at once. Students of native history and of the history of sport will find it a careful, source-based study.
indian-nullification-of-the-unconstituti:
William Apess, a Pequot preacher who spelled his name Apes on the title page, published Indian Nullification in 1835. The book defends the Marshpee Tribe against Massachusetts laws he calls unconstitutional. A letter from the tribe opens it, calling Apess a brother raised up for them. White men, it says, are the only ones who imposed on them.

Apess speaks in a fearless and eloquent speech quoted in the book. He shows how overseers extorted from poor Indians, in his account. The tribe, he argues, could manage its own affairs better. The pretended riot is explained in their favor.
international-short-stories-french:
Francis J. Reynolds compiled International Short Stories: French, issued in 1910. Coppee's A Piece of Bread opens the volume, with a young duke at Aix in Savoy. Balzac, Bourget, Merimee, and Maupassant are all represented. Voltaire's Zadig and Hugo's fight with a cannon add older and grander names.

Vidocq's Jean Monette brings a detective's memoir into the set. An inspector asks help to take the robber Despreau near the Rue St. Antoine at eleven at night. Daudet's Last Lesson and Zola's Four Days close the range. Reynolds gives English readers a broad French shelf in one book.
jack-ranger-s-western-trip-or-from-board:
Clarence Young's Jack Ranger's Western Trip takes its hero from boarding school to ranch and range. The story opens at Washington Hall, where Jack falls into trouble, faces a threatening letter, and turns tables on a plot with a chemistry lesson.

A burglar scare, Nat's invitation, and a grand wind-up send Jack west, where an old acquaintance, Professor Punjab's trick, and shooting an oil well await. The wild steer, the old stockman, a thief in the night, a cattle stampede, and hunting mountain lions follow. Young readers who enjoy school stories that become western adventures will find Jack Ranger brisk and cheerful.
judith-of-blue-lake-ranch:
Judith of Blue Lake Ranch is a Western novel by Jackson Gregory, published in March 1919 by Charles Scribner's Sons. W. Herbert Dunton drew the pictures. The frontispiece shows Judith's spurs turning a bucking, devil-hearted horse. Twenty chapters are listed, opening with Bud Lee Wants to Know.

Judith takes a hand, rides an outlaw, and puts matters straight in the early chapters. Later titles promise rifle shots from cliffs, a happening in Squaw Creek Cañon, and time under fire in an old cabin. Young Hampton registers a protest, and a partners theme closes the list shown. Gregory writes ranch adventure with a heroine who rides and decides for herself.
laennec-auscultation-mediate-vol1-1819-f:
French readers met Laennec's invention in its first form in De l'auscultation mediate, printed in 1819. Tome one opens the treatise on diagnosing diseases of the lungs and heart. Laennec describes the stethoscope, a simple wooden tube of his own devising. He then sets out the sounds it reveals and what each one means.

Healthy and sick chests are compared sound by sound. Laennec writes from hospital wards, testing each sign against what autopsies later showed. That link between sound and lesion made his method scientific. The French first edition is the founding text of chest examination. A separate English translation by Forbes is also held.
laennec-auscultation-mediate-vol2-1819-f:
Tome two of Laennec's De l'auscultation mediate, also from 1819, completes the original French treatise. The first tome set out the stethoscope and its basic signs. The second carries the method through the diseases of the lungs and heart in full. Case evidence and lesion records fill its pages.

Laennec matches what the ear hears to what the opened body shows. That discipline turned listening into diagnosis. French medicine gained a tool that spread across the world within years. The two tomes together form one work and should be read as such. This second half holds much of the clinical detail. It rewards doctors and historians alike.
language-an-introduction-to-the-study-of:
Edward Sapir published Language in 1921, as an introduction to the study of speech. Nine chapters move from a definition of language to its history. Sapir calls language a cultural act, not an inborn one.

He rejects simple theories that speech began with cries or sound copying. Chapters treat sounds, words, grammar, and how languages change. He also asks whether thought is possible without language. Sapir writes for general readers, not only scholars. His book remains a classic doorway into linguistics, the science of language. Sapir's examples come from many tongues, including Native American languages. They show how widely human speech patterns can differ.
lois-the-witch:
Elizabeth Gaskell's story of Lois appears in this 1861 work. A modern Penguin introduction traces Gaskell's life first. She was born in London in 1810, it explains. Cheshire, Stratford, and the north formed her early years.

In 1832 she married the Reverend William Gaskell of Manchester. Household, parish work, and motherhood filled sixteen busy years. Mary Barton, her first full fiction, succeeded instantly in 1848. Charlotte Brontë became her close friend from 1850 onward. Dickens's Household Words carried her fiction for thirteen years. North and South, another Manchester novel, appeared in 1855. She also wrote for Dickens's magazine Household Words over thirteen years.
madam-how-and-lady-why-or-first-lessons-:
Madam How and Lady Why gives first lessons in earth lore for children. Charles Kingsley wrote it, and this text follows the 1889 Macmillan edition. He dedicated it to his son Grenville Arthur and his schoolfellows. His preface scolds the dull, ugly children's books of his own boyhood.

Kingsley urges boys to use their eyes, ears, and common sense. Madam How and Lady Why are his two guiding figures. One shows how things happen; the other asks why they happen. Volcanoes, tides, fossils, and cliffs become stories under their lead. Kingsley was a clergyman who loved natural science deeply. His book taught wonder first and facts close behind.
mrs-piper-the-society-for-psychical-rese:
Michael Sage wrote this study of Mrs. Piper, a famed trance medium. Noralie Robertson translated it from French, slightly cut. Sir Oliver Lodge wrote the preface for the 1904 New York edition. The book asks if mediumship is a sickness of the nerves.

Chapters weigh fraud, muscle reading, and thought transfer as rival claims. Professor William James of Harvard watched her early trances with care. Dr. Richard Hodgson led much of the research. A full sitting with Mrs. Piper is set out for readers. The book is a calm, close look at the science of ghosts in its early days.
mrs-wiggs-of-the-cabbage-patch:
Alice Caldwell Hegan Rice wrote this tale of a poor city district, copyrighted in 1901. She dedicated it to her mother, angel of the Cabbage Patch. The contents open with Mrs. Wiggs's philosophy. Ways and means, a Christmas lady, and a benefit dance follow.

Mrs. Wiggs keeps cheer in a hard place and helps her neighbors. A theater party and Mr. Bob bring town folk into the Patch. One chapter tells how spring came to the district. Rice writes poverty with humor and respect, not pity. The small book won wide love for its claim that joy can live on very little.
nasa-tm-19650019857-highlights-of-recent:
Robert Jastrow is named in the surviving pages of this survey of recent space research. Space science, he writes, is not one field by itself. It draws on Earth sciences, physics, and astronomy, where spacecraft can do what ground experiments cannot. In later years, he adds, the life sciences would join that group in a major role.

Jastrow links that growth to exploration of the Moon and planets. The survey reviews work in the physical sciences and discusses it for a broad reader. As a snapshot, it shows how a leading space scientist framed the field while the first wave of spacecraft results was still fresh.
nasa-tm-19660020064-advances-in-particle:
W Hess, G Mead, and M P Nakada of Goddard's Theoretical Division reviewed gains in particles and fields research in January 1965. Their era is the satellite age, counted from 1958. Subjects include the solar wind's effect on Earth and the radiation belts. Earth's magnetic field, solar energetic particles, and cosmic rays all receive treatment, along with neutrons and ground effects.

Before satellites, most of these topics rested on hints from the ground. Seven years of flight data had remade the field. A review by three of its workers marks the change in one place. It also tells later readers exactly what was known, and what was still guesswork, at that early date.
nasa-tm-19670012812-radiometry-research:
The Radiometry Section at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland issued this summary in February 1967. Radiometry is the science of measuring radiation, and the section supported spacecraft work. The report sums up the section's activities for the latter part of 1966.

It is divided into three parts. One covers work by the section's own staff, and the others cover on-site and off-site contractor work. The catalog record lists work on spacecraft coatings and solar simulators. It also names vortex arc studies, measurements of solar flux and spectra, and tests of radiation effects on solar cells.
nasa-tm-19690028207-cloud-statistics-in-:
Vincent V. Salomonson wrote this Goddard preprint, numbered X-622-69-386, on cloud statistics for Earth Resources Technology Satellite mission planning. ERTS craft, due in the early nineteen seventies, would map mineral, ocean, water, and farm resources from orbit. Their sensors need clear skies, so planners need to know how often any given place is actually cloud free.

Few studies give cloud cover as a frequency distribution over place and time, Salomonson finds. Those few show only small portions of Earth clear often enough for good odds on repeated passes. Over the United States, fall viewing is best and spring viewing worst. He also warns that satellite sensors misjudge broken cumulus and thin cirrus in opposite directions.
nasa-tm-19700015897-magnetometers-for-sp:
Norman F. Ness wrote this review in March 1970, while on leave from the Goddard Space Flight Center. He was based at a plasma laboratory in Rome, Italy. His subject is magnetometers, the tools spacecraft carry to measure magnetic fields in space.

Ness opens with a short summary of major results gained with these tools. He then explains how each main type works. The types covered are search coil, fluxgate, proton, alkali vapor, and helium vapor instruments. He closes with how the tools are tested and calibrated. The review served builders and users of field-measuring gear on space missions.
nasa-tm-19700025444-a-simulated-study-of:
Ronald W. Simpson wrote this Apollo study of manual control techniques for lunar orbit rendezvous. It is a simulation study, run with the concentrated flight plan for that rendezvous. Crews would need such hand-flying skills if automatic systems fell short near the Moon, far from any quick help.

The study grows out of earlier work on backup monitoring and control for rendezvous flights. Those efforts asked how a crew could watch the primary guidance system and step in after a partial or complete failure. A recent guidance division simulation had tested control modes that might back up the primary system. Simpson's runs apply that thinking to the tighter, concentrated plan for meeting in lunar orbit.
nasa-tm-19710006420-summer-institute-for:
The Goddard Space Flight Center issued this final report in January 1971. It closes out the Summer Institute for Biomedical Research in Technology Utilization. The institute ran from June 22 to August 28, 1970.

The program brought space technology into medical work. NASA instruments built to watch astronauts could also watch patients. The report covers both the running of the institute and its technical side. It is classed as an administrative and technical report, the closing record of the session. Programs of this kind were NASA's way of paying back its research cost in daily life.
orchesography-or-the-art-of-dancing-the-: Orchesography is John Weaver's 1706 English translation of Raoul-Auger Feuillet's French manual of baroque dance notation. It was printed in London. Its title promises the whole art explained through characters and demonstrative figures. Tables of steps and rules for the arms are also promised. The hosted sample contains only the title page. A transcriber's note warns that the work leans so heavily on diagrams that no plain text version exists. The steps themselves cannot be read here.
poor-miss-finch:
Wilkie Collins dedicated Poor Miss Finch to Mrs. Elliot of the Deanery, Bristol, in memory of an uninterrupted friendship, and used his preface to state a daring aim. Fiction had shown charming blind girls before, he writes, but always from the ideal and sentimental side; his Lucilla would exhibit blindness as it really is. Collins gathered his facts from competent authorities, and everything Lucilla does or says about her condition rests on what blind people had actually done and said.

Around Lucilla he built an intricate plot of love, identity, and deception, with the twin Nugent Dubourg and the narrator Madame Pratolungo as studies in human inconsistency. Collins argues in the preface that readers wrongly demand logical consistency from fictional motives. The novel, part sensation story and part serious experiment, asks sympathy for its heroine without a drop of the usual syrup.
racine-mithridate-french:
Racine's Mithridate, a tragedy of 1673 in French, stages the last days of a famed king. The cast lists Mithridate, king of Pontus, with Monime, promised to him and named queen. His sons Pharnace and Xiphares, born of different mothers, stand beside them.

The scene is Nymphee, a seaport on the Cimmerian Bosphorus. In his preface Racine notes that Sulla, Lucullus, and Pompey won glory against this foe. Old and beaten, the king still schemes, famed for guarding himself against poison. A love triangle in his shadow sharpens this most political of Racine's plays, a study of pride facing ruin.
racketty-packetty-house-as-told-by-queen:
Racketty-Packetty House, as told by Queen Crosspatch, is a children's story by Frances Hodgson Burnett, with illustrations by Harrison Cady. Queen Crosspatch begins with a rule: dolls do anything they choose when people are not looking, dancing, singing, and playing the piano, but they stop the moment anyone turns to watch.

The house of the title stands in a corner of Cynthia's nursery, behind the door, the worst spot in the room. It was pushed there when Tidy Castle arrived for Cynthia's birthday. Tidy Castle is a grand new dolls' house. It has elegant furniture and a knocker on the door. Cynthia is ashamed of the shabby old house beside it.
samuel-butler-a-sketch:
Henry Festing Jones wrote Samuel Butler: A Sketch to introduce the life of the writer Samuel Butler. The piece first appeared in 1913 inside a Butler essay volume and came out again from Jonathan Cape in London in 1921. Jones had already written a full memoir of Butler, and the sketch gives the family background in short form.

Butler was born on December 4, 1835, at Langar Rectory in Nottinghamshire, where his father Thomas then served as rector. His mother, Fanny Worsley, came from a Bristol sugar family, and his grandfather had led Shrewsbury School before becoming Bishop of Lichfield. Jones stresses that these Butlers were kin to neither the Hudibras poet nor the Analogy writer. Butler's schooldays began at home, and a family trip to Italy in 1843 gave the boy, at eight, his first great event.
slips-of-speech:
John H. Bechtel wrote Slips of Speech to help readers fix the day-to-day faults of speech and writing. Bechtel, also the author of Practical Synonyms and a work on how words are said, saw the book printed at Philadelphia by the Penn Publishing Company in 1901, under an 1895 copyright. Chapters treat taste, choice of words, short forms, the possessive case, pronouns, and number.

Later chapters cover adverbs, word links, the infinitive, participles, and small words of place and time. Redundancy, two negatives, and the match of verb with subject close the list, with an index at the end. Bechtel opens by noting that Homer knew no rules yet wrote verse that lasts. Most men, he argues, are no Homer, and so they need rules to guide them.
stories-about-animals-with-pictures-to-m:
Francis C. Woodworth, editor of The Youth's Cabinet and author of Stories About Birds, published Stories About Animals, With Pictures to Match at Boston in 1851; the work was entered for copyright in 1849. His preface says the pages group together short accounts chosen to show animal character.

Woodworth wrote for young readers, pairing each story with a picture so the lesson lands twice. The tales draw out traits like faithfulness, cleverness, and kindness in common and wild creatures. Books of this kind taught children natural history through story rather than dry lists, and Woodworth's plain, warm style made him a steady name in American homes.
the-arctic-prairies-a-canoe-journey-of-2:
Ernest Thompson Seton, billed as author of Wild Animals I Have Known, recounts a canoe journey of two thousand miles in search of the caribou. The book is dedicated to Sir Wilfrid Laurier, premier of Canada. Its subtitle calls it an account of a voyage to the region north of Aylmer Lake.

Seton's preface asks what young man would not give a year of his life to roll back time five decades. He dreams of the old Missouri with buffalo on its banks, big game in sight, and red men roaming free of fences. Trading posts stood hundreds of miles apart then, he notes, and news moved by horse or canoe. His own northern trip, he hints, bought a share of that lost world at far less cost.
the-boy-life-of-napoleon-afterwards-empe:
Boy Life of Napoleon, Afterwards Emperor of the French, came out in 1895 with art by Vesper L. George. It was adapted and made larger for American boys and girls from the French work of Madame Eugénie Foa. Foa had written Little Princes and Princesses and Little Robinson. A preface tells how her name had been known in French homes for more than a generation.

The preface praises Foa as the most loved French writer of tales from past times for the young, some forty years back. Her tone is pure, her morals high, and her teaching direct, it says. It also credits her with true facts and strong action. For this form, new study was drawn on to round out her sketch of Napoleon's boyhood. The hope is that young readers will go on to his later life with minds free of party bias, hate, and hero worship.
the-delights-of-wisdom-pertaining-to-con:
Emanuel Swedenborg, named on the title page as a Swede, wrote The Delights of Wisdom Pertaining to Conjugial Love, with The Pleasures of Insanity Pertaining to Scortatory Love added. The English text translates his Latin work printed at Amsterdam in 1768. The opening relations concern the joys of heaven and weddings there.

Swedenborg solemnly declares that what follows is no fiction of the imagination. He says the scenes were truly done and seen, not in sleep but in full wakefulness. The Lord opened the inner parts of his mind and spirit. He was granted to be in the spiritual world with angels and in the natural world with men at once, for twenty-five years as of 1768. An angel then appears beneath the eastern heaven, sounding a trumpet toward the north, the west, and the south.
the-flying-u-ranch:
B. M. Bower wrote Flying U Ranch as a western tale of the Happy Family, a crew of cowhands on a Montana ranch. Sheep trouble stands near the heart of the contents.

The tale opens as the crew waits for Sunday supper at the bunkhouse door. The Old Man comes back from Helena with a stranger, Miguel Rapponi, a flashy dresser straight from San Francisco. The boys eye his silk scarf, stamped cuffs, and high boot heels with one mind of doubt. Sheep camps, false friends, and range pride test the crew's trust in the books that follow.
the-fourth-watch: H. A. Cody wrote The Fourth Watch as a novel of a clergyman's life, and only the front matter and contents are present here. Cody gives the book to the watchmen and stewards of the Lord who toil through life's long night. The chapter heads name Glendow Rectory, the breath of slander, an auction, a golden key, camp scenes, a long night, and light at eventide. Cody's past books named here include The Frontiersman and The Long Patrol. No chapter text appears in these opening pages.
the-golden-calf-which-the-world-adores-a: John Frederick Helvetius wrote The Golden Calf, Which the World Adores and Desires. Helvetius was a doctor at the Hague. The tract was first set down in Latin. It is here faithfully Englished. John Starkey printed it in London in 1670. Only front matter is present here: the long title page and dedications. The title page states the claim of the tract. At the Hague in 1666, the whole substance of lead was changed in one moment. It became gold-obrizon. A tiny grain of the true philosophick stone did the work.
the-house-of-heine-brothers-in-munich:
A small Munich banking firm sits at the center of this story. The text comes from the 1864 Chapman and Hall edition of Tales of All Countries. The Heine brothers keep a modest office in the old market-place. Only three clerks work there. One old man never deals with the public. A young Englishman assists him. A boy runs messages and tends the stoves. Nobody doubts the brothers' word or their solvency. Their business is tiny beside the great London banks.

London houses employ legions of clerks. Their partners stay hidden from customers. The Heines instead sit visibly in two dingy rooms. A broad staircase leads up to them. The elder brother is a bachelor in the suburbs. The younger, Ernest Heine, has a wife much younger than himself. They have two daughters and a son. Firm and family stand side by side. The story is ready to entangle them.
the-immortals-masterpieces-of-fiction-cr: Project Gutenberg's 1905 edition of the French Immortals gathers nineteen novels crowned by the French Academy, each also issued separately. Only the series contents and the opening title page of the first volume are present here, so the novels themselves do not appear. The list runs from Georges Ohnet's Serge Panine and Anatole France's The Red Lily through Daudet's Fromont and Risler, Pierre Loti's Madame Chrysanthème, and Alfred de Vigny's Cinq Mars. Serge Panine carries a general introduction to the series by Gaston Boissier, perpetual secretary of the Academy.
the-lighted-match: Charles Neville Buck published his novel with W. J. Watt in New York in 1911, illustrated by R. F. Schabelitz. Only the title pages and the start of the contents are present here, showing a frontispiece of a woman holding out her hand to a man named Benton. The first chapter listed is called An Omen Is Construed. The novel itself, a Kentucky mountain romance by the author of The Key to Yesterday, does not appear here.
the-man-who-knew-too-much:
Gilbert K. Chesterton's The Man Who Knew Too Much gathers eight detective tales. They include The Face in the Target, The Vanishing Prince, The Soul of the Schoolboy, and The Bottomless Well. The Fad of the Fisherman, The Hole in the Wall, The Temple of Silence, and The Vengeance of the Statue follow. The first story sends Harold March, a rising reviewer and social critic, walking briskly across a great tableland of moors toward Torwood Park. March is on a political errand: the Chancellor of the Exchequer, Sir Howard Horne, will expound his so-called Socialist budget to him in an interview.

March knows all about politics and nothing about politicians, Chesterton says, and much about art and philosophy, but little about the world he lives in. Midway across the sunny flats he finds a narrow cleft carrying a small stream, and curiosity pulls him down into it.
the-master-detective-being-some-further-:
Percy James Brebner published The Master Detective in 1916, a set of further investigations by his sleuth Christopher Quarles. Fifteen cases fill the contents, from a kidnapping and a stolen aeroplane model to a contessa's pearls and a crime in a yellow taxi. Other cases involve a jeweled chalice, a forty-ton yawl, and the Grange Park mystery. The first case opens with the death of Sir Grenville Rusholm, baronet.

Obituary notices fill the papers, wreaths crowd the Lodge in Queen's Square, and Lady Rusholm receives floods of sympathy. Brebner notes that the dead man counted for little in politics, having refused to stand for Parliament. His social success owed much, perhaps, to his wife's charm. Yet a man so prominent leaves questions behind him when he dies. Quarles steps into a world of wealth, reputation, and hidden difficulty.
the-miller-of-old-church: Ellen Glasgow's novel The Miller of Old Church shows only its dedication and contents here, so the story itself does not appear. Glasgow dedicated the book to her sister Cary Glasgow McCormack, in loving acknowledgment of help and sympathy through the years. The contents divide the novel into Jordan's Journey and The Cross-Roads. Chapter titles promise a mill, a flirtatious Molly, a sermon by the Reverend Orlando Mullen, and chapters treating the ladies' sphere, contradictions, and life's ironies.
the-moon-out-of-reach:
Margaret Pedler's novel The Moon Out of Reach holds a 1921 copyright. Grosset and Dunlap published it in New York. Only title page and contents are present here, so the story does not appear. Pedler is billed as author of The House of Dreams-Come-True, The Splendid Folly, and The Lamp of Fate.

Eighteen chapters are listed. The Shining Ship and The Good Samaritan open the book, followed by A Question of Externals and The Skeleton in the Cupboard. Preux Chevalier, A Forgotten Fan, and The Other Side of the Door lead toward A Skirmish with Death. By the Lovers' Bridge, Relations-in-Law, King Arthur's Castle, and Till Death Us Do Part close the list on a romantic note.
the-old-peabody-pew-a-christmas-romance-: A Christmas romance of a country church, The Old Peabody Pew appeared in a 1907 edition. No author is named in the pages present here, which hold the dedication only, so the story itself does not appear. The dedication speaks to New England women of a quiet village who worked with the writer in a Dorcas Society, and recalls their white-spired meeting house. The writer admits there never was a Peabody Pew, and offers the imagined tale back with rosemary, for remembrance.
the-personal-touch: J. Wilbur Chapman, D.D., wrote The Personal Touch, a book on personal evangelism. The pages present hold the contents and the opening of a foreword headed simply "If," so the chapters themselves do not appear. The contents list A Testimony, A General Principle, No Man Cared for My Soul, Winning the Young, and Conversion Is a Miracle. The foreword argues that if being a Christian is worthwhile, ordinary concern should prompt us to speak of Christ to those we meet.
the-slowcoach:
E. V. Lucas's The Slowcoach runs to twenty-four chapters, its contents say. The Avories open the book. Mysterious wheels, a thorough examination, and the plans follow. The first day and first night of travel come at chapters eight and nine. Adventures punctuate the list: a second caravan, a young policeman, runaway ponies, and a lost baby. Stratford-on-Avon appears at chapter twelve. The most surprising adventure of all precedes the end.

Chapter one introduces the Avory family in an old house at Chiswick. Once upon a time there was a nice family, Lucas begins. Captain Avory was dead, wounded at Spion Kop, the narrator explains. Mrs. Avory was thirty-five, with four children. Janet, aged fourteen, was the eldest, and Gregory Bruce, aged seven, the youngest. They were all very fond of each other, Lucas adds.
the-true-story-of-my-life-a-sketch: Hans Christian Andersen's True Story of My Life, a sketch translated by Mary Howitt, is introduced in this record by Howitt's own letter to her Boston publishers, dated London, 29 June 1847. She forwards the proof sheets of Andersen's unpublished life, translated from a copy the author sent her, and notes that this is the author's edition, in whose proceeds he shares. The translation is inscribed to Jenny Lind, in admiration of her talents and her beautiful life. Andersen's autobiography itself begins after these formal leaves.
the-vagabond-and-other-poems-from-punch: R. C. Lehmann collected The Vagabond and Other Poems from Punch in a volume published by John Lane in 1918. A short note explains that all but two pieces first appeared in Punch, whose proprietors allowed the reprinting. For Wilma came instead from Blackwood's Magazine. The poems themselves are not present in this record; the note and contents list are what appear. Titles include The Vagabond, Singing Water, Cragwell End, The Bird in the Room, and Killed in Action. Later entries name a poem to Flight-Lieutenant Robinson, V. C.
the-way-of-salvation-in-the-lutheran-chu: G. H. Gerberding wrote The Way of Salvation in the Lutheran Church for a Lutheran Publication Society edition in Philadelphia. A transcriber's note explains that accents dropped from transliterated Greek words and that italics were expanded for readability. Only the title page and that note are present here, so Gerberding's chapters do not appear. Readers learn the book's subject and its Lutheran frame from the title alone. The society's imprint shows it reached readers through the church's own publishing house.
the-yoke-a-romance-of-the-days-when-the-: Elizabeth Miller's The Yoke, copyrighted in 1904, is presented here by its title pages and contents. Its subtitle calls it a romance of the days when Israel left Egyptian bondage. Miller dedicates the book to her brother Percy, who constructed the plot. Twelve chapters are listed, from Choosing the Tens to Canaan. The Lady Miriam and Athor the Golden appear. The novel's chapters themselves do not follow in the pages present.
thomas-henry-huxley-a-character-sketch: Leonard Huxley wrote a character sketch of his father, Thomas Henry Huxley, issued for the Rationalist Press Association and published by Watts in London in 1920. A frontispiece photograph by Elliott and Fry faces the title page. Sixteen chapters are listed. Headings move from early days and medical training to the Rattlesnake voyage, agnosticism, and the battle over Darwin's Origin. Later chapters treat public speaking, popular education, ethics, friendships, Darwin, Hooker, and Tyndall. The opening pages and contents are what is present here, so Leonard Huxley's sketch itself is not shown.
thomas-jefferson-a-character-sketch:
Edward S. Ellis wrote a character sketch of Thomas Jefferson for the Great Americans of History series, with a supplementary essay by G. Mercer Adam. The volume also promises an account of the Louisiana Purchase, anecdotes, characteristics, and a chronology. Ellis compares Jefferson's mark on early government to a mint stamp.

He calls Jefferson an aristocrat by birth and a democrat by nature, learned yet fond of a farmer's simple tastes. Jefferson refused birthday celebrations and disliked titles and ceremony. Readers get an admiring popular biography built from traits, stories, and praise for his foresight about the young nation.
three-frenchmen-in-bengal-the-commercial: S. C. Hill, officer in charge of the records of the Government of India, published Three Frenchmen in Bengal in 1903. His subtitle names the commercial ruin of the French settlements in 1757. Maps and plans accompany the book, including the Ganges valley after Rennell. Four chapters treat the quarrel with the English, then Renault at Chandernagore, Law at Cossimbazar, and Courtin at Dacca. Hill dedicated the work to his wife. The front pages and contents are what is held in this record, so Hill's history itself is not shown.
tillie-a-mennonite-maid-a-story-of-the-p: Helen Reimensnyder Martin wrote a story of the Pennsylvania Dutch, and its contents list twenty-six chapters in the characters' own dialect. Headings quote Tillie's father threatening to learn her once, the Doc combining business and pleasure, and debates over whether novels are moral. Later headings promise Tillie's revolt, her last fight, and Getz learning Tillie. Chapter one is announced with the cry Oh, I love her, but no text follows. The contents pages are what is given in this record, so Martin's novel itself is not shown.
un-doc-yasser-arafat-s-1974-un-general-a:
Yasser Arafat, leader of the Palestine Liberation Organization, addressed the United Nations General Assembly in November 1974. No Palestinian leader had spoken to the Assembly before. The hall heard him say he had come bearing an olive branch and a freedom fighter's gun, and he begged the world not to let the branch fall.

The speech argues that Palestinians are a people with a right to their own state. It rejects the label of terrorist and blames the conflict on dispossession. The address won the PLO observer status at the UN and stands as a landmark of Palestinian diplomacy.
what-the-schools-teach-and-might-teach: The opening shown here is made up of the title page and lists of tables, so Franklin Bobbitt's findings do not appear. Bobbitt, of the University of Chicago, wrote the book in 1915 for the Cleveland Education Survey. Its tables count time spent on reading, spelling, and handwriting in school. Other tables cover sums, history, geography, drawing, and manual training. Science, health, gym work, and music close the list. The tables alone show a study built on hours and counts.
widger-s-quotations-from-project-gutenbe: Only a Project Gutenberg header is present here, so none of David Widger's quotations appear. The header names the set as number 16 in Widger's Quotations series. Its source is The Immortals of the French Academy. The header gives a release date of May 2003 and etext number 4001. It also notes a first posting on October 6, 2001, and calls the file edition 10. The rest is standard Gutenberg license and donation text. Readers learn the set's source and issue data, but see no quoted lines.
